paragraphs: This paper presents a neural model of how visual cortex segments and groups motion. A central problem is that local motion measurements can be ambiguous: the movement visible in a small part of a shape may not uniquely determine how the whole shape moves. The model addresses how these local signals become a coherent global interpretation.

Its processing combines a Motion Oriented Contrast Filter with longer-range interactions in a Cooperative Competitive Loop. The filter preprocesses motion signals, while the interacting mechanisms organize their broader relationships. The combined system is used to explain phenomena including induced motion, motion capture, and motion aftereffects.

The resulting motion Boundary Contour System operates in parallel with a system for static boundaries. The two then cooperate to represent boundaries for three-dimensional form perception. The paper clarifies how mechanisms for static segmentation can be adapted to motion, particularly by suppressing and reorganizing ambiguous local movements. Its contribution is an integrated account of motion filtering, global grouping, and cooperation between moving and static visual structure.
summary.tldr: A neural motion model combines local filtering and long-range interactions to organize ambiguous movements into coherent visual boundaries.

title: Neural Dynamics of Motion Segmentation and Grouping

paragraphs: The paper studies how learning within individuals affects evolution across a population of neural networks. It examines the Baldwin effect through simulations on a pattern recognition problem. The main question is how the amount of training, and its distribution among individuals, changes the speed at which the population's genes evolve.

The simulations show that both no learning and excessive learning lead to slow genetic evolution, with an intermediate amount producing the fastest progress. This means that increasing individual training does not produce a steadily increasing evolutionary benefit. In the studied setting, the balance between learning and evolution matters more than maximizing the learning allocated to each individual.

The distribution of training also matters. With the total number of training presentations held fixed, evolution is fastest when individuals within a generation receive different numbers of presentations. The authors further connect hybrid learning and genetic algorithms with difficult, high-dimensional pattern recognition, citing the ability of genetic algorithms to help avoid local minima. Training allocation is therefore an important design choice in the combined system.
summary.tldr: Neural-network simulations find that intermediate learning and unequal training allocations can accelerate genetic evolution.

title: Evolution and Learning in Neural Networks: The Number and Distribution of Learning Trials Affect the Rate of Evolution

abstract: A network model with temporal sequencing and state-dependent modula(cid:173) tory features is described. The model is motivated by neurocognitive data characterizing different states of waking and sleeping. Computer studies demonstrate how unique states of sequencing can exist within the same network under different aminergic and cholinergic modulatory influences. Relationships between state-dependent modulation, memory, sequencing and learning are discussed.

paragraphs: This paper presents a neural network model whose temporal sequencing depends on its modulatory state. Temporal sequencing concerns how activity develops in an ordered progression over time. The model is motivated by neurocognitive observations of waking and sleeping, making changes in overall brain state central to the behavior the authors seek to explain.

Computer studies examine the network under different aminergic and cholinergic modulatory influences. They demonstrate that distinct sequencing states can occur within the same network. The key result is therefore a change in the organization of activity associated with modulation, rather than a requirement to introduce a different network for each sequencing state.

The paper discusses how this state dependence relates to memory, sequencing, and learning. Its explanatory value is that a shared network can support different temporal behaviors under different influences. This makes modulatory state part of the account of what the network does: understanding its sequence behavior requires considering both the network itself and the conditions under which its activity unfolds.
summary.tldr: A neural network exhibits distinct temporal sequencing states under different aminergic and cholinergic modulation.

title: Network Model of State-Dependent Sequencing

The direct visual pathway (photoreceptors, bipolar and ganglion cells) and the horizontal units, as well as the D-amacrine cells were sim(cid:173) ulated. The computer program simulated the analog non-spiking transmission between photoreceptor and bipolar cells, and between bipolar and ganglion cells, as well as the gap-junctions between hor(cid:173) izontal cells, and the release of dopamine by D-amacrine cells and its diffusion in the extra-cellular space. A 64 x 64 photoreceptors retina, containing 16,448 units, was carried out. This retina dis(cid:173) played contour extraction with a Mach effect, and adaptation to brightness. The simulation showed that the dopaminergic amacrine cells were necessary to ensure adaptation to local brightness.

paragraphs: The authors simulate the mammalian fovea to investigate how the retina processes images locally. Their model includes photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and ganglion cells along the direct visual pathway, together with horizontal cells and dopamine-releasing amacrine cells. The aim is to connect image-processing behavior to detailed biological interactions within this network.

The simulation represents analog, non-spiking transmission along the direct pathway and gap-junction connections between horizontal cells. It also models dopamine release and diffusion through the space outside cells. Including this chemical process allows the study to examine how modulation of retinal activity contributes to visual processing alongside the network's direct signal transmission.

The implemented retina contains a 64 by 64 photoreceptor array and 16,448 units overall. It extracts contours, displays a Mach effect associated with edge contrast, and adapts to brightness. Within this simulation, dopaminergic amacrine cells are necessary for adaptation to local brightness. The finding assigns these cells a specific functional role in adjusting retinal processing to illumination across an image.
summary.tldr: A detailed retinal simulation finds that dopamine-releasing amacrine cells are necessary for its adaptation to local brightness.

title: Dopaminergic Neuromodulation Brings a Dynamical Plasticity to the Retina

abstract: I describe a silicon network consisting of a group of excitatory neu(cid:173) rons and a global inhibitory neuron. The output of the inhibitory neuron is normalized with respect to the input strengths. This out(cid:173) put models the normalization property of the wide-field direction(cid:173) selective cells in the fly visual system. This normalizing property is also useful in any system where we wish the output signal to code only the strength of the inputs, and not be dependent on the num(cid:173) ber of inputs. The circuitry in each neuron is equivalent to that in Lazzaro's winner-take-all (WTA) circuit with one additional tran(cid:173) sistor and a voltage reference. Just as in Lazzaro's circuit, the outputs of the excitatory neurons code the neuron with the largest input. The difference here is that multiple winners can be chosen. By varying the voltage reference of the neuron, the network can transition between a soft-max behavior and a hard WTA behav(cid:173) ior. I show results from a fabricated chip of 20 neurons in a 1.2J.Lm CMOS technology.

paragraphs: This paper describes a silicon neural circuit that can vary how strongly its inputs compete. The circuit combines a group of excitatory neurons with one inhibitory neuron shared across the group. As in a winner-take-all circuit, the excitatory outputs identify the neuron receiving the strongest input, but this design can also allow multiple winners.

The adjustable behavior comes from adding one transistor and a voltage reference to each neuron's circuitry relative to the referenced winner-take-all design. Changing the voltage reference moves the network between softer competition and hard winner selection. This makes the competition adjustable within the circuit rather than fixing it to a single selection behavior.

The inhibitory output also has a normalization property intended to represent input strength without depending on the number of inputs. The author connects this behavior to wide-field direction-selective cells in fly vision. Results come from a fabricated chip containing 20 neurons in 1.2-micrometer CMOS technology, grounding the proposed behavior in a physical implementation.
summary.tldr: A fabricated neural circuit uses an adjustable voltage reference to move between soft competition and hard winner-take-all selection.

title: A Winner-Take-All Circuit with Controllable Soft Max Property

abstract: In a Bayesian mixture model it is not necessary a priori to limit the num(cid:173) ber of components to be finite. In this paper an infinite Gaussian mixture model is presented which neatly sidesteps the difficult problem of find(cid:173) ing the "right" number of mixture components. Inference in the model is done using an efficient parameter-free Markov Chain that relies entirely on Gibbs sampling.
originalAbstract: In a Bayesian mixture model it is not necessary a priori to limit the num(cid:173) ber of components to be finite. In this paper an infinite Gaussian mixture model is presented which neatly sidesteps the difficult problem of find(cid:173) ing the "right" number of mixture components. Inference in the model is done using an efficient parameter-free Markov Chain that relies entirely on Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: A Gaussian mixture represents a distribution by combining Gaussian components. A difficult modeling choice is deciding how many components to allow. This paper presents a Bayesian formulation in which that number does not have to be restricted to a finite value in advance, addressing the component-count question through the model's construction.

The infinite mixture changes what must be specified before inference begins. Instead of requiring the modeler to settle on the right finite number of components, it permits an unbounded collection within the Bayesian formulation. The significance of infinity here is the removal of an advance finite restriction, which sidesteps the particular model-selection problem identified by the authors.

Inference uses a Markov chain described as efficient and parameter-free, relying entirely on Gibbs sampling. This supplies a computational procedure alongside the modeling proposal. The paper's contribution is therefore both a way to formulate Gaussian mixtures without fixing a finite component count and a sampling-based way to carry out inference in that formulation.
summary.tldr: An infinite Bayesian Gaussian mixture avoids fixing a finite component count and supports inference through a parameter-free Gibbs-sampling chain.

title: The Infinite Gaussian Mixture Model

abstract: In theory, the Winnow multiplicative update has certain advantages over the Perceptron additive update when there are many irrelevant attributes. Recently, there has been much effort on enhancing the Perceptron algo(cid:173) rithm by using regularization, leading to a class of linear classification methods called support vector machines. Similarly, it is also possible to apply the regularization idea to the Winnow algorithm, which gives meth(cid:173) ods we call regularized Winnows. We show that the resulting methods compare with the basic Winnows in a similar way that a support vector machine compares with the Perceptron. We investigate algorithmic is(cid:173) sues and learning properties of the derived methods. Some experimental results will also be provided to illustrate different methods.

Recently, there has been much effort on enhancing the Perceptron algo(cid:173) rithm by using regularization, leading to a class of linear classification methods called support vector machines. Similarly, it is also possible to apply the regularization idea to the Winnow algorithm, which gives meth(cid:173) ods we call regularized Winnows. We investigate algorithmic is(cid:173) sues and learning properties of the derived methods. Some experimental results will also be provided to illustrate different methods.

paragraphs: Winnow updates a classifier's weights multiplicatively, while the Perceptron uses additive updates. The paper starts from the theoretical observation that Winnow has certain advantages when many input attributes are irrelevant. It asks how regularization, already important in developing support vector machines from the Perceptron setting, can be applied to Winnow.

The resulting family of methods is called regularized Winnows. The authors show that these methods relate to basic Winnow in a way analogous to the relationship between support vector machines and the Perceptron. This gives regularized Winnow a place within a broader comparison of classification methods, linking the update rule to the treatment of regularization.

The paper investigates both algorithmic questions and learning properties, and includes experiments illustrating differences among the methods. Its stated motivation combines Winnow's theoretical behavior with irrelevant attributes and the benefits of developing a regularized counterpart. The abstract does not claim universal experimental superiority; its main contribution is the derived family of methods and the analysis of their relationship to existing classifiers.
summary.tldr: Regularized Winnow methods extend multiplicative-update classification through a relationship analogous to that between support vector machines and the Perceptron.

title: Regularized Winnow Methods

abstract: It has been known that people, after being exposed to sentences generated by an artificial grammar, acquire implicit grammatical knowledge and are able to transfer the knowledge to inputs that are generated by a modified grammar. We show that a second order recurrent neural network is able to transfer grammatical knowledge from one language (generated by a Finite State Machine) to another language which differ both in vocabularies and syntax. Representa(cid:173) tion of the grammatical knowledge in the network is analyzed using linear discriminant analysis.
originalAbstract: It has been known that people, after being exposed to sentences generated by an artificial grammar, acquire implicit grammatical knowledge and are able to transfer the knowledge to inputs that are generated by a modified grammar. We show that a second order recurrent neural network is able to transfer grammatical knowledge from one language (generated by a Finite State Machine) to another language which differ both in vocabularies and syntax. Representa(cid:173) tion of the grammatical knowledge in the network is analyzed using linear discriminant analysis.

paragraphs: People exposed to sentences from an artificial grammar can acquire implicit grammatical knowledge and transfer it to inputs produced by a modified grammar. This paper examines a related capability in a second-order recurrent neural network. The question is whether knowledge acquired from one structured language can remain useful when the language changes.

The authors demonstrate transfer from a language generated by a finite state machine to another language that differs in both vocabulary and syntax. This makes the demonstrated transfer broader than retaining knowledge when only the words change. The network carries useful grammatical knowledge across a setting in which both the symbols and their organization differ.

The paper also uses linear discriminant analysis to examine how the network represents grammatical knowledge. This adds an analysis of the learned representation to the behavioral demonstration of transfer. The result establishes the reported capability for the artificial-language setting studied, while the human findings provide the motivating phenomenon rather than proof that people and the network use the same mechanism.
summary.tldr: A second-order recurrent network transfers grammatical knowledge between artificial languages that differ in vocabulary and syntax.

title: Grammar Transfer in a Second Order Recurrent Neural Network

abstract: We present a novel strategy for automatically debugging programs given sampled data from thousands of actual user runs. Our goal is to pinpoint those features that are most correlated with crashes. This is accomplished by maximizing an appropriately deﬁned utility function. It has analogies with intuitive debugging heuristics, and, as we demonstrate, is able to deal with various types of bugs that occur in real programs.
originalAbstract: We present a novel strategy for automatically debugging programs given sampled data from thousands of actual user runs. Our goal is to pinpoint those features that are most correlated with crashes. This is accomplished by maximizing an appropriately deﬁned utility function. It has analogies with intuitive debugging heuristics, and, as we demonstrate, is able to deal with various types of bugs that occur in real programs.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an automated debugging strategy based on sampled information from thousands of actual user executions. Its goal is to identify program features most strongly associated with crashes. This makes evidence from many real runs the starting point for deciding where debugging attention should be directed.

The authors formulate that search as maximizing a defined utility function. The function provides a quantitative way to choose features that are informative about failures, and the approach has connections to intuitive debugging heuristics. The central move is to express the search for useful debugging clues as an optimization problem over collected execution data.

Demonstrations show that the strategy can handle several types of bugs occurring in real programs. The findings support using statistical patterns across many sampled runs to help pinpoint relevant features. Because the stated target is correlation with crashes, the selected features serve as evidence for debugging; the abstract's claim is about finding useful crash-associated clues rather than automatically proving the causal explanation of every failure.
summary.tldr: A utility-maximizing method uses sampled user executions to identify program features associated with crashes.

title: Statistical Debugging of Sampled Programs

abstract: This paper presents an algorithm for learning the time-varying shape of a non-rigid 3D object from uncalibrated 2D tracking data. We model shape motion as a rigid component (rotation and translation) combined with a non-rigid deformation. Reconstruction is ill-posed if arbitrary deforma- tions are allowed. We constrain the problem by assuming that the object shape at each time instant is drawn from a Gaussian distribution. Based on this assumption, the algorithm simultaneously estimates 3D shape and motion for each time frame, learns the parameters of the Gaussian, and robustly ﬁlls-in missing data points. We then extend the algorithm to model temporal smoothness in object shape, thus allowing it to handle severe cases of missing data.
originalAbstract: This paper presents an algorithm for learning the time-varying shape of a non-rigid 3D object from uncalibrated 2D tracking data. We model shape motion as a rigid component (rotation and translation) combined with a non-rigid deformation. Reconstruction is ill-posed if arbitrary deforma- tions are allowed. We constrain the problem by assuming that the object shape at each time instant is drawn from a Gaussian distribution. Based on this assumption, the algorithm simultaneously estimates 3D shape and motion for each time frame, learns the parameters of the Gaussian, and robustly ﬁlls-in missing data points. We then extend the algorithm to model temporal smoothness in object shape, thus allowing it to handle severe cases of missing data.

paragraphs: The paper reconstructs the changing three-dimensional shape of a deformable object from uncalibrated two-dimensional tracking data. It separates motion into a rigid component, consisting of rotation and translation, and a non-rigid deformation. Allowing completely arbitrary deformations would make reconstruction ill-posed, so the model needs a constraint on how shapes can vary.

The authors assume that the object’s shape at each time is drawn from a Gaussian distribution. Under this assumption, the algorithm jointly estimates shape and motion for every frame and learns the Gaussian’s parameters. It also fills in missing tracked points, making missing-data reconstruction part of the same estimation procedure.

An extension incorporates temporal smoothness in object shape. This adds information about how shapes evolve across frames and allows the method to handle severe missing-data cases. The contribution links a distributional assumption about shape variation with joint reconstruction and, in the extension, temporal structure. The Gaussian assumption is the stated device that constrains the otherwise ambiguous reconstruction problem.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian model of shape variation enables joint recovery of deforming 3D shape, motion, and missing points from uncalibrated 2D tracks.

title: Learning Non-Rigid 3D Shape from 2D Motion

abstract: We have developed a novel algorithm for integrating source localization and noise suppression based on a probabilistic graphical model of stimulus-evoked MEG/EEG data. Our algorithm localizes multiple dipoles while suppressing noise sources with the computational complexity equivalent to a single dipole scan, and is therefore more ef(cid:2)cient than traditional multidipole (cid:2)tting procedures. In simulation, the algorithm can accurately localize and estimate the time course of several simultaneously-active dipoles, with rotating or (cid:2)xed orientation, at noise levels typical for averaged MEG data. Furthermore, the algorithm is superior to beamforming techniques, which we show to be an approximation to our graphical model, in estimation of temporally correlated sources. Success of this algorithm for localizing auditory cortex in a tumor patient and for localizing an epileptic spike source are also demonstrated.

Our algorithm localizes multiple dipoles while suppressing noise sources with the computational complexity equivalent to a single dipole scan, and is therefore more ef(cid:2)cient than traditional multidipole (cid:2)tting procedures. In simulation, the algorithm can accurately localize and estimate the time course of several simultaneously-active dipoles, with rotating or (cid:2)xed orientation, at noise levels typical for averaged MEG data. paragraphs: The paper combines two tasks in analyzing stimulus-evoked MEG and EEG: locating the sources of measured activity and suppressing noise. It uses a probabilistic graphical model to estimate multiple dipoles together. The stated computational complexity is equivalent to scanning for a single dipole, making the procedure more efficient than traditional multidipole fitting.

In simulations, the algorithm accurately locates several simultaneously active dipoles and estimates how their activity changes over time. These demonstrations include both fixed and rotating source orientations, at noise levels described as typical of averaged MEG measurements. The results therefore address source position and temporal activity within the same estimation framework.

The authors also show that beamforming techniques can be viewed as an approximation to their graphical model. Their algorithm performs better when estimating sources whose activity is correlated over time. Additional demonstrations locate auditory cortex in a tumor patient and an epileptic spike source, extending the evidence beyond simulated signals to the reported applications.
summary.tldr: A graphical-model algorithm jointly localizes multiple MEG/EEG sources and suppresses noise with the complexity of a single-dipole scan.

title: A Probabilistic Algorithm Integrating Source Localization and Noise Suppression of MEG and EEG data

abstract: Adaptively optimizing experiments can significantly reduce the number of trials needed to characterize neural responses using parametric statistical models. However, the potential for these methods has been limited to date by severe computational challenges: choosing the stimulus which will provide the most information about the (typically high-dimensional) model parameters requires evaluating a high-dimensional integration and optimization in near-real time. Here we present a fast algorithm for choosing the optimal (most informative) stimulus based on a Fisher approximation of the Shannon information and specialized numerical linear algebra techniques. This algorithm requires only low-rank matrix manipulations and a one-dimensional linesearch to choose the stimulus and is therefore efficient even for high-dimensional stimulus and parameter spaces; for example, we require just 15 milliseconds on a desktop computer to optimize a 100-dimensional stimulus. Our algorithm therefore makes real-time adaptive experimental design feasible. Simulation results show that model parameters can be estimated much more efficiently using these adaptive techniques than by using random (nonadaptive) stimuli. Finally, we generalize the algorithm to efficiently handle both fast adaptation due to spike-history effects and slow, non-systematic drifts in the model parameters.

paragraphs: Adaptive neurophysiology experiments choose stimuli to learn about a neural-response model efficiently. The computational obstacle is selecting the most informative stimulus quickly when both stimuli and model parameters have many dimensions. This paper develops an algorithm that makes this choice practical using an approximation to the information gained from an experiment.

The method combines a Fisher approximation of Shannon information with specialized numerical linear algebra. Stimulus selection requires low-rank matrix operations and a one-dimensional line search, reducing the computational burden of the high-dimensional problem. The authors report optimizing a 100-dimensional stimulus in 15 milliseconds on a desktop computer, supporting real-time use.

Simulations show that adaptive stimulus choices estimate model parameters much more efficiently than random, nonadaptive choices. The authors also extend the algorithm to account for rapid adaptation caused by spike history and slower, nonsystematic parameter drift. Together, these contributions address both the speed of experimental decisions and changes in neural responses, while the reported estimation advantage comes from simulation results.
summary.tldr: An information-approximation algorithm selects high-dimensional stimuli in real time and improves parameter estimation over random stimuli in simulations.

title: Real-time adaptive information-theoretic optimization of neurophysiology experiments

abstract: Multi-level hierarchical models provide an attractive framework for incorporating correlations induced in a response variable organized in a hierarchy. Model fitting is challenging, especially for hierarchies with large number of nodes. We provide a novel algorithm based on a multi-scale Kalman filter that is both scalable and easy to implement. For non-Gaussian responses, quadratic approximation to the log-likelihood results in biased estimates. We suggest a bootstrap strategy to correct such biases. Our method is illustrated through simulation studies and analyses of real world data sets in health care and online advertising.

Model fitting is challenging, especially for hierarchies with large number of nodes. We provide a novel algorithm based on a multi-scale Kalman filter that is both scalable and easy to implement. For non-Gaussian responses, quadratic approximation to the log-likelihood results in biased estimates. We suggest a bootstrap strategy to correct such biases. Our method is illustrated through simulation studies and analyses of real world data sets in health care and online advertising.

paragraphs: Multi-level hierarchical models describe responses whose relationships follow a hierarchy. Observations linked through that hierarchy can be correlated, and the model incorporates those connections when fitting the data. The paper addresses the computational difficulty that arises when the hierarchy contains many nodes and the posterior mode must be found efficiently.

The authors propose an algorithm based on a multi-scale Kalman filter, describing it as scalable and easy to implement. Its role is to make fitting these structured models more manageable as the hierarchy grows. The algorithm is paired with attention to an estimation issue: for non-Gaussian responses, using a quadratic approximation to the log-likelihood produces biased estimates.

To address that bias, the paper suggests a bootstrap correction strategy. The computational approximation and the correction serve complementary purposes: one supports tractable fitting, while the other addresses distortion introduced in the non-Gaussian case. Simulation studies and applications to healthcare and online advertising illustrate the method, showing its use in both controlled examples and real datasets with hierarchical modeling needs.
summary.tldr: A multi-scale Kalman-filter algorithm accelerates hierarchical model fitting, with a proposed bootstrap correction for non-Gaussian approximation bias.

title: Fast Computation of Posterior Mode in Multi-Level Hierarchical Models

abstract: Cell assemblies exhibiting episodes of recurrent coherent activity have been observed in several brain regions including the striatum and hippocampus CA3. Here we address the question of how coherent dynamically switching assemblies appear in large networks of biologically realistic spiking neurons interacting deterministically. We show by numerical simulations of large asymmetric inhibitory networks with fixed external excitatory drive that if the network has intermediate to sparse connectivity, the individual cells are in the vicinity of a bifurcation between a quiescent and firing state and the network inhibition varies slowly on the spiking timescale, then cells form assemblies whose members show strong positive correlation, while members of different assemblies show strong negative correlation. We show that cells and assemblies switch between firing and quiescent states with time durations consistent with a power-law. Our results are in good qualitative agreement with the experimental studies. The deterministic dynamical behaviour is related to winner-less competition shown in small closed loop inhibitory networks with heteroclinic cycles connecting saddle-points.
originalAbstract: Cell assemblies exhibiting episodes of recurrent coherent activity have been observed in several brain regions including the striatum and hippocampus CA3. Here we address the question of how coherent dynamically switching assemblies appear in large networks of biologically realistic spiking neurons interacting deterministically. We show by numerical simulations of large asymmetric inhibitory networks with fixed external excitatory drive that if the network has intermediate to sparse connectivity, the individual cells are in the vicinity of a bifurcation between a quiescent and firing state and the network inhibition varies slowly on the spiking timescale, then cells form assemblies whose members show strong positive correlation, while members of different assemblies show strong negative correlation. We show that cells and assemblies switch between firing and quiescent states with time durations consistent with a power-law. Our results are in good qualitative agreement with the experimental studies. The deterministic dynamical behaviour is related to winner-less competition shown in small closed loop inhibitory networks with heteroclinic cycles connecting saddle-points.

paragraphs: Groups of neurons can repeatedly become active together, with activity switching between groups. The paper asks how such assemblies can arise in large networks of biologically realistic spiking neurons whose interactions are deterministic. It investigates this question through numerical simulations of asymmetric inhibitory networks receiving fixed external excitation.

The reported assembly formation depends on several conditions. Connectivity ranges from intermediate to sparse, individual neurons sit near the transition between silence and firing, and inhibition changes slowly relative to individual spikes. Under these conditions, neurons within an assembly show strongly correlated activity, while neurons belonging to different assemblies show strongly opposing activity patterns.

Cells and assemblies alternate between active and quiet periods whose durations are consistent with a power-law distribution. The authors report good qualitative agreement with experimental observations. They also relate the dynamics to winner-less competition in smaller inhibitory networks, where activity moves among states without settling on a permanent winner. The simulations thus offer a conditional dynamical explanation for coherent assemblies that keep changing over time.
summary.tldr: Simulations show that deterministic inhibitory networks can form switching neuronal assemblies under specific connectivity and dynamical conditions.

title: Cell Assemblies in Large Sparse Inhibitory Networks of Biologically Realistic Spiking Neurons

abstract: We consider an online decision problem over a discrete space in which the loss function is submodular. We give algorithms which are computationally efficient and are Hannan-consistent in both the full information and bandit settings.
originalAbstract: We consider an online decision problem over a discrete space in which the loss function is submodular. We give algorithms which are computationally efficient and are Hannan-consistent in both the full information and bandit settings.
title: Beyond Convexity: Online Submodular Minimization

abstract: This paper explores links between basis construction methods in Markov decision processes and power series expansions of value functions. This perspective provides a useful framework to analyze properties of existing bases, as well as provides insight into constructing more effective bases. Krylov and Bellman error bases are based on the Neumann series expansion. These bases incur very large initial Bellman errors, and can converge rather slowly as the discount factor approaches unity. The Laurent series expansion, which relates discounted and average-reward formulations, provides both an explanation for this slow convergence as well as suggests a way to construct more efficient basis representations. The first two terms in the Laurent series represent the scaled average-reward and the average-adjusted sum of rewards, and subsequent terms expand the discounted value function using powers of a generalized inverse called the Drazin (or group inverse) of a singular matrix derived from the transition matrix. Experiments show that Drazin bases converge considerably more quickly than several other bases, particularly for large values of the discount factor. An incremental variant of Drazin bases called Bellman average-reward bases (BARBs) is described, which provides some of the same benefits at lower computational cost.

paragraphs: A value function in a Markov decision process can be represented using a collection of basis functions. This paper studies how choosing those functions relates to series expansions of the value function. That connection provides a way to explain existing methods and design representations that converge more efficiently.

The paper also introduces Bellman average-reward bases, an incremental variant that retains some of these benefits at lower computational cost. The results connect representation design to the structure of long-horizon rewards.
summary.tldr: Series expansions motivate new value-function bases that empirically converge faster, particularly when the discount factor is close to one.

title: Basis Construction from Power Series Expansions of Value Functions

abstract: Singular Value Decomposition (and Principal Component Analysis) is one of the most widely used techniques for dimensionality reduction: successful and efficiently computable, it is nevertheless plagued by a well-known, well-documented sensitivity to outliers. Recent work has considered the setting where each point has a few arbitrarily corrupted components. Yet, in applications of SVD or PCA such as robust collaborative filtering or bioinformatics, malicious agents, defective genes, or simply corrupted or contaminated experiments may effectively yield entire points that are completely corrupted. We present an efficient convex optimization-based algorithm we call Outlier Pursuit, that under some mild assumptions on the uncorrupted points (satisfied, e.g., by the standard generative assumption in PCA problems) recovers the exact optimal low-dimensional subspace, and identifies the corrupted points. Such identification of corrupted points that do not conform to the low-dimensional approximation, is of paramount interest in bioinformatics and financial applications, and beyond. Our techniques involve matrix decomposition using nuclear norm minimization, however, our results, setup, and approach, necessarily differ considerably from the existing line of work in matrix completion and matrix decomposition, since we develop an approach to recover the correct column space of the uncorrupted matrix, rather than the exact matrix itself.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis can be strongly affected by outliers. This paper considers corruption of entire data points, a setting relevant when a whole experiment, gene, or participant's contribution is unreliable. Such corruption requires a different recovery goal from problems where only a few components of each point are damaged.

The authors introduce Outlier Pursuit, an efficient convex optimization algorithm using matrix decomposition and nuclear norm minimization. Under stated mild assumptions on the uncorrupted points, the method recovers the exact optimal low-dimensional subspace and identifies corrupted points. The abstract notes that these assumptions are satisfied, for example, by a standard generative assumption used in PCA.

The target is the correct column space of the uncorrupted matrix, rather than exact reconstruction of the matrix itself. This distinction aligns the method with the underlying purpose of dimensionality reduction: recovering the structure supported by reliable observations. Identifying points that fail to conform to that structure is an additional output, making the method relevant when detecting contaminated observations is itself valuable.
summary.tldr: Outlier Pursuit uses convex optimization to recover the underlying PCA subspace and identify corrupted points under assumptions on the clean data.

title: Robust PCA via Outlier Pursuit

abstract: Learning the number of clusters is a key problem in data clustering. We present dip-means, a novel robust incremental method to learn the number of data clusters that may be used as a wrapper around any iterative clustering algorithm of the k-means family. In contrast to many popular methods which make assumptions about the underlying cluster distributions, dip-means only assumes a fundamental cluster property: each cluster to admit a unimodal distribution. The proposed algorithm considers each cluster member as a ''viewer'' and applies a univariate statistic hypothesis test for unimodality (dip-test) on the distribution of the distances between the viewer and the cluster members. Two important advantages are: i) the unimodality test is applied on univariate distance vectors, ii) it can be directly applied with kernel-based methods, since only the pairwise distances are involved in the computations. Experimental results on artificial and real datasets indicate the effectiveness of our method and its superiority over analogous approaches.

paragraphs: Dip-means addresses the problem of determining how many clusters a dataset contains. It is an incremental method that can wrap around iterative clustering algorithms in the k-means family. Its stated assumption is that each cluster admits a unimodal distribution, giving it a criterion for judging whether a proposed cluster behaves like one group.

The method treats each member of a cluster as a viewer. For that viewer, it collects distances to the other cluster members and applies the dip-test, a statistical test of unimodality, to the resulting one-dimensional distribution. This turns a question about a potentially high-dimensional cluster into tests on univariate distance vectors.

Because its computations use pairwise distances, the method can also work directly with kernel-based clustering methods. Experiments on artificial and real datasets report effectiveness and superiority over analogous approaches. The contribution is a way to estimate cluster count through a specific distributional property, while retaining compatibility with existing iterative clustering machinery and avoiding a prescribed detailed family of cluster distributions.
summary.tldr: Dip-means estimates cluster count by testing unimodality in within-cluster distance distributions.

title: Dip-means: an incremental clustering method for estimating the number of clusters

abstract: Owing to several applications in large scale learning and vision problems, fast submodular function minimization (SFM) has become a critical problem. Theoretically, unconstrained SFM can be performed in polynomial time (Iwata and Orlin 2009), however these algorithms are not practical. In 1976, Wolfe proposed an algorithm to find the minimum Euclidean norm point in a polytope, and in 1980, Fujishige showed how Wolfe's algorithm can be used for SFM. For general submodular functions, the Fujishige-Wolfe minimum norm algorithm seems to have the best empirical performance. Despite its good practical performance, theoretically very little is known about Wolfe's minimum norm algorithm -- to our knowledge the only result is an exponential time analysis due to Wolfe himself. In this paper we give a maiden convergence analysis of Wolfe's algorithm. We prove that in t iterations, Wolfe's algorithm returns a O(1/t)-approximate solution to the min-norm point. We also prove a robust version of Fujishige's theorem which shows that an O(1/n^2)-approximate solution to the min-norm point problem implies exact submodular minimization. As a corollary, we get the first pseudo-polynomial time guarantee for the Fujishige-Wolfe minimum norm algorithm for submodular function minimization. In particular, we show that the min-norm point algorithm solves SFM in O(n^7F^2)-time, where $F$ is an upper bound on the maximum change a single element can cause in the function value.

paragraphs: Submodular function minimization appears in learning and vision, but algorithms with strong general polynomial-time guarantees can be impractical. The Fujishige-Wolfe approach has strong reported empirical performance, yet its theoretical behavior was poorly understood. It solves a geometric problem involving the point of minimum Euclidean norm in a polytope.

The authors prove that after t iterations, Wolfe's algorithm obtains an O(1/t)-approximate solution to this minimum-norm problem. They also establish a robust version of the theorem linking that geometric problem to submodular minimization: an O(1/n²)-accurate minimum-norm solution suffices to obtain an exact submodular minimum. This connects approximate geometric progress to exact discrete optimization.

Combining these results gives a pseudo-polynomial runtime guarantee for the Fujishige-Wolfe method. The stated bound is O(n⁷F²), where F bounds the largest change in function value caused by one element. Its dependence on F is part of the guarantee. The contribution supplies a convergence explanation for a practically successful method and a quantitative route from its iterations to an exact solution.
summary.tldr: Convergence and robustness results give the Fujishige-Wolfe submodular minimization algorithm a pseudo-polynomial runtime guarantee.

title: Provable Submodular Minimization using Wolfe's Algorithm

abstract: This paper presents a Bayesian optimization method with exponential convergence without the need of auxiliary optimization and without the delta-cover sampling. Most Bayesian optimization methods require auxiliary optimization: an additional non-convex global optimization problem, which can be time-consuming and hard to implement in practice. Also, the existing Bayesian optimization method with exponential convergence requires access to the delta-cover sampling, which was considered to be impractical. Our approach eliminates both requirements and achieves an exponential convergence rate.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a Bayesian optimization method with exponential convergence without the need of auxiliary optimization and without the delta-cover sampling. Most Bayesian optimization methods require auxiliary optimization: an additional non-convex global optimization problem, which can be time-consuming and hard to implement in practice. Also, the existing Bayesian optimization method with exponential convergence requires access to the delta-cover sampling, which was considered to be impractical. Our approach eliminates both requirements and achieves an exponential convergence rate.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization can require a difficult optimization problem inside the main optimization process. According to this paper, most existing approaches select their next step through an auxiliary nonconvex global optimization. That extra problem can be time-consuming and difficult to implement, making the machinery used to guide optimization a substantial burden of its own.

The paper introduces a method that removes this auxiliary optimization requirement. It also avoids delta-cover sampling, a requirement of an existing Bayesian optimization method with exponential convergence. The abstract describes that sampling requirement as having been considered impractical, so eliminating it addresses a second obstacle to using an approach with this convergence behavior.

The main result is that the proposed method achieves exponential convergence while dispensing with both requirements. The significance is the combination: the convergence result is retained alongside a simpler set of required operations. This establishes a route to exponential convergence that does not depend on either of the two specific computational components identified as problematic.
summary.tldr: The proposed Bayesian optimization method achieves exponential convergence without auxiliary global optimization or delta-cover sampling.

title: Bayesian Optimization with Exponential Convergence

abstract: Asynchronous parallel optimization received substantial successes and extensive attention recently. One of core theoretical questions is how much speedup (or benefit) the asynchronous parallelization can bring to us. This paper provides a comprehensive and generic analysis to study the speedup property for a broad range of asynchronous parallel stochastic algorithms from the zeroth order to the first order methods. Our result recovers or improves existing analysis on special cases, provides more insights for understanding the asynchronous parallel behaviors, and suggests a novel asynchronous parallel zeroth order method for the first time. Our experiments provide novel applications of the proposed asynchronous parallel zeroth order method on hyper parameter tuning and model blending problems.
originalAbstract: Asynchronous parallel optimization received substantial successes and extensive attention recently. Our experiments provide novel applications of the proposed asynchronous parallel zeroth order method on hyper parameter tuning and model blending problems.

paragraphs: Running optimization work in parallel raises a basic question: how much faster does the overall learning process become? This paper studies that question for asynchronous stochastic optimization, where parallel work proceeds without requiring all workers to advance together. Its focus is the relationship between parallel execution and optimization speed, rather than simply whether parallel computation is possible.

The authors develop a shared analysis covering a broad range of methods, from zeroth-order approaches to first-order approaches. These categories distinguish methods that work with objective evaluations from methods that use gradient information. Treating them within one framework makes it possible to connect speedup results that would otherwise be studied as separate algorithm-specific cases.

The analysis recovers or improves existing results for particular methods and provides further insight into asynchronous behavior. It also motivates a new asynchronous parallel zeroth-order algorithm. The experiments apply that algorithm to hyperparameter tuning and model blending. Together, these contributions connect a general theoretical treatment of speedup with concrete uses of optimization based on function evaluations.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis studies asynchronous optimization speedups and motivates a new parallel zeroth-order method.

title: A Comprehensive Linear Speedup Analysis for Asynchronous Stochastic Parallel Optimization from Zeroth-Order to First-Order

abstract: In this paper, we propose a multi-step inertial Forward--Backward splitting algorithm for minimizing the sum of two non-necessarily convex functions, one of which is proper lower semi-continuous while the other is differentiable with a Lipschitz continuous gradient. We first prove global convergence of the scheme with the help of the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property. Then, when the non-smooth part is also partly smooth relative to a smooth submanifold, we establish finite identification of the latter and provide sharp local linear convergence analysis. The proposed method is illustrated on a few problems arising from statistics and machine learning.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a multi-step inertial Forward--Backward splitting algorithm for minimizing the sum of two non-necessarily convex functions, one of which is proper lower semi-continuous while the other is differentiable with a Lipschitz continuous gradient. We first prove global convergence of the scheme with the help of the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property. Then, when the non-smooth part is also partly smooth relative to a smooth submanifold, we establish finite identification of the latter and provide sharp local linear convergence analysis. The proposed method is illustrated on a few problems arising from statistics and machine learning.

paragraphs: The paper develops an optimization algorithm for objectives made from two functions, neither of which has to be convex. One function may be nonsmooth, while the other must be differentiable with a Lipschitz continuous gradient. This structure lets the method treat the two parts separately while using information from several previous steps through an inertial update.

The main theoretical contribution is a global convergence result using the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property. This establishes convergence of the scheme under the stated mathematical framework; it should not be read as a claim that arbitrary nonconvex problems can be solved to their global minimum. The distinction matters because convergence and global optimality are different properties.

With an additional partial-smoothness assumption, the authors show that the method identifies a relevant smooth submanifold after finitely many iterations. They then give a sharp analysis of local linear convergence. Together, these results explain both eventual structural identification and the behavior near a solution. Examples from statistics and machine learning illustrate the proposed method.
summary.tldr: A multistep inertial optimization method has convergence guarantees and, under additional structure, finite manifold identification and local linear convergence.

title: A Multi-step Inertial Forward-Backward Splitting Method for Non-convex Optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of non-parametric Conditional Independence testing (CI testing) for continuous random variables. Given i.i.d samples from the joint distribution $f(x,y,z)$ of continuous random vectors $X,Y$ and $Z,$ we determine whether $X \independent Y \vert Z$. We approach this by converting the conditional independence test into a classification problem. This allows us to harness very powerful classifiers like gradient-boosted trees and deep neural networks. These models can handle complex probability distributions and allow us to perform significantly better compared to the prior state of the art, for high-dimensional CI testing. The main technical challenge in the classification problem is the need for samples from the conditional product distribution $f^{CI}(x,y,z) = f(x|z)f(y|z)f(z)$ -- the joint distribution if and only if $X \independent Y \vert Z.$ -- when given access only to i.i.d. samples from the true joint distribution $f(x,y,z)$. To tackle this problem we propose a novel nearest neighbor bootstrap procedure and theoretically show that our generated samples are indeed close to $f^{CI}$ in terms of total variational distance. We then develop theoretical results regarding the generalization bounds for classification for our problem, which translate into error bounds for CI testing. We provide a novel analysis of Rademacher type classification bounds in the presence of non-i.i.d \textit{near-independent} samples. We empirically validate the performance of our algorithm on simulated and real datasets and show performance gains over previous methods.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether two continuous random vectors, X and Y, are independent once a third vector, Z, is taken into account. Starting from independent samples of their joint distribution, the authors turn this conditional-independence question into a classification problem. This permits powerful classifiers, including boosted trees and deep neural networks, to handle complex distributions.

The authors propose a nearest-neighbor bootstrap for this purpose. They theoretically show that the generated samples are close to the desired conditional-product distribution in total variation distance.

The analysis also connects classification generalization bounds to errors in conditional-independence testing. It accounts for the generated samples being nearly independent rather than fully independent. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show gains over previous methods, especially for high-dimensional testing. The contribution combines a practical classification-based test with theoretical treatment of the synthetic comparison samples on which it relies.
summary.tldr: A conditional-independence test combines powerful classifiers with a theoretically analyzed nearest-neighbor bootstrap to improve high-dimensional testing.

title: Model-Powered Conditional Independence Test

abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress with the quick evolvement of model structures. In this paper, we propose the concept of layer-wise coordination for NMT, which explicitly coordinates the learning of hidden representations of the encoder and decoder together layer by layer, gradually from low level to high level. Specifically, we design a layer-wise attention and mixed attention mechanism, and further share the parameters of each layer between the encoder and decoder to regularize and coordinate the learning. Experiments show that combined with the state-of-the-art Transformer model, layer-wise coordination achieves improvements on three IWSLT and two WMT translation tasks. More specifically, our method achieves 34.43 and 29.01 BLEU score on WMT16 English-Romanian and WMT14 English-German tasks, outperforming the Transformer baseline.

Specifically, we design a layer-wise attention and mixed attention mechanism, and further share the parameters of each layer between the encoder and decoder to regularize and coordinate the learning. Experiments show that combined with the state-of-the-art Transformer model, layer-wise coordination achieves improvements on three IWSLT and two WMT translation tasks. paragraphs: A neural translation model uses an encoder and a decoder, each building hidden representations across multiple layers. This paper proposes coordinating those representations layer by layer as they progress from lower to higher levels. The goal is to make the two sides learn together at corresponding stages of their processing.

The method introduces layer-wise attention and mixed attention mechanisms to support this coordination. It also shares parameters between encoder and decoder layers, providing a way to regularize their learning and tie their representations together. These changes make cooperation between the two components an explicit part of the model's architecture and training.

When combined with the Transformer, layer-wise coordination improves results on three IWSLT and two WMT translation tasks. The reported scores are 34.43 BLEU for WMT16 English–Romanian and 29.01 BLEU for WMT14 English–German, both above the Transformer baseline. The findings support coordinating intermediate representations as a useful architectural change across the evaluated translation tasks.
summary.tldr: Layer-wise attention and parameter sharing coordinate Transformer encoders and decoders, improving results on five translation tasks.

title: Layer-Wise Coordination between Encoder and Decoder for Neural Machine Translation

abstract: Novelty detection is the problem of identifying whether a new data point is considered to be an inlier or an outlier. We assume that training data is available to describe only the inlier distribution. Recent approaches primarily leverage deep encoder-decoder network architectures to compute a reconstruction error that is used to either compute a novelty score or to train a one-class classifier. While we too leverage a novel network of that kind, we take a probabilistic approach and effectively compute how likely it is that a sample was generated by the inlier distribution. We achieve this with two main contributions. First, we make the computation of the novelty probability feasible because we linearize the parameterized manifold capturing the underlying structure of the inlier distribution, and show how the probability factorizes and can be computed with respect to local coordinates of the manifold tangent space. Second, we improve the training of the autoencoder network. An extensive set of results show that the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.

We assume that training data is available to describe only the inlier distribution. Recent approaches primarily leverage deep encoder-decoder network architectures to compute a reconstruction error that is used to either compute a novelty score or to train a one-class classifier. While we too leverage a novel network of that kind, we take a probabilistic approach and effectively compute how likely it is that a sample was generated by the inlier distribution. We achieve this with two main contributions. First, we make the computation of the novelty probability feasible because we linearize the parameterized manifold capturing the underlying structure of the inlier distribution, and show how the probability factorizes and can be computed with respect to local coordinates of the manifold tangent space. Second, we improve the training of the autoencoder network. An extensive set of results show that the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Novelty detection asks whether a new observation belongs to the familiar data distribution or is an outlier. This paper assumes that training examples describe only the inlier distribution. It develops an encoder-decoder approach that estimates how likely an observation is to have been generated by that distribution, giving the detection decision an explicitly probabilistic basis.

The main computational idea is to linearize the parameterized manifold representing the structure of inlier data. This local approximation makes the probability calculation feasible. The authors show how the probability factorizes and can be evaluated using local coordinates associated with the manifold's tangent space, connecting the learned representation to a calculable measure of inlier likelihood.

The paper also improves training of its autoencoder network. Together, the probability computation and training changes achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets in the reported evaluation. These results support using the learned geometry of familiar data for probabilistic novelty detection under the assumption that training provides examples of inliers only.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic autoencoder method uses local manifold geometry to estimate whether an observation comes from the learned inlier distribution.

title: Generative Probabilistic Novelty Detection with Adversarial Autoencoders

abstract: Given two candidate models, and a set of target observations, we address the problem of measuring the relative goodness of fit of the two models. We propose two new statistical tests which are nonparametric, computationally efficient (runtime complexity is linear in the sample size), and interpretable. As a unique advantage, our tests can produce a set of examples (informative features) indicating the regions in the data domain where one model fits significantly better than the other. In a real-world problem of comparing GAN models, the test power of our new test matches that of the state-of-the-art test of relative goodness of fit, while being one order of magnitude faster.
originalAbstract: Given two candidate models, and a set of target observations, we address the problem of measuring the relative goodness of fit of the two models. We propose two new statistical tests which are nonparametric, computationally efficient (runtime complexity is linear in the sample size), and interpretable. As a unique advantage, our tests can produce a set of examples (informative features) indicating the regions in the data domain where one model fits significantly better than the other. In a real-world problem of comparing GAN models, the test power of our new test matches that of the state-of-the-art test of relative goodness of fit, while being one order of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Comparing two models against observed data often calls for more than a single ranking. A useful comparison can also identify where one model captures the data better. This paper develops two statistical tests for relative goodness of fit that combine a model comparison with interpretable evidence about the source of the difference.

The tests are nonparametric and have runtime that grows linearly with the number of samples. Their distinguishing feature is the ability to return informative examples indicating regions of the data domain where one model fits significantly better than its competitor. This connects a statistical conclusion to concrete parts of the observations that help explain it.

In a real-world comparison of generative adversarial networks, the reported test matches the statistical power of a state-of-the-art relative-fit test while running about ten times faster. That result supports the practical value of combining efficiency with interpretation: the comparison can retain sensitivity to model differences while also helping users locate those differences.
summary.tldr: Two efficient statistical tests compare model fit and identify informative examples showing where one model performs significantly better.

title: Informative Features for Model Comparison

abstract: Many probabilistic models of interest in scientific computing and machine learning have expensive, black-box likelihoods that prevent the application of standard techniques for Bayesian inference, such as MCMC, which would require access to the gradient or a large number of likelihood evaluations. We introduce here a novel sample-efficient inference framework, Variational Bayesian Monte Carlo (VBMC). VBMC combines variational inference with Gaussian-process based, active-sampling Bayesian quadrature, using the latter to efficiently approximate the intractable integral in the variational objective. Our method produces both a nonparametric approximation of the posterior distribution and an approximate lower bound of the model evidence, useful for model selection. We demonstrate VBMC both on several synthetic likelihoods and on a neuronal model with data from real neurons. Across all tested problems and dimensions (up to D = 10), VBMC performs consistently well in reconstructing the posterior and the model evidence with a limited budget of likelihood evaluations, unlike other methods that work only in very low dimensions. Our framework shows great promise as a novel tool for posterior and model inference with expensive, black-box likelihoods.

The quadrature component approximates an otherwise intractable integral in the variational objective, while active sampling guides where evaluations are made. summary.tldr: VBMC combines variational inference and active Bayesian quadrature to estimate posteriors and model evidence with few expensive likelihood evaluations.

title: Variational Bayesian Monte Carlo

abstract: We present a new algorithm for stochastic variational inference that targets at models with non-differentiable densities. One of the key challenges in stochastic variational inference is to come up with a low-variance estimator of the gradient of a variational objective. We tackle the challenge by generalizing the reparameterization trick, one of the most effective techniques for addressing the variance issue for differentiable models, so that the trick works for non-differentiable models as well. Our algorithm splits the space of latent variables into regions where the density of the variables is differentiable, and their boundaries where the density may fail to be differentiable. For each differentiable region, the algorithm applies the standard reparameterization trick and estimates the gradient restricted to the region. For each potentially non-differentiable boundary, it uses a form of manifold sampling and computes the direction for variational parameters that, if followed, would increase the boundary’s contribution to the variational objective. The sum of all the estimates becomes the gradient estimate of our algorithm. Our estimator enjoys the reduced variance of the reparameterization gradient while remaining unbiased even for non-differentiable models. The experiments with our preliminary implementation confirm the benefit of reduced variance and unbiasedness.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference depends on estimating gradients of an objective using random samples. The reparameterization trick can reduce the variance of those estimates for differentiable models, but densities with nondifferentiable regions complicate its use. This paper extends the technique to account explicitly for those regions and their boundaries.

The algorithm divides latent-variable space into regions where the density is differentiable and boundaries where differentiability may fail. Within each region, it uses the standard reparameterization approach. At the boundaries, it applies a form of manifold sampling to estimate how changes to the variational parameters affect the boundary’s contribution to the objective.

Adding the regional and boundary estimates produces the final gradient estimate. Accounting for both kinds of contributions allows the estimator to remain unbiased for nondifferentiable models while retaining reduced variance associated with reparameterization gradients. Experiments with a preliminary implementation confirm benefits from those properties. The central contribution is therefore a gradient construction that handles boundary effects as part of the inference calculation.
summary.tldr: Combining regional reparameterization gradients with sampled boundary contributions yields an unbiased, reduced-variance estimator for nondifferentiable models.

title: Reparameterization Gradient for Non-differentiable Models

abstract: Classically, the time complexity of a first-order method is estimated by its number of gradient computations. In this paper, we study a more refined complexity by taking into account the ``lingering'' of gradients: once a gradient is computed at $x_k$, the additional time to compute gradients at $x_{k+1},x_{k+2},\dots$ may be reduced. We show how this improves the running time of gradient descent and SVRG. For instance, if the "additional time'' scales linearly with respect to the traveled distance, then the "convergence rate'' of gradient descent can be improved from $1/T$ to $\exp(-T^{1/3})$. On the empirical side, we solve a hypothetical revenue management problem on the Yahoo! Front Page Today Module application with 4.6m users to $10^{-6}$ error (or $10^{-12}$ dual error) using 6 passes of the dataset.

paragraphs: Optimization methods are often assessed by counting gradient computations, implicitly treating each computation as a fresh expense. This paper studies a more detailed cost model: after computing a gradient at one point, some of that work may remain useful at later points. The authors call this persistence the lingering of gradients.

They show how exploiting lingering can improve the running time of gradient descent and SVRG. One result assumes that the additional work needed for gradients scales linearly with the distance traveled. Under that condition, gradient descent's convergence rate in the refined computational accounting can improve from 1/T to exp(−T^(1/3)). The condition is central to that comparison.

The empirical study considers a hypothetical revenue-management problem using the Yahoo! Front Page Today Module application with 4.6 million users. It reaches 10⁻⁶ error, or 10⁻¹² dual error, in six passes through the dataset. The contribution highlights reusable gradient computation as a source of efficiency that a simple count of complete gradient evaluations can overlook.
summary.tldr: Reusing lingering gradient information improves optimization runtime, with faster conditional convergence under a distance-sensitive computation model.

title: The Lingering of Gradients: How to Reuse Gradients Over Time

abstract: We demonstrate, theoretically and empirically, that adversarial robustness can significantly benefit from semisupervised learning. Theoretically, we revisit the simple Gaussian model of Schmidt et al. that shows a sample complexity gap between standard and robust classification. We prove that unlabeled data bridges this gap: a simple semisupervised learning procedure (self-training) achieves high robust accuracy using the same number of labels required for achieving high standard accuracy. Empirically, we augment CIFAR-10 with 500K unlabeled images sourced from 80 Million Tiny Images and use robust self-training to outperform state-of-the-art robust accuracies by over 5 points in (i) $\ell_\infty$ robustness against several strong attacks via adversarial training and (ii) certified $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ robustness via randomized smoothing. On SVHN, adding the dataset's own extra training set with the labels removed provides gains of 4 to 10 points, within 1 point of the gain from using the extra labels.

paragraphs: Learning to resist adversarial input changes can require more data than learning ordinary classification. This paper investigates whether the extra examples need human-provided labels. It combines theory and experiments to show that semisupervised learning, specifically self-training, can substantially improve robustness by making use of unlabeled examples.

In a simple Gaussian model, the authors prove that self-training bridges the label-complexity gap between standard and robust classification. It achieves high robust accuracy with the same number of labels needed for high standard accuracy, using unlabeled data as additional information. This is a result for the analyzed model, with label requirements distinguished from the total amount of data used.

For CIFAR-10, adding 500,000 unlabeled images improves leading robust accuracies by more than five points in the reported adversarial-training and certified-smoothing settings. On SVHN, using its extra training set without labels yields gains of four to ten points, within one point of the gains obtained with those labels. The experiments show that additional labels account for relatively little of the benefit in that SVHN comparison.
summary.tldr: Self-training with unlabeled data closes a theoretical robustness label gap in a Gaussian model and substantially improves reported robust image-classification results.

title: Unlabeled Data Improves Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Recent works have shown the effectiveness of randomized smoothing as a scalable technique for building neural network-based classifiers that are provably robust to $\ell_2$-norm adversarial perturbations. In this paper, we employ adversarial training to improve the performance of randomized smoothing. We design an adapted attack for smoothed classifiers, and we show how this attack can be used in an adversarial training setting to boost the provable robustness of smoothed classifiers. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation that our method consistently outperforms all existing provably $\ell_2$-robust classifiers by a significant margin on ImageNet and CIFAR-10, establishing the state-of-the-art for provable $\ell_2$-defenses. Moreover, we find that pre-training and semi-supervised learning boost adversarially trained smoothed classifiers even further. Our code and trained models are available at http://github.com/Hadisalman/smoothing-adversarial.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing is a scalable way to construct neural classifiers with provable robustness to adversarial perturbations measured in the l2 norm. This paper seeks to improve the performance of those smoothed classifiers through adversarial training. The focus is on strengthening robustness that can be certified, within the stated perturbation model.

The authors design an attack adapted specifically to smoothed classifiers and use it during adversarial training. Aligning the training attack with the smoothed classifier provides a way to improve the classifier whose robustness will be evaluated. They show how this combination boosts provable robustness rather than treating smoothing and adversarial training as separate procedures.

Extensive experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 report consistent, significant improvements over the existing provably l2-robust classifiers considered in the paper. The authors also find that pretraining and semi-supervised learning improve the adversarially trained smoothed classifiers further. These findings establish the reported state of the art for provable l2 defenses and show that additional learning strategies can strengthen the combined approach.
summary.tldr: Adversarial training with an attack tailored to smoothed classifiers improves their provable l2 robustness on ImageNet and CIFAR-10.

title: Provably Robust Deep Learning via Adversarially Trained Smoothed Classifiers

abstract: Bayesian optimisation is a popular technique for hyperparameter learning but typically requires initial exploration even in cases where similar prior tasks have been solved. We propose to transfer information across tasks using learnt representations of training datasets used in those tasks. This results in a joint Gaussian process model on hyperparameters and data representations. Representations make use of the framework of distribution embeddings into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The developed method has a faster convergence compared to existing baselines, in some cases requiring only a few evaluations of the target objective.
