paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for useful hyperparameter settings by evaluating a training objective and using those results to guide subsequent choices. Even when related tasks have already been solved, the search may still spend effort exploring initially. This paper proposes transferring information from earlier tasks through learned representations of their training datasets.

The method represents datasets using distribution embeddings in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. These representations describe a task through its data distribution and enter a joint Gaussian process model alongside hyperparameters. The model can therefore relate objective behavior to both the chosen settings and the dataset on which those settings are used. Dataset information becomes part of the mechanism for transferring experience.

The authors report faster convergence than existing baselines, with some cases needing only a few evaluations of the target objective. That qualification matters: the abstract does not claim that every new task needs so few evaluations. The result supports using distributional descriptions of datasets to make prior optimization experience useful when tuning a target task.
summary.tldr: Learning representations of dataset distributions lets Bayesian optimization transfer across tasks and converge faster in reported comparisons.

title: Hyperparameter Learning via Distributional Transfer

abstract: Various evaluation measures have been developed for multi-label classification, including Hamming Loss (HL), Subset Accuracy (SA) and Ranking Loss (RL). However, there is a gap between empirical results and the existing theories: 1) an algorithm often empirically performs well on some measure(s) while poorly on others, while a formal theoretical analysis is lacking; and 2) in small label space cases, the algorithms optimizing HL often have comparable or even better performance on the SA measure than those optimizing SA directly, while existing theoretical results show that SA and HL are conflicting measures. This paper provides an attempt to fill up this gap by analyzing the learning guarantees of the corresponding learning algorithms on both SA and HL measures. We show that when a learning algorithm optimizes HL with its surrogate loss, it enjoys an error bound for the HL measure independent of $c$ (the number of labels), while the bound for the SA measure depends on at most $O(c)$. On the other hand, when directly optimizing SA with its surrogate loss, it has learning guarantees that depend on $O(\sqrt{c})$ for both HL and SA measures. This explains the observation that when the label space is not large, optimizing HL with its surrogate loss can have promising performance for SA. We further show that our techniques are applicable to analyze the learning guarantees of algorithms on other measures, such as RL. Finally, the theoretical analyses are supported by experimental results.

paragraphs: Multi-label classifiers can be evaluated by individual label errors or by whether the entire predicted label set is correct. These correspond to Hamming loss and subset accuracy. Although existing theory describes the measures as conflicting, experiments sometimes show that optimizing Hamming loss also performs well on subset accuracy, particularly when relatively few labels are involved.

The paper analyzes learning guarantees for algorithms that optimize surrogate losses for either measure. With c labels, optimizing the Hamming-loss surrogate gives a Hamming-loss error bound independent of c and a subset-accuracy bound with at most linear dependence on c. Optimizing the subset-accuracy surrogate instead gives guarantees for both measures that depend on the square root of c.

These different dependencies help explain why targeting Hamming loss can still produce promising subset accuracy in smaller label spaces. The results concern learning bounds, so they clarify the empirical pattern without requiring one objective to win in every case. The authors also extend their techniques to ranking loss and present experiments supporting the theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: Label-count-dependent learning bounds explain why optimizing Hamming loss can also yield promising subset accuracy when the label space is small.

title: Multi-label classification: do Hamming loss and subset accuracy really conflict with each other?

abstract: We present an extension of the conditional gradient method to problems whose feasible sets are convex cones. We provide a convergence analysis for the method and for variants with nonconvex objectives, and we extend the analysis to practical cases with effective line search strategies. For the specific case of the positive semidefinite cone, we present a memory-efficient version based on randomized matrix sketches and advocate a heuristic greedy step that greatly improves its practical performance. Numerical results on phase retrieval and matrix completion problems indicate that our method can offer substantial advantages over traditional conditional gradient and Burer-Monteiro approaches.

paragraphs: This paper extends conditional gradient optimization to problems whose feasible solutions form a convex cone. The cone structure is the organizing feature of the proposed method. The authors analyze convergence both for the method and for variants involving nonconvex objectives, and extend that analysis to practical versions using effective line search strategies.

For optimization over positive semidefinite matrices, the paper develops a version designed to use less memory. It relies on randomized matrix sketches, which provide compact representations for the matrix computations. The authors also recommend a heuristic greedy step that substantially improves practical performance. The abstract distinguishes this practical improvement from the convergence analysis supporting the broader optimization framework.

Numerical experiments examine phase retrieval and matrix completion. In these problems, the results indicate that the proposed method can offer substantial advantages over traditional conditional gradient methods and Burer-Monteiro approaches. The contribution therefore combines a general extension of an optimization method with a memory-conscious implementation for an important matrix setting, supported by favorable results on the tested applications.
summary.tldr: Conic descent extends conditional gradient methods to convex cones, with a matrix-sketching version that offers memory efficiency and favorable numerical results.

title: Conic Descent and its Application to Memory-efficient Optimization over Positive Semidefinite Matrices

abstract: We study the problem of inferring communication structures that can solve cooperative multi-agent planning problems while minimizing the amount of communication. We quantify the amount of communication as the maximum degree of the communication graph; this metric captures settings where agents have limited bandwidth. Minimizing communication is challenging due to the combinatorial nature of both the decision space and the objective; for instance, we cannot solve this problem by training neural networks using gradient descent. We propose a novel algorithm that synthesizes a control policy that combines a programmatic communication policy used to generate the communication graph with a transformer policy network used to choose actions. Our algorithm first trains the transformer policy, which implicitly generates a "soft" communication graph; then, it synthesizes a programmatic communication policy that "hardens" this graph, forming a neurosymbolic transformer. Our experiments demonstrate how our approach can synthesize policies that generate low-degree communication graphs while maintaining near-optimal performance.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need to choose actions and decide whom to communicate with. This paper seeks communication structures that preserve effective joint planning while limiting each agent's communication burden. It measures that burden through the maximum degree of the communication graph, reflecting settings where agents have limited bandwidth.

Choosing a sparse graph is a combinatorial problem that the authors cannot solve directly through neural-network gradient descent. Their approach splits the task into two stages. First, they train a transformer policy that implicitly creates a soft communication graph. They then synthesize a programmatic policy that converts this soft structure into explicit communication choices.

The resulting neurosymbolic transformer combines a program that generates the communication graph with a transformer network that selects actions. This makes the communication structure an explicit part of the control policy. Experiments demonstrate low-degree communication graphs while maintaining near-optimal performance, supporting the two-stage approach as a way to reduce communication without sacrificing much coordination quality in the tested problems.
summary.tldr: A learned transformer and synthesized communication program produce sparse multi-agent communication graphs with near-optimal experimental performance.

title: Neurosymbolic Transformers for Multi-Agent Communication

abstract: Entropic causal inference is a framework for inferring the causal direction between two categorical variables from observational data. The central assumption is that the amount of unobserved randomness in the system is not too large. This unobserved randomness is measured by the entropy of the exogenous variable in the underlying structural causal model, which governs the causal relation between the observed variables. Kocaoglu et al. conjectured that the causal direction is identifiable when the entropy of the exogenous variable is not too large. In this paper, we prove a variant of their conjecture. Namely, we show that for almost all causal models where the exogenous variable has entropy that does not scale with the number of states of the observed variables, the causal direction is identifiable from observational data. We also consider the minimum entropy coupling-based algorithmic approach presented by Kocaoglu et al., and for the first time demonstrate algorithmic identifiability guarantees using a finite number of samples. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of the method to relaxing some of the assumptions in our theory and demonstrate that both the constant-entropy exogenous variable and the no latent confounder assumptions can be relaxed in practice. We also empirically characterize the number of observational samples needed for causal identification. Finally, we apply the algorithm on Tuebingen cause-effect pairs dataset.

paragraphs: Entropic causal inference seeks the causal direction between two categorical variables using observational data. Its central assumption limits the amount of hidden randomness driving their relationship. The framework measures that randomness through the entropy of an exogenous variable in a structural causal model, making a restriction on unseen variation central to identifying direction.

The paper proves a variant of an earlier conjecture: direction is identifiable for almost all causal models whose exogenous entropy does not grow with the number of observed-variable states. The authors also provide finite-sample algorithmic identifiability guarantees for an approach based on minimum entropy coupling, connecting the structural result to inference from a limited dataset.

Experiments investigate robustness when theoretical assumptions are relaxed. They indicate that constant exogenous entropy and the absence of latent confounders can be relaxed in practice, without making those relaxations part of the general theorem. The authors also examine sample requirements empirically and apply the algorithm to Tuebingen cause-effect pairs. The work separates formal identifiability conditions from evidence of broader practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes causal-direction identifiability under bounded hidden entropy and gives finite-sample guarantees for an entropy-based inference method.

title: Entropic Causal Inference: Identifiability and Finite Sample Results

abstract: Wasserstein barycenters provide a geometrically meaningful way to aggregate probability distributions, built on the theory of optimal transport. They are difficult to compute in practice, however, leading previous work to restrict their supports to finite sets of points. Leveraging a new dual formulation for the regularized Wasserstein barycenter problem, we introduce a stochastic algorithm that constructs a continuous approximation of the barycenter. We establish strong duality and use the corresponding primal-dual relationship to parametrize the barycenter implicitly using the dual potentials of regularized transport problems. The resulting problem can be solved with stochastic gradient descent, which yields an efficient online algorithm to approximate the barycenter of continuous distributions given sample access. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and compare against previous work on synthetic examples and real-world applications.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter aggregates probability distributions in a way that respects the geometry used by optimal transport. Computing one is difficult, and earlier approaches often restrict the result to a finite collection of support points. This paper develops a method for constructing a continuous approximation instead.

The starting point is a new dual formulation of the regularized barycenter problem. The authors establish strong duality, linking the original problem to this alternative formulation. They use that relationship to represent the barycenter implicitly through the dual potentials of regularized transport problems. The representation avoids requiring the barycenter to be specified directly as a finite set of points.

The resulting optimization can be carried out with stochastic gradient descent, yielding an online algorithm that needs sample access to the input distributions. Experiments on synthetic examples and real-world applications demonstrate the approach and compare it with prior work. Its main significance is a computational route from sampled continuous distributions to a continuous barycenter approximation, supported by the primal-dual relationship underlying the construction.
summary.tldr: A new dual formulation enables online stochastic optimization of continuous approximations to regularized Wasserstein barycenters from samples.

title: Continuous Regularized Wasserstein Barycenters

abstract: It is known that the current graph neural networks (GNNs) are difficult to make themselves deep due to the problem known as over-smoothing. Multi-scale GNNs are a promising approach for mitigating the over-smoothing problem. However, there is little explanation of why it works empirically from the viewpoint of learning theory. In this study, we derive the optimization and generalization guarantees of transductive learning algorithms that include multi-scale GNNs. Using the boosting theory, we prove the convergence of the training error under weak learning-type conditions. By combining it with generalization gap bounds in terms of transductive Rademacher complexity, we show that a test error bound of a specific type of multi-scale GNNs that decreases corresponding to the number of node aggregations under some conditions. Our results offer theoretical explanations for the effectiveness of the multi-scale structure against the over-smoothing problem. We apply boosting algorithms to the training of multi-scale GNNs for real-world node prediction tasks. We confirm that its performance is comparable to existing GNNs, and the practical behaviors are consistent with theoretical observations. Code is available at https://github.com/delta2323/GB-GNN.

In this study, we derive the optimization and generalization guarantees of transductive learning algorithms that include multi-scale GNNs. Using the boosting theory, we prove the convergence of the training error under weak learning-type conditions. By combining it with generalization gap bounds in terms of transductive Rademacher complexity, we show that a test error bound of a specific type of multi-scale GNNs that decreases corresponding to the number of node aggregations under some conditions. Our results offer theoretical explanations for the effectiveness of the multi-scale structure against the over-smoothing problem. We apply boosting algorithms to the training of multi-scale GNNs for real-world node prediction tasks. We confirm that its performance is comparable to existing GNNs, and the practical behaviors are consistent with theoretical observations. Code is available at https://github.com/delta2323/GB-GNN.

paragraphs: Repeatedly aggregating information across a graph can make node representations overly similar, a problem called over-smoothing. Multi-scale graph neural networks are a promising response, but their empirical success has lacked a clear learning-theoretic explanation. This paper analyzes optimization and generalization for transductive learning algorithms that include these networks.

The authors use boosting theory to establish convergence of training error under weak learning-type conditions. They combine this analysis with generalization gap bounds expressed through transductive Rademacher complexity. For a particular type of multi-scale graph network, the resulting test error bound decreases as the number of node aggregations increases, provided certain conditions hold. The conclusion therefore concerns a specified architecture and conditional bound.

This gives a theoretical account of how multi-scale structure can help counter over-smoothing while benefiting from further aggregation. The authors also train multi-scale networks using boosting algorithms on real-world node prediction tasks. Performance is comparable to existing graph neural networks, and the observed practical behavior agrees with their theoretical analysis. The empirical finding supports the explanation without claiming universal superiority.
summary.tldr: Boosting-based analysis gives conditional optimization and generalization guarantees explaining why multi-scale graph networks can resist over-smoothing.

title: Optimization and Generalization Analysis of Transduction through Gradient Boosting and Application to Multi-scale Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student network using a teacher’s soft outputs, which convey more than a single class label. Although this approach has worked for model compression and knowledge transfer, its theoretical explanation has been less developed. This paper studies distillation in wide neural networks through a neural tangent kernel approximation.

That approximation represents the network as a linear model built from its random features. Within this linearized setting, the authors derive a transfer risk bound and introduce data inefficiency, a measure of how difficult a task is to learn from data. The measure provides a way to analyze how the choice of training targets affects learning.

For a perfect teacher, the analysis shows that using a high proportion of soft labels can be beneficial. For an imperfect teacher, hard labels can correct erroneous teacher predictions. These findings explain why combining hard and soft labels can be useful: the teacher provides guidance, while ground-truth labels can counter its mistakes. The conclusions are developed through the paper’s wide-network, linearized analysis.
summary.tldr: A linearized analysis of wide networks explains when teacher soft labels help and how hard labels can correct an imperfect teacher.

title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher

abstract: Hyperparameter optimization of neural networks can be elegantly formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. While research on bilevel optimization of neural networks has been dominated by implicit differentiation and unrolling, hypernetworks such as Self-Tuning Networks (STNs) have recently gained traction due to their ability to amortize the optimization of the inner objective. In this paper, we diagnose several subtle pathologies in the training of STNs. Based on these observations, we propose the Delta-STN, an improved hypernetwork architecture which stabilizes training and optimizes hyperparameters much more efficiently than STNs. The key idea is to focus on accurately approximating the best-response Jacobian rather than the full best-response function; we achieve this by reparameterizing the hypernetwork and linearizing the network around the current parameters. We demonstrate empirically that our Delta-STN can tune regularization hyperparameters (e.g. weight decay, dropout, number of cutout holes) with higher accuracy, faster convergence, and improved stability compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: Choosing neural-network hyperparameters can be viewed as a nested optimization problem: network parameters are optimized within a broader search over hyperparameters. Self-Tuning Networks use a hypernetwork to amortize the inner optimization. This paper identifies training pathologies in that approach and develops an architecture intended to make the process more stable and efficient.

Delta-STN changes what the hypernetwork must approximate accurately. Instead of concentrating on the entire best-response function, which describes optimized network parameters across hyperparameter choices, it focuses on the best-response Jacobian. This Jacobian describes how those parameters respond locally to hyperparameter changes. The method obtains this focus by reparameterizing the hypernetwork and linearizing the network around its current parameters.

Experiments evaluate tuning regularization choices such as weight decay, dropout, and the number of cutout holes. The authors report higher accuracy, faster convergence, and improved stability compared with existing approaches. These findings support the practical value of approximating local response information carefully, rather than requiring an equally accurate approximation of the full parameter-response function.
summary.tldr: Delta-STN improves hyperparameter tuning by focusing its hypernetwork on local parameter responses, yielding faster and more stable optimization in experiments.

title: Delta-STN: Efficient Bilevel Optimization for Neural Networks using Structured Response Jacobians

abstract: Existing semi-supervised learning (SSL) algorithms use a single weight to balance the loss of labeled and unlabeled examples, i.e., all unlabeled examples are equally weighted. But not all unlabeled data are equal. In this paper we study how to use a different weight for “every” unlabeled example. Manual tuning of all those weights -- as done in prior work -- is no longer possible. Instead, we adjust those weights via an algorithm based on the influence function, a measure of a model's dependency on one training example. To make the approach efficient, we propose a fast and effective approximation of the influence function. We demonstrate that this technique outperforms state-of-the-art methods on semi-supervised image and language classification tasks.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled examples with examples whose labels are unavailable. Common approaches use one weight to balance the labeled and unlabeled losses, giving every unlabeled example the same relative importance. This paper asks whether training can benefit from assigning a separate weight to each unlabeled example.

With one adjustable weight per example, manual tuning is no longer practical. The authors instead update the weights using an influence-function-based algorithm. An influence function measures how dependent a model is on an individual training observation, supplying a way to reason about examples separately. To make this approach efficient, the paper introduces a fast approximation to the influence function.

The method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches on semi-supervised image and language classification tasks. These results support replacing a single shared balance with learned example-specific contributions. The contribution combines that finer control over unlabeled data with an approximation that makes the weighting procedure practical, rather than leaving the additional weights as a large manual tuning problem.
summary.tldr: An efficient influence-function approximation learns separate weights for unlabeled examples and improves semi-supervised image and language classification.

title: Not All Unlabeled Data are Equal: Learning to Weight Data in Semi-supervised Learning

abstract: Over-parametrization is an important technique in training neural networks. In both theory and practice, training a larger network allows the optimization algorithm to avoid bad local optimal solutions. In this paper we study a closely related tensor decomposition problem: given an $l$-th order tensor in $(R^d)^{\otimes l}$ of rank $r$ (where $r\ll d$), can variants of gradient descent find a rank $m$ decomposition where $m > r$? We show that in a lazy training regime (similar to the NTK regime for neural networks) one needs at least $m = \Omega(d^{l-1})$, while a variant of gradient descent can find an approximate tensor when $m = O^*(r^{2.5l}\log d)$. Our results show that gradient descent on over-parametrized objective could go beyond the lazy training regime and utilize certain low-rank structure in the data.

paragraphs: This paper uses tensor decomposition to study why over-parameterized optimization can benefit from moving beyond lazy training. The task is to represent an order-l tensor with dimension d and rank r using m components, where the underlying rank is much smaller than the dimension and m exceeds r. Extra components provide flexibility during optimization.

The authors prove a large requirement for a lazy training regime analogous to the neural tangent kernel regime in neural networks: m must be at least on the order of d raised to l minus one. They then show that a variant of gradient descent can approximate the tensor using m = O*(r^(2.5l) log d), giving a substantially different dependence on dimension and rank.

This comparison demonstrates that over-parameterized gradient-based optimization can exploit low-rank structure beyond what the studied lazy regime permits. The result concerns approximate tensor recovery by a particular gradient-descent variant. Its broader significance is to provide a concrete setting where analysis beyond lazy training reveals capabilities that a lazy-regime description would miss.
summary.tldr: A tensor-decomposition analysis shows that a gradient-descent variant can exploit low-rank structure with fewer components than lazy training requires.

title: Beyond Lazy Training for Over-parameterized Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Collecting training data from untrusted sources exposes machine learning services to poisoning adversaries, who maliciously manipulate training data to degrade the model accuracy. When trained on offline datasets, poisoning adversaries have to inject the poisoned data in advance before training, and the order of feeding these poisoned batches into the model is stochastic. In contrast, practical systems are more usually trained/fine-tuned on sequentially captured real-time data, in which case poisoning adversaries could dynamically poison each data batch according to the current model state. In this paper, we focus on the real-time settings and propose a new attacking strategy, which affiliates an accumulative phase with poisoning attacks to secretly (i.e., without affecting accuracy) magnify the destructive effect of a (poisoned) trigger batch. By mimicking online learning and federated learning on MNIST and CIFAR-10, we show that model accuracy significantly drops by a single update step on the trigger batch after the accumulative phase. Our work validates that a well-designed but straightforward attacking strategy can dramatically amplify the poisoning effects, with no need to explore complex techniques.

paragraphs: This paper studies poisoning attacks against models trained or fine-tuned on incoming data. In this setting, an attacker can adapt poisoned batches to the model’s current state. That differs from poisoning a fixed offline dataset, where malicious examples must be prepared before training and may reach the model in an unpredictable order.

The proposed strategy adds an accumulative preparation phase before a poisoned trigger batch. During preparation, the attack preserves accuracy while making the model more vulnerable to the later trigger. Its central idea is that the effects of malicious training data can build up without immediately appearing as worse predictive performance.

Experiments mimicking online and federated learning on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show a substantial accuracy drop after a single update using the trigger batch. These results demonstrate that a relatively straightforward strategy can amplify poisoning damage in the studied settings. They also show why accuracy during the preparation phase does not reveal the full effect: the visible degradation arrives only after the model encounters the trigger.
summary.tldr: An accumulative poisoning strategy preserves accuracy during preparation while amplifying the damage caused by a later poisoned training batch.

title: Accumulative Poisoning Attacks on Real-time Data

abstract: For many reinforcement learning (RL) applications, specifying a reward is difficult. In this paper, we consider an RL setting where the agent can obtain information about the reward only by querying an expert that can, for example, evaluate individual states or provide binary preferences over trajectories. From such expensive feedback, we aim to learn a model of the reward function that allows standard RL algorithms to achieve high expected return with as few expert queries as possible. For this purpose, we propose Information Directed Reward Learning (IDRL), which uses a Bayesian model of the reward function and selects queries that maximize the information gain about the difference in return between potentially optimal policies. In contrast to prior active reward learning methods designed for specific types of queries, IDRL naturally accommodates different query types. Moreover, by shifting the focus from reducing the reward approximation error to improving the policy induced by the reward model, it achieves similar or better performance with significantly fewer queries. We support our findings with extensive evaluations in multiple environments and with different types of queries.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs a reward signal that tells an agent which outcomes are desirable, but specifying that signal can be difficult. This paper studies a setting where information about rewards comes only from asking an expert. The expert might assess individual states or choose between two trajectories. Because this feedback is expensive, the goal is to learn a useful reward model with few queries.

The proposed method, Information Directed Reward Learning (IDRL), maintains a Bayesian reward model, representing uncertainty about the reward function. It selects questions to maximize information about differences in expected return between policies that could be optimal. This directs feedback toward uncertainty relevant to choosing how the agent should behave. A standard reinforcement learning algorithm can then use the learned reward model.

The approach matters because improving reward estimates and improving the resulting policy are different objectives. IDRL focuses on the latter and accommodates different kinds of expert questions. Across evaluations involving multiple environments and query types, the authors report similar or better performance with significantly fewer queries than prior active reward learning methods. These findings support selecting feedback for its usefulness in comparing promising policies.
summary.tldr: IDRL selects expert questions that clarify which promising policies have higher returns, achieving similar or better performance with significantly fewer queries in the reported evaluations.

title: Information Directed Reward Learning for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Numerous models for supervised and reinforcement learning benefit from combinations of discrete and continuous model components. End-to-end learnable discrete-continuous models are compositional, tend to generalize better, and are more interpretable. A popular approach to building discrete-continuous computation graphs is that of integrating discrete probability distributions into neural networks using stochastic softmax tricks. Prior work has mainly focused on computation graphs with a single discrete component on each of the graph's execution paths. We analyze the behavior of more complex stochastic computations graphs with multiple sequential discrete components. We show that it is challenging to optimize the parameters of these models, mainly due to small gradients and local minima. We then propose two new strategies to overcome these challenges. First, we show that increasing the scale parameter of the Gumbel noise perturbations during training improves the learning behavior. Second, we propose dropout residual connections specifically tailored to stochastic, discrete-continuous computation graphs. With an extensive set of experiments, we show that we can train complex discrete-continuous models which one cannot train with standard stochastic softmax tricks. We also show that complex discrete-stochastic models generalize better than their continuous counterparts on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Models that combine discrete choices with continuous neural computations can offer compositional structure and better interpretability. A common training approach uses stochastic softmax tricks to integrate discrete distributions into neural networks. This paper investigates what happens when several discrete components occur sequentially along a computation path, extending beyond the simpler structures emphasized in earlier work.

The analysis identifies small gradients and local minima as major obstacles to optimizing these deeper combinations of discrete and continuous operations. The authors propose two remedies: increasing the scale of Gumbel noise perturbations during training, and adding dropout residual connections designed specifically for stochastic discrete-continuous computation graphs. Both changes target the difficulty of learning through multiple discrete stages.

Experiments show that these strategies train complex models that standard stochastic softmax methods cannot successfully train in the studied settings. The resulting discrete-stochastic models also generalize better than continuous counterparts on several benchmarks. The findings suggest that optimization design is crucial to realizing the potential of richer discrete-continuous architectures.
summary.tldr: Stronger Gumbel perturbations and tailored residual connections make complex discrete-continuous networks easier to train.

title: Efficient Learning of Discrete-Continuous Computation Graphs

abstract: Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs) are a powerful approach to unsupervised learning. They enable scalable approximate posterior inference in latent-variable models using variational inference. A VAE posits a variational family parameterized by a deep neural network---called an encoder---that takes data as input. This encoder is shared across all the observations, which amortizes the cost of inference. However the encoder of a VAE has the undesirable property that it maps a given observation and a semantics-preserving transformation of it to different latent representations. This "inconsistency" of the encoder lowers the quality of the learned representations, especially for downstream tasks, and also negatively affects generalization. In this paper, we propose a regularization method to enforce consistency in VAEs. The idea is to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the variational distribution when conditioning on the observation and the variational distribution when conditioning on a random semantics-preserving transformation of this observation. This regularization is applicable to any VAE. In our experiments we apply it to four different VAE variants on several benchmark datasets and found it always improves the quality of the learned representations but also leads to better generalization. In particular, when applied to the Nouveau VAE (NVAE), our regularization method yields state-of-the-art performance on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CELEBA. We also applied our method to 3D data and found it learns representations of superior quality as measured by accuracy on a downstream classification task. Finally, we show our method can even outperform the triplet loss, an advanced and popular contrastive learning-based method for representation learning.

paragraphs: A variational auto-encoder uses a shared encoder to infer a distribution over hidden representations for each observation. Sharing this encoder makes inference scalable, but does not ensure that two versions of the same meaningful content receive consistent representations. The paper identifies disagreement under meaning-preserving transformations as a problem for representation quality and generalization.

The proposed regularizer compares the encoder's distribution for an observation with its distribution for a randomly transformed version. Training minimizes their Kullback–Leibler divergence, encouraging agreement at the distribution level. The key requirement is that the transformation preserve semantics: the regularizer is intended to suppress sensitivity to changes that should not alter what the observation means.

The authors describe the regularizer as applicable to any VAE and test it on four variants. Representation quality improves throughout their experiments, alongside better generalization. Applied to NVAE, it achieves reported state-of-the-art results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CELEBA. Experiments on 3D data also show better downstream classification, and additional comparisons show that the method can outperform triplet-loss representation learning.
summary.tldr: Encouraging a VAE to encode meaning-preserving transformations consistently improves representations and generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Consistency Regularization for Variational Auto-Encoders

abstract: We present a new perspective of achieving image synthesis by viewing this task as a visual token generation problem. Different from existing paradigms that directly synthesize a full image from a single input (e.g., a latent code), the new formulation enables a flexible local manipulation for different image regions, which makes it possible to learn content-aware and fine-grained style control for image synthesis. Specifically, it takes as input a sequence of latent tokens to predict the visual tokens for synthesizing an image. Under this perspective, we propose a token-based generator (i.e., TokenGAN). Particularly, the TokenGAN inputs two semantically different visual tokens, i.e., the learned constant content tokens and the style tokens from the latent space. Given a sequence of style tokens, the TokenGAN is able to control the image synthesis by assigning the styles to the content tokens by attention mechanism with a Transformer. We conduct extensive experiments and show that the proposed TokenGAN has achieved state-of-the-art results on several widely-used image synthesis benchmarks, including FFHQ and LSUN CHURCH with different resolutions. In particular, the generator is able to synthesize high-fidelity images with (1024x1024) size, dispensing with convolutions entirely.

paragraphs: This paper treats image synthesis as generating visual tokens from a sequence of latent tokens. The formulation creates opportunities to manipulate different image regions locally and learn fine-grained style control that depends on content. It changes how the generator organizes its input and intermediate representation, making regional control an explicit part of the synthesis process.

The resulting generator, TokenGAN, uses two semantically different token types: learned constant content tokens and style tokens drawn from latent space. A Transformer attention mechanism assigns styles to content tokens. This supplies a mechanism for deciding how the style information should influence different content components when constructing an image.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results on several image-synthesis benchmarks, including FFHQ and LSUN CHURCH at different resolutions. The generator also produces high-fidelity images at 1024 by 1024 pixels without using convolutions. These results demonstrate that the proposed token-and-attention formulation can support high-resolution synthesis while providing the local manipulation capabilities that motivate the approach.
summary.tldr: TokenGAN uses Transformer attention to assign style tokens to content tokens, enabling fine-grained control and high-resolution image synthesis without convolutions.

title: Improving Visual Quality of Image Synthesis by A Token-based Generator with Transformers

abstract: We study the inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) problem under a transition dynamics mismatch between the expert and the learner. Specifically, we consider the Maximum Causal Entropy (MCE) IRL learner model and provide a tight upper bound on the learner's performance degradation based on the $\ell_1$-distance between the transition dynamics of the expert and the learner. Leveraging insights from the Robust RL literature, we propose a robust MCE IRL algorithm, which is a principled approach to help with this mismatch. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the stable performance of our algorithm compared to the standard MCE IRL algorithm under transition dynamics mismatches in both finite and continuous MDP problems.
originalAbstract: We study the inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) problem under a transition dynamics mismatch between the expert and the learner. Specifically, we consider the Maximum Causal Entropy (MCE) IRL learner model and provide a tight upper bound on the learner's performance degradation based on the $\ell_1$-distance between the transition dynamics of the expert and the learner. Leveraging insights from the Robust RL literature, we propose a robust MCE IRL algorithm, which is a principled approach to help with this mismatch. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the stable performance of our algorithm compared to the standard MCE IRL algorithm under transition dynamics mismatches in both finite and continuous MDP problems.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning uses expert behavior to learn about the objective behind that behavior. This paper studies what happens when the expert and learner have different transition dynamics: the same action can lead to different outcomes in their respective environments. Such a mismatch can reduce the learner’s performance even when expert demonstrations are available.

The analysis focuses on Maximum Causal Entropy inverse reinforcement learning. The authors derive a tight upper bound on performance degradation in terms of the L1 distance between expert and learner transition dynamics. This connects the extent of environmental mismatch to a quantitative limit on the resulting loss in performance.

Using ideas from robust reinforcement learning, the paper then proposes a robust version of the MCE IRL algorithm to address the mismatch. Experiments cover both finite and continuous MDP problems and show stable performance compared with standard MCE IRL under differing dynamics. The contribution pairs a theoretical account of mismatch-related degradation with a principled algorithm whose reported behavior is more stable in those settings.
summary.tldr: A robust Maximum Causal Entropy IRL method addresses expert–learner dynamics mismatch, supported by a tight degradation bound and empirical stability.

title: Robust Inverse Reinforcement Learning under Transition Dynamics Mismatch

abstract: The joint probabilities of potential outcomes are fundamental components of causal inference in the sense that (i) if they are identifiable, then the causal risk is also identifiable, but not vise versa (Pearl, 2009; Tian and Pearl, 2000) and (ii) they enable us to evaluate the probabilistic aspects of ``necessity'', ``sufficiency'', and ``necessity and sufficiency'', which are important concepts of successful explanation (Watson, et al., 2020). However, because they are not identifiable without any assumptions, various assumptions have been utilized to evaluate the joint probabilities of potential outcomes, e.g., the assumption of monotonicity (Pearl, 2009; Tian and Pearl, 2000), the independence between potential outcomes (Robins and Richardson, 2011), the condition of gain equality (Li and Pearl, 2019), and the specific functional relationships between cause and effect (Pearl, 2009). Unlike existing identification conditions, in order to evaluate the joint probabilities of potential outcomes without such assumptions, this paper proposes two types of novel identification conditions using covariate information. In addition, when the joint probabilities of potential outcomes are identifiable through the proposed conditions, the estimation problem of the joint probabilities of potential outcomes reduces to that of singular models and thus they can not be evaluated by standard statistical estimation methods. To solve the problem, this paper proposes a new statistical estimation method based on the augmented Lagrangian method and shows the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators. Given space constraints, the proofs, the details on the statistical estimation method, some numerical experiments, and the case study are provided in the supplementary material.

The contribution is a different route to identification that avoids those listed assumptions while still requiring the proposed conditions.

The authors develop an estimator using the augmented Lagrangian method and establish its asymptotic normality. The work therefore addresses both when the causal quantities can be recovered and how to estimate them in the resulting nonstandard statistical setting.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces covariate-based identification conditions for joint potential outcomes and an estimator suited to the resulting singular models.

title: Identification and Estimation of Joint Probabilities of Potential Outcomes in Observational Studies with Covariate Information

abstract: We study the online learning with feedback graphs framework introduced by Mannor and Shamir (2011), in which the feedback received by the online learner is specified by a graph $G$ over the available actions. We develop an algorithm that simultaneously achieves regret bounds of the form: $O(\sqrt{\theta(G) T})$ with adversarial losses; $O(\theta(G)\mathrm{polylog}{T})$ with stochastic losses; and $O(\theta(G)\mathrm{polylog}{T} + \sqrt{\theta(G) C})$ with stochastic losses subject to $C$ adversarial corruptions. Here, $\theta(G)$ is the $clique~covering~number$ of the graph $G$. Our algorithm is an instantiation of Follow-the-Regularized-Leader with a novel regularization that can be seen as a product of a Tsallis entropy component (inspired by Zimmert and Seldin (2019)) and a Shannon entropy component (analyzed in the corrupted stochastic case by Amir et al. (2020)), thus subtly interpolating between the two forms of entropies. One of our key technical contributions is in establishing the convexity of this regularizer and controlling its inverse Hessian, despite its complex product structure.

paragraphs: In online learning with feedback graphs, a graph over actions specifies what feedback the learner receives. This paper develops one algorithm with regret guarantees for adversarial losses, stochastic losses, and stochastic losses affected by adversarial corruption. The objective is to retain protection against difficult sequences while benefiting from more regular data.

The bounds depend on the graph's clique covering number, denoted theta, and the number of rounds T. Adversarial regret is of order square root of theta times T. Stochastic regret is theta times a polylogarithmic function of T. With C adversarial corruptions, the guarantee adds a square-root-of-theta-times-C term to the stochastic bound, explicitly accounting for the corruption level.

The algorithm uses Follow-the-Regularized-Leader with a regularizer combining Tsallis and Shannon entropy components through a product structure. Establishing convexity and controlling the inverse Hessian of this regularizer are key technical contributions. These properties support the simultaneous guarantees, connecting a carefully designed optimization penalty to adaptation across different loss environments.
summary.tldr: A combined-entropy regularizer gives one feedback-graph learning algorithm regret guarantees for adversarial, stochastic, and corrupted stochastic losses.

title: Towards Best-of-All-Worlds Online Learning with Feedback Graphs

abstract: Diffusion models are recent state-of-the-art methods for image generation and likelihood estimation. In this work, we generalize continuous-time diffusion models to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds and derive a variational framework for likelihood estimation. Computationally, we propose new methods for computing the Riemannian divergence which is needed for likelihood estimation. Moreover, in generalizing the Euclidean case, we prove that maximizing this variational lower-bound is equivalent to Riemannian score matching. Empirically, we demonstrate the expressive power of Riemannian diffusion models on a wide spectrum of smooth manifolds, such as spheres, tori, hyperboloids, and orthogonal groups. Our proposed method achieves new state-of-the-art likelihoods on all benchmarks.

paragraphs: Diffusion models are powerful tools for generation and likelihood estimation, but the geometry of the space being modeled matters. This paper extends continuous-time diffusion models to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds. These spaces include smooth geometric structures beyond ordinary Euclidean space, allowing the modeling framework to address data with corresponding geometric organization.

The authors derive a variational framework for estimating likelihoods and introduce methods for computing Riemannian divergence, a quantity required by that framework. They also prove that maximizing the resulting variational lower bound is equivalent to Riemannian score matching. This establishes a theoretical connection between the likelihood objective and a score-based learning objective in the manifold setting.

Experiments demonstrate the models on spheres, tori, hyperboloids, and orthogonal groups. The method achieves the best reported likelihoods on every benchmark evaluated in the paper. Together, the results show both a mathematical extension of diffusion modeling and empirical expressive power across several smooth spaces, with the benchmark claim applying to the evaluations actually conducted.
summary.tldr: The paper extends continuous-time diffusion modeling to Riemannian manifolds and connects variational likelihood learning to Riemannian score matching.

title: Riemannian Diffusion Models

abstract: Generating temporally coherent high fidelity video is an important milestone in generative modeling research. We make progress towards this milestone by proposing a diffusion model for video generation that shows very promising initial results. Our model is a natural extension of the standard image diffusion architecture, and it enables jointly training from image and video data, which we find to reduce the variance of minibatch gradients and speed up optimization. To generate long and higher resolution videos we introduce a new conditional sampling technique for spatial and temporal video extension that performs better than previously proposed methods. We present the first results on a large text-conditioned video generation task, as well as state-of-the-art results on established benchmarks for video prediction and unconditional video generation. Supplementary material is available at https://video-diffusion.github.io/.

This paper extends an image diffusion architecture to video and presents promising initial results toward that goal. The architecture supports joint training on images and videos, allowing both kinds of data to contribute to the same model.

The authors find that this joint training reduces minibatch-gradient variance and speeds optimization. They also introduce conditional sampling for extending videos in space and time, addressing the generation of longer and higher-resolution outputs. The proposed sampling technique performs better than previously proposed methods in the reported comparison.

These findings cover both conditioning on available information and generating videos without such conditioning. The contribution combines an architectural extension, a useful joint-training strategy, and a sampling method for expanding outputs, while describing the broader progress in high-fidelity coherent video generation as promising.
summary.tldr: A video diffusion architecture combines image-video training with conditional sampling for longer, higher-resolution generation.

title: Video Diffusion Models

abstract: Predictive coding (PC) has emerged as an influential normative model of neural computation with numerous extensions and applications. As such, much effort has been put into mapping PC faithfully onto the cortex, but there are issues that remain unresolved or controversial. In particular, current implementations often involve separate value and error neurons and require symmetric forward and backward weights across different brain regions. These features have not been experimentally confirmed. In this work, we show that the PC framework in the linear regime can be modified to map faithfully onto the cortical hierarchy in a manner compatible with empirical observations. By employing a disentangling-inspired constraint on hidden-layer neural activities, we derive an upper bound for the PC objective. Optimization of this upper bound leads to an algorithm that shows the same performance as the original objective and maps onto a biologically plausible network. The units of this network can be interpreted as multi-compartmental neurons with non-Hebbian learning rules, with a remarkable resemblance to recent experimental findings. There exist prior models which also capture these features, but they are phenomenological, while our work is a normative derivation. This allows us to determine which features are necessary for the functioning of the model. For instance, the network we derive does not involve one-to-one connectivity or signal multiplexing, which the phenomenological models require, indicating that these features are not necessary for learning in the cortex. The normative nature of our algorithm in the simplified linear case also allows us to prove interesting properties of the framework and analytically understand the computational role of our network's components. The parameters of our network have natural interpretations as physiological quantities in a multi-compartmental model of pyramidal neurons, providing a concrete link between PC and experimental measurements carried out in the cortex.

This paper asks whether a modified predictive-coding model can better match observed cortical organization while retaining its computational purpose.

The contribution is a principled bridge between a learning objective and a proposed biological implementation.
summary.tldr: A constrained linear predictive-coding objective yields a network with biologically interpretable components and performance matching the original objective.

title: Constrained Predictive Coding as a Biologically Plausible Model of the Cortical Hierarchy

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essentially a process of transferring a teacher model's behavior, e.g., network response, to a student model. The network response serves as additional supervision to formulate the machine domain, which uses the data collected from the human domain as a transfer set. Traditional KD methods hold an underlying assumption that the data collected in both human domain and machine domain are both independent and identically distributed (IID). We point out that this naive assumption is unrealistic and there is indeed a transfer gap between the two domains. Although the gap offers the student model external knowledge from the machine domain, the imbalanced teacher knowledge would make us incorrectly estimate how much to transfer from teacher to student per sample on the non-IID transfer set. To tackle this challenge, we propose Inverse Probability Weighting Distillation (IPWD) that estimates the propensity of a training sample belonging to the machine domain, and assigns its inverse amount to compensate for under-represented samples. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet demonstrate the effectiveness of \ours~for both two-stage distillation and one-stage self-distillation.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using additional supervision from a teacher's responses. This paper examines a mismatch between the human domain supplying the training data and the machine domain represented by teacher behavior. The authors argue that treating these domains as independent and identically distributed overlooks a meaningful transfer gap.

That gap can supply useful external knowledge, but the teacher's knowledge may be unevenly represented across examples. As a result, the amount transferred from teacher to student can be misestimated for individual samples. The proposed Inverse Probability Weighting Distillation method estimates a sample's propensity to belong to the machine domain and weights it by the inverse of that estimate.

The weighting is designed to compensate for underrepresented samples during knowledge transfer. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet demonstrate effectiveness in both two-stage distillation and one-stage self-distillation. The paper therefore treats the balance of teacher-provided supervision as a learning issue in its own right, using estimated domain propensity to adjust how strongly different samples contribute to distillation.
summary.tldr: Inverse Probability Weighting Distillation adjusts sample weights to compensate for uneven teacher knowledge across a human-to-machine transfer gap.

title: Respecting Transfer Gap in Knowledge Distillation

abstract: We study a class of generalized linear programs (GLP) in a large-scale setting, which includes simple, possibly nonsmooth convex regularizer and simple convex set constraints. By reformulating (GLP) as an equivalent convex-concave min-max problem, we show that the linear structure in the problem can be used to design an efficient, scalable first-order algorithm, to which we give the name Coordinate Linear Variance Reduction (CLVR; pronounced ``clever''). CLVR yields improved complexity results for (GLP) that depend on the max row norm of the linear constraint matrix in (GLP) rather than the spectral norm. When the regularization terms and constraints are separable, CLVR admits an efficient lazy update strategy that makes its complexity bounds scale with the number of nonzero elements of the linear constraint matrix in (GLP) rather than the matrix dimensions. On the other hand, for the special case of linear programs, by exploiting sharpness, we propose a restart scheme for CLVR to obtain empirical linear convergence. Then we show that Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problems with ambiguity sets based on both $f$-divergence and Wasserstein metrics can be reformulated as (GLPs) by introducing sparsely connected auxiliary variables. We complement our theoretical guarantees with numerical experiments that verify our algorithm's practical effectiveness, in terms of wall-clock time and number of data passes.

The problem class permits simple convex constraints and regularizers that may be nonsmooth. By expressing these programs as equivalent convex-concave min-max problems, the authors use their linear structure to design a scalable first-order optimization algorithm.

The complexity guarantees depend on the largest row norm of the constraint matrix rather than its spectral norm. When the regularization and constraints separate across components, a lazy update strategy makes the bounds scale with the number of nonzero matrix entries instead of the matrix dimensions. They also reformulate distributionally robust optimization problems with f-divergence or Wasserstein ambiguity sets as generalized linear programs, introducing sparsely connected auxiliary variables. Numerical experiments assess practical effectiveness through elapsed time and data passes, complementing the complexity analysis and showing applications beyond the initial formulation.
summary.tldr: CLVR exploits linear and, under separability, sparse structure to improve generalized linear programming complexity and practical optimization performance.

title: Coordinate Linear Variance Reduction for Generalized Linear Programming

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims at learning policies from previously collected static trajectory data without interacting with the real environment. Recent works provide a novel perspective by viewing offline RL as a generic sequence generation problem, adopting sequence models such as Transformer architecture to model distributions over trajectories and repurposing beam search as a planning algorithm. However, the training datasets utilized in general offline RL tasks are quite limited and often suffering from insufficient distribution coverage, which could me harmful to training sequence generation models yet has not drawn enough attention in the previous works. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm named Bootstrapped Transformer, which incorporates the idea of bootstrapping and leverages the learned model to self-generate more offline data to further boost the training of sequence model. We conduct extensive experiments on two offline RL benchmarks and demonstrate that our model can largely remedy the limitations of the existing offline RL training and beat other strong baseline methods. We also analyze the generated pseudo data and the revealed characteristics may shed some light on offline RL training.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains an agent from previously collected trajectories without allowing new interaction with the environment. One approach treats these trajectories as sequences: a Transformer learns their distribution, and sequence search becomes a way to plan actions. The paper focuses on a weakness of this approach: limited datasets may cover too little of the behavior the sequence model needs to learn.

Bootstrapped Transformer uses the learned model to generate additional artificial trajectory data, then uses that data to further train the sequence model. This creates a feedback process in which the model contributes examples to its own training. The additional examples come from the model rather than fresh experience in the real environment, preserving the offline setting.

Experiments on two offline reinforcement learning benchmarks report substantial improvements over existing training approaches and strong competing methods. The authors also examine characteristics of the generated data to better understand its contribution. These findings support model-generated training data as a useful way to address limited coverage in the evaluated settings, without establishing that it can replace arbitrary missing experience.
summary.tldr: Bootstrapped Transformer improves offline reinforcement learning by generating additional training trajectories with its own learned model.

title: Bootstrapped Transformer for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Both supervised and unsupervised machine learning algorithms have been used to learn partition-based index structures for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. Existing supervised algorithms formulate the learning task as finding a partition in which the nearest neighbors of a training set point belong to the same partition element as the point itself, so that the nearest neighbor candidates can be retrieved by naive lookup or backtracking search. We formulate candidate set selection in ANN search directly as a multilabel classification problem where the labels correspond to the nearest neighbors of the query point, and interpret the partitions as partitioning classifiers for solving this task. Empirical results suggest that the natural classifier based on this interpretation leads to strictly improved performance when combined with any unsupervised or supervised partitioning strategy. We also prove a sufficient condition for consistency of a partitioning classifier for ANN search, and illustrate the result by verifying this condition for chronological $k$-d trees.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest neighbor search tries to find nearby data points without examining every possible match. Partition-based indexes make this manageable by dividing the search space. Existing supervised approaches learn partitions that place a training point together with its neighbors, making those neighbors accessible through lookup or backtracking.

This paper changes the learning target: it treats selecting candidate neighbors as a multilabel classification problem. Each possible neighbor corresponds to a label, and a query can have several correct labels. The partitions then act as classifiers for predicting which candidates should be considered. This connects the index structure directly to the candidate-selection task, rather than relying only on shared partition membership.

The empirical results suggest that the resulting classifier improves performance when paired with supervised or unsupervised partitioning strategies. The authors also establish a sufficient condition for a partitioning classifier to be consistent and verify it for chronological k-d trees. That condition provides a theoretical route to consistency; it does not establish that every partitioning strategy automatically satisfies it.
summary.tldr: Recasting candidate selection as multilabel classification improves partition-based neighbor search empirically and yields a sufficient condition for consistency.

title: A Multilabel Classification Framework for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing coupled networks (e.g., biological neural networks) connecting large numbers of variables (e.g.,nerve cells), of which state evolution is governed by dissipative dynamics consisting of strong self-drive (dominants the evolution) and weak coupling-drive. The core difficulty is sparseness of coupling effect that emerges (the coupling force is significant) only momentarily and otherwise remains quiescent in time series (e.g., neuronal activity sequence). Here we learn the idea from attention mechanism to guide the classifier to make inference focusing on the critical regions of time series data where coupling effect may manifest. Specifically, attention coefficients are assigned autonomously by artificial neural networks trained to maximise the Attentive Transfer Entropy (ATEn), which is a novel generalization of the iconic transfer entropy metric. Our results show that, without any prior knowledge of dynamics, ATEn explicitly identifies areas where the strength of coupling-drive is distinctly greater than zero. This innovation substantially improves reconstruction performance for both synthetic and real directed coupling networks using data generated by neuronal models widely used in neuroscience.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reconstruct directed connections among variables from their changing states, with neural networks in biology as a motivating example. The difficult setting is one where each variable's own dynamics dominate its behavior and interactions with other variables are weak. Evidence of those interactions appears only briefly, leaving much of the time series relatively uninformative about the connections.

The proposed Attentive Transfer Entropy, or ATEn, adapts transfer entropy by incorporating learned attention. Artificial neural networks assign attention coefficients and are trained to maximize this new measure. Those coefficients guide inference toward time intervals where coupling may become visible, concentrating the analysis on brief informative events within otherwise strongly self-driven activity.

The reported results show that ATEn identifies regions with distinctly nonzero coupling influence without prior knowledge of the dynamics. The authors also report substantially better reconstruction of synthetic and real directed coupling networks using data generated by neuronal models common in neuroscience. The findings support attention as a way to uncover interactions whose observable effects are sparse in time.
summary.tldr: ATEn learns to focus on brief moments of interaction, improving reconstruction of directed networks from strongly self-driven time series.

title: Attentive Transfer Entropy to Exploit Transient Emergence of Coupling Effect

abstract: Self-training and contrastive learning have emerged as leading techniques for incorporating unlabeled data, both under distribution shift (unsupervised domain adaptation) and when it is absent (semi-supervised learning). However, despite the popularity and compatibility of these techniques, their efficacy in combination remains surprisingly unexplored. In this paper, we first undertake a systematic empirical investigation of this combination, finding (i) that in domain adaptation settings, self-training and contrastive learning offer significant complementary gains; and (ii) that in semi-supervised learning settings, surprisingly, the benefits are not synergistic. Across eight distribution shift datasets (e.g., BREEDs, WILDS), we demonstrate that the combined method obtains 3--8\% higher accuracy than either approach independently. Finally, we theoretically analyze these techniques in a simplified model of distribution shift demonstrating scenarios under which the features produced by contrastive learning can yield a good initialization for self-training to further amplify gains and achieve optimal performance, even when either method alone would fail.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning and self-training both make use of unlabeled data, but their usefulness together is a separate question from their individual success. This paper systematically studies their combination in two settings: domain adaptation, where the data distribution changes, and semi-supervised learning without that distribution shift.

The experiments reveal an important distinction. Under distribution shift, the two techniques provide substantial complementary benefits. Across eight distribution-shift datasets, their combination achieves accuracy reported as 3–8% higher than either method alone. In the semi-supervised setting without shift, however, the authors do not find synergistic benefits. The practical value of combining them therefore differs across the investigated settings.

A theoretical analysis offers an explanation within a simplified model of distribution shift. It identifies scenarios where contrastive learning produces features that give self-training a useful starting point. Self-training can then strengthen those gains and reach optimal performance, even when either technique alone would fail. This is a conditional account of how the methods can cooperate, supporting the empirical finding without asserting that their combination always helps.
summary.tldr: Contrastive learning and self-training provide complementary gains under distribution shift, but the same synergy was not observed without shift.

title: Complementary Benefits of Contrastive Learning and Self-Training Under Distribution Shift

abstract: Algorithmic recommender systems such as Spotify and Netflix affect not only consumer behavior but also *producer incentives*. Producers seek to create content that will be shown by the recommendation algorithm, which can impact both the diversity and quality of their content. In this work, we investigate the resulting supply-side equilibria in personalized content recommender systems. We model the decisions of producers as choosing *multi-dimensional* content vectors and users as having *heterogenous* preferences, which contrasts with classical low-dimensional models. Multi-dimensionality and heterogeneity creates the potential for *specialization*, where different producers create different types of content at equilibrium. Using a duality argument, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for whether specialization occurs. Then, we characterize the distribution of content at equilibrium in concrete settings with two populations of users. Lastly, we show that specialization can enable producers to achieve *positive profit at equilibrium*, which means that specialization can reduce the competitiveness of the marketplace. At a conceptual level, our analysis of supply-side competition takes a step towards elucidating how personalized recommendations shape the marketplace of digital goods.

Its contribution is a theoretical account of how heterogeneous demand and multidimensional content interact with recommendation incentives to shape digital supply.
summary.tldr: A theoretical model characterizes when personalized recommendations encourage producer specialization and how that specialization can sustain positive profits.

title: Supply-Side Equilibria in Recommender Systems

abstract: Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) have recently experienced a resurgence in popularity due to their interpretability, which arises from expressing the target value as a sum of non-linear transformations of the features. Despite the current enthusiasm for GAMs, their susceptibility to concurvity — i.e., (possibly non-linear) dependencies between the features — has hitherto been largely overlooked. Here, we demonstrate how concurvity can severly impair the interpretability of GAMs and propose a remedy: a conceptually simple, yet effective regularizer which penalizes pairwise correlations of the non-linearly transformed feature variables. This procedure is applicable to any differentiable additive model, such as Neural Additive Models or NeuralProphet, and enhances interpretability by eliminating ambiguities due to self-canceling feature contributions. We validate the effectiveness of our regularizer in experiments on synthetic as well as real-world datasets for time-series and tabular data. Our experiments show that concurvity in GAMs can be reduced without significantly compromising prediction quality, improving interpretability and reducing variance in the feature importances.

paragraphs: Generalized additive models express a prediction as a sum of separate, potentially nonlinear feature contributions. That structure makes them appealing for interpretation because each contribution can be examined individually. However, dependencies between features can create concurvity: different contribution curves can compensate for one another, making the apparent explanation ambiguous even when the combined prediction remains useful.

This paper shows how seriously that ambiguity can undermine interpretation and proposes a regularizer to reduce it. The regularizer penalizes pairwise correlations between the transformed feature variables that enter the additive prediction. It therefore targets dependence in the learned contributions, including dependence arising through nonlinear transformations, rather than considering only relationships between the original input values.

The approach applies to differentiable additive models, including Neural Additive Models and NeuralProphet. Experiments use synthetic and real-world tabular and time-series data. They show that the regularizer can reduce concurvity without significantly sacrificing prediction quality, while also reducing variation in feature importance. The practical benefit is a clearer allocation of contributions among features, with less ambiguity from contributions that cancel each other.
summary.tldr: Penalizing correlations between learned feature contributions makes additive models more interpretable without significantly reducing predictive quality in the reported experiments.

title: Curve Your Enthusiasm: Concurvity Regularization in Differentiable Generalized Additive Models

abstract: In value-based deep reinforcement learning with replay memories, the batch size parameter specifies how many transitions to sample for each gradient update. Although critical to the learning process, this value is typically not adjusted when proposing new algorithms. In this work we present a broad empirical study that suggests reducing the batch size can result in a number of significant performance gains; this is surprising, as the general tendency when training neural networks is towards larger batch sizes for improved performance. We complement our experimental findings with a set of empirical analyses towards better understanding this phenomenon.
