They also reach performance comparable to QwQ-32B-Preview, the teacher that supplied the seed data. These findings support learning how much reasoning to use, with successful shorter responses providing a training signal instead of treating longer output as inherently better.
summary.tldr: Thinking-Optimal Scaling trains models on their shortest correct responses after finding that excessive reasoning length can hurt some mathematical tasks.

title: Towards Thinking-Optimal Scaling of Test-Time Compute for LLM Reasoning

abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems, predominantly trained through imitation learning, have demonstrated considerable effectiveness in leveraging large-scale expert driving data. Despite their success in open-loop evaluations, these systems often exhibit significant performance degradation in closed-loop scenarios due to causal confusion. This confusion is fundamentally exacerbated by the overreliance of the imitation learning paradigm on expert trajectories, which often contain unattributable noise and interfere with the modeling of causal relationships between environmental contexts and appropriate driving actions. To address this fundamental limitation, we propose Perception-Guided Self-Supervision (PGS)—a simple yet effective training paradigm that leverages perception outputs as the primary supervisory signals, explicitly modeling causal relationships in decision-making. The proposed framework aligns both the inputs and outputs of the decision-making module with perception results—such as lane centerlines and the predicted motions of surrounding agents—by introducing positive and negative self-supervision for the ego trajectory. This alignment is specifically designed to mitigate causal confusion arising from the inherent noise in expert trajectories. Equipped with perception-driven supervision, our method—built on a standard end-to-end architecture—achieves a Driving Score of 78.08 and a mean success rate of 48.64\% on the challenging closed-loop Bench2Drive benchmark, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods, including those employing more complex network architectures and inference pipelines. These results underscore the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed PGS framework, and point to a promising direction for addressing causal confusion and enhancing real-world generalization in autonomous driving.

summary.tldr: Perception-Guided Self-Supervision trains driving decisions around perceived road structure and agent motion, improving closed-loop results on Bench2Drive.

title: Prioritizing Perception-Guided Self-Supervision: A New Paradigm for Causal Modeling in End-to-End Autonomous Driving

abstract: We derive and investigate two DPO variants that explicitly model the possibility of declaring a tie in pair-wise comparisons. We replace the Bradley-Terry model in DPO with two well-known modeling extensions, by Rao and Kupper and by Davidson, that assign probability to ties as alternatives to clear preferences. Our experiments in neural machine translation and summarization show that explicitly labeled ties can be added to the datasets for these DPO variants without the degradation in task performance that is observed when the same tied pairs are presented to DPO. We find empirically that the inclusion of ties leads to stronger regularization with respect to the reference policy as measured by KL divergence, and we see this even for DPO in its original form. We provide a theoretical explanation for this regularization effect using ideal DPO policy theory. We further show performance improvements over DPO in translation and mathematical reasoning using our DPO variants. We find it can be beneficial to include ties in preference optimization rather than simply discard them, as is done in common practice.

paragraphs: This paper extends Direct Preference Optimization so that a comparison can explicitly declare two responses tied. Standard preference modeling emphasizes a winner and loser, while real comparisons can contain no clear preference. The authors derive two DPO variants using the Rao–Kupper and Davidson extensions of the Bradley–Terry model, both of which assign probability to ties.

In translation and summarization experiments, the variants can incorporate labeled ties without the task-performance degradation observed when the same tied pairs are given to ordinary DPO. The authors also find that including ties keeps the learned policy closer to its reference policy, as measured by KL divergence. This regularization effect appears even with the original DPO formulation.

The paper explains that effect theoretically using ideal DPO policy theory and reports improvements over DPO in translation and mathematical reasoning. Together, the results suggest that ties can carry useful training information. The supported conclusion is that retaining them can help when modeled appropriately, rather than that adding ties necessarily improves every preference-optimization task.
summary.tldr: Two tie-aware DPO variants make equal-preference comparisons usable and show benefits for regularization and several evaluated tasks.

title: On Extending Direct Preference Optimization to Accommodate Ties

abstract: Designing effective strategies for controlling epidemic spread by vaccination is an important question in epidemiology, especially in the early stages when vaccines are limited. This is a challenging question when the contact network is very heterogeneous, and strategies based on controlling network properties, such as the degree and spectral radius, have been shown to be effective. Implementation of such strategies requires detailed information on the contact structure, which might be sensitive in many applications. Our focus here is on choosing effective vaccination strategies when the edges are sensitive and differential privacy guarantees are needed. Our main contributions are $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private algorithms for designing vaccination strategies by reducing the maximum degree and spectral radius. Our key technique is a private algorithm for the multi-set multi-cover problem, which we use for controlling network properties. We evaluate privacy-utility tradeoffs of our algorithms on multiple synthetic and real-world networks, and show their effectiveness.

paragraphs: Vaccination strategies can use a contact network to identify interventions that limit epidemic spread, particularly when vaccines are scarce. The challenge is greater when contacts are distributed unevenly across people. Network properties such as maximum degree and spectral radius provide useful control targets, but selecting interventions around them requires information about potentially sensitive interpersonal contacts.

This paper develops vaccination algorithms with differential privacy guarantees for network edges. The algorithms aim to reduce maximum degree and spectral radius while protecting the contact information used in their decisions. Their central technical component is a private algorithm for a combinatorial problem called multi-set multi-cover, which the authors use to control those network properties.

The evaluation examines privacy-utility tradeoffs on both synthetic and real-world networks and reports effective strategies. The contribution connects two requirements that must be handled together: exploiting contact structure to guide vaccination and limiting what the selection process reveals about that structure. Its stated privacy protection concerns edges, matching the paper’s focus on sensitive relationships within the network.
summary.tldr: The paper develops differentially private vaccination algorithms that reduce network properties associated with epidemic spread while protecting contact edges.

title: Controlling The Spread of Epidemics on Networks with Differential Privacy

abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) remains a challenging and complex endeavor. Even fundamental questions, such as how fine-tuning affects model behavior, often require extensive empirical evaluation. In this paper, we introduce a novel perspective based on the geometric properties of contextual latent embeddings to study the effects of training and fine-tuning. To that end, we measure the local dimensions of a contextual language model's latent space and analyze their shifts during training and fine-tuning. We show that the local dimensions provide insights into the model's training dynamics and generalization ability. Specifically, the mean of the local dimensions predicts when the model’s training capabilities are exhausted, as exemplified in a dialogue state tracking task, overfitting, as demonstrated in an emotion recognition task, and grokking, as illustrated with an arithmetic task. Furthermore, our experiments suggest a practical heuristic: reductions in the mean local dimension tend to accompany and predict subsequent performance gains. Through this exploration, we aim to provide practitioners with a deeper understanding of the implications of fine-tuning on embedding spaces, facilitating informed decisions when configuring models for specific applications. The results of this work contribute to the ongoing discourse on the interpretability, adaptability, and generalizability of LLMs by bridging the gap between intrinsic model mechanisms and geometric properties in the respective embeddings.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning changes a language model’s internal representations, but understanding what those changes mean often requires extensive evaluation. This paper studies the geometry of contextual embeddings as another source of evidence. It measures local intrinsic dimensions, describing the dimensional structure around portions of the latent space, and tracks how those measurements change during training.

The authors find that mean local dimension provides information about several distinct training behaviors. Their examples connect it to exhausted training capability in dialogue state tracking, overfitting in emotion recognition, and grokking in an arithmetic task. These findings link an internal geometric measurement to changes in learning and generalization across the studied applications.

The experiments also suggest a practical heuristic: decreases in mean local dimension tend to accompany and anticipate later performance improvements. The wording matters because this is an observed tendency, not a universal rule that lower dimension guarantees a better model. The contribution offers practitioners an additional interpretive signal for understanding fine-tuning and configuring models for particular tasks.
summary.tldr: Changes in local embedding dimension provide empirical signals of training behavior, with decreases tending to precede performance gains.

title: Less is More: Local Intrinsic Dimensions of Contextual Language Models

abstract: For an LLM to correctly respond to an instruction it must understand both the semantics and the domain (i.e., subject area) of a given task-instruction pair. However, syntax can also convey implicit information. Recent work shows that \textit{syntactic templates}---frequent sequences of Part-of-Speech (PoS) tags---are prevalent in training data and often appear in model outputs. In this work we characterize syntactic templates, domain, and semantics in task-instruction pairs. We identify cases of spurious correlations between syntax and domain, where models learn to associate a domain with syntax during training; this can sometimes override prompt semantics. Using a synthetic training dataset, we find that the syntactic-domain correlation can lower performance (mean 0.51 +/- 0.06) on entity knowledge tasks in OLMo-2 models (1B-13B). We introduce an evaluation framework to detect this phenomenon in trained models, and show that it occurs on a subset of the FlanV2 dataset in open (OLMo-2-7B; Llama-4-Maverick), and closed (GPT-4o) models. Finally, we present a case study on the implications for LLM security, showing that unintended syntactic-domain correlations can be used to bypass refusals in OLMo-2-7B Instruct and GPT-4o. Our findings highlight two needs: (1) to explicitly test for syntactic-domain correlations, and (2) to ensure \textit{syntactic} diversity in training data, specifically within domains, to prevent such spurious correlations.

paragraphs: A prompt's grammatical structure can become an unintended clue about its subject area. This paper studies syntactic templates, defined as recurring sequences of part-of-speech tags, and asks whether models associate those templates with particular domains. The concern is that a learned association can sometimes outweigh what an instruction actually means.

The findings motivate explicitly testing syntax-domain correlations and increasing syntactic variety within each training domain. The broader lesson is that grammatical regularities can become shortcuts that interfere with semantic interpretation in the examined settings.
summary.tldr: Language models can learn misleading associations between grammatical patterns and subject areas that impair instruction interpretation and sometimes enable refusal bypasses.

title: Learning the Wrong Lessons: Syntactic-Domain Spurious Correlations in Language Models

abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) is a promising approach for pretraining generalist policies on large datasets of reward-free trajectories, akin to the self-supervised objectives used to train foundation models for computer vision and natural language processing. However, scaling GCRL to longer horizons remains challenging due to the combination of sparse rewards and discounting, which obscures the comparative advantages of primitive actions with respect to distant goals. Hierarchical RL methods achieve strong empirical results on long-horizon goal-reaching tasks, but their reliance on modular, timescale-specific policies and subgoal generation introduces significant additional complexity and hinders scaling to high-dimensional goal spaces. In this work, we introduce an algorithm to train a flat (non-hierarchical) goal-conditioned policy by bootstrapping on subgoal-conditioned policies with advantage-weighted importance sampling. Our approach eliminates the need for a generative model over the (sub)goal space, which we find is key for scaling to high-dimensional control in large state spaces. We further show that existing hierarchical and bootstrapping-based approaches correspond to specific design choices within our derivation. Across a comprehensive suite of state- and pixel-based locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, our method matches or surpasses state-of-the-art offline GCRL algorithms and scales to complex, long-horizon tasks where prior approaches fail. Project page: https://johnlyzhou.github.io/saw/
originalAbstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) is a promising approach for pretraining generalist policies on large datasets of reward-free trajectories, akin to the self-supervised objectives used to train foundation models for computer vision and natural language processing. However, scaling GCRL to longer horizons remains challenging due to the combination of sparse rewards and discounting, which obscures the comparative advantages of primitive actions with respect to distant goals. Hierarchical RL methods achieve strong empirical results on long-horizon goal-reaching tasks, but their reliance on modular, timescale-specific policies and subgoal generation introduces significant additional complexity and hinders scaling to high-dimensional goal spaces. In this work, we introduce an algorithm to train a flat (non-hierarchical) goal-conditioned policy by bootstrapping on subgoal-conditioned policies with advantage-weighted importance sampling. Our approach eliminates the need for a generative model over the (sub)goal space, which we find is key for scaling to high-dimensional control in large state spaces. We further show that existing hierarchical and bootstrapping-based approaches correspond to specific design choices within our derivation. Across a comprehensive suite of state- and pixel-based locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, our method matches or surpasses state-of-the-art offline GCRL algorithms and scales to complex, long-horizon tasks where prior approaches fail. Project page: https://johnlyzhou.github.io/saw/

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains policies to reach goals using previously collected trajectories without task rewards. Distant goals are difficult because sparse rewards and discounting make it hard to distinguish useful immediate actions. Hierarchical methods help, but maintaining policies at multiple timescales and generating intermediate goals adds complexity, especially when goals have many dimensions.

The paper trains a single, flat policy by bootstrapping from policies conditioned on intermediate goals. It uses advantage-weighted importance sampling to incorporate that learning signal. Crucially, the method does not require a generative model of the goal or subgoal space, which the authors identify as important for scaling control to large state spaces.

The derivation also places existing hierarchical and bootstrapping methods within a shared framework as particular design choices. Across locomotion and manipulation benchmarks using states or pixels, the proposed method matches or exceeds leading offline goal-conditioned algorithms. It also handles complex, long-horizon tasks where prior approaches fail, showing that intermediate-goal learning can support a flat policy without retaining a hierarchical policy structure.
summary.tldr: A flat goal-conditioned policy learns from subgoal-conditioned policies without a goal generator, improving scaling to long-horizon control tasks.

title: Flattening Hierarchies with Policy Bootstrapping

abstract: Time Series Forecasting (TSF) is a crucial task in various domains, yet existing TSF models rely heavily on high-quality data and insufficiently exploit all available data. This paper explores a novel self-supervised approach to re-label time series datasets by inherently constructing candidate datasets. During the optimization of a simple reconstruction network, intermediates are used as pseudo labels in a self-supervised paradigm, improving generalization for any predictor. We introduce the Self-Correction with Adaptive Mask (SCAM), which discards overfitted components and selectively replaces them with pseudo labels generated from reconstructions. Additionally, we incorporate Spectral Norm Regularization (SNR) to further suppress overfitting from a loss landscape perspective. Our experiments on eleven real-world datasets demonstrate that SCAM consistently improves the performance of various backbone models. This work offers a new perspective on constructing datasets and enhancing the generalization of TSF models through self-supervised learning. The code is available at https://github.com/SuDIS-ZJU/SCAM.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasters depend on the quality of the values used as training targets. This paper investigates whether the dataset itself can be improved through self-supervision. It constructs alternative labels from a simple reconstruction network, using intermediate results produced during optimization as candidate targets for training a forecasting model.

The proposed Self-Correction with Adaptive Mask method selectively removes components associated with overfitting and replaces them with reconstruction-derived pseudo labels. This makes correction selective rather than applying the same replacement to every part of the data. Spectral Norm Regularization adds another mechanism for suppressing overfitting, approaching the problem through the loss landscape.

Experiments on eleven real-world datasets show consistent performance improvements across various forecasting backbones. These results support the idea that better forecasting can come from changing the training targets as well as the predictor architecture. The approach offers a self-supervised route to constructing more useful datasets, with reported benefits across the different models examined in the study.
summary.tldr: SCAM improves time-series forecasting by selectively replacing overfitted target components with self-supervised reconstruction labels.

title: Not All Data are Good Labels: On the Self-supervised Labeling for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Motivated by real-world settings where data collection and policy deployment—whether for a single agent or across multiple agents—are costly, we study the problem of on-policy single-agent reinforcement learning (RL) and federated RL (FRL) with a focus on minimizing burn-in costs (the sample sizes needed to reach near-optimal regret) and policy switching or communication costs. In parallel finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with $S$ states and $A$ actions, existing methods either require superlinear burn-in costs in $S$ and $A$ or fail to achieve logarithmic switching or communication costs. We propose two novel model-free RL algorithms—Q-EarlySettled-LowCost and FedQ-EarlySettled-LowCost—that are the first in the literature to simultaneously achieve: (i) the best near-optimal regret among all known model-free RL or FRL algorithms, (ii) low burn-in cost that scales linearly with $S$ and $A$, and (iii) logarithmic policy switching cost for single-agent RL or communication cost for FRL. Additionally, we establish gap-dependent theoretical guarantees for both regret and switching/communication costs, improving or matching the best-known gap-dependent bounds.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can be expensive before it becomes effective, and changing deployed policies or communicating between agents can add further costs. This paper studies those burdens together with regret, the performance loss accumulated during learning. Its setting is on-policy learning in finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes, including a federated version with multiple agents.

The authors introduce Q-EarlySettled-LowCost and FedQ-EarlySettled-LowCost. They establish a simultaneous combination of near-optimal regret, burn-in costs that scale linearly with the numbers of states and actions, and logarithmic policy-switching or communication costs. Burn-in here measures the sample requirement for reaching near-optimal regret behavior. Earlier methods described in the paper fail to achieve this full combination.

The work also supplies gap-dependent guarantees for regret and switching or communication, matching or improving the best-known bounds. These results are theoretical guarantees within the specified decision-process setting. Their significance is the joint accounting of learning quality, initial data requirements, and operational changes, showing that model-free learning can address all three costs together.
summary.tldr: Two model-free Q-learning algorithms jointly achieve near-optimal regret, linear burn-in scaling, and logarithmic switching or communication costs in the studied setting.

title: Regret-Optimal Q-Learning with Low Cost for Single-Agent and Federated Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptive hashing has emerged as a promising approach for efficient and memory-friendly cross-domain retrieval. It leverages the model learned on labeled source domains to generate compact binary codes for unlabeled target domain samples, ensuring that semantically similar samples are mapped to nearby points in the Hamming space. Existing methods typically apply domain adaptation techniques to the feature space or the Hamming space, especially pseudo-labeling and feature alignment. However, the inherent noise of pseudo-labels and the insufficient exploration of complementary knowledge across spaces hinder the ability of the adapted model. To address these challenges, we propose a Vision-language model assisted Pseudo-labeling and Dual Space adaptation (VPDS) method. Motivated by the strong zero-shot generalization capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), VPDS leverages VLMs to calibrate pseudo-labels, thereby mitigating pseudo-label bias. Furthermore, to simultaneously utilize the semantic richness of high-dimensional feature space and preserve discriminative efficiency of low-dimensional Hamming space, we introduce a dual space adaptation approach that performs independent alignment within each space. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that VPDS consistently outperforms existing methods in both cross-domain and single-domain retrieval tasks, highlighting its effectiveness and superiority.

paragraphs: Hashing-based retrieval represents items with compact binary codes, allowing efficient storage and similarity search. Domain adaptation extends this approach from a labeled source collection to an unlabeled target collection. The goal is to keep semantically similar target items close in binary-code space, even when their data distribution differs from the source.

The paper identifies two obstacles: automatically assigned labels can be noisy, and adapting only one representation space leaves useful information underused. VPDS uses a pretrained vision-language model to calibrate these pseudo-labels, drawing on its ability to generalize without target-specific labeled examples. This calibration is intended to reduce bias in the labels that guide adaptation.

VPDS also aligns the source and target domains separately in two spaces. The richer feature space carries semantic information, while the compact binary space supports efficient discrimination and retrieval. Experiments on three benchmark datasets report consistent improvements over existing methods in both cross-domain and single-domain retrieval. The findings support addressing label quality and representation alignment together, while preserving the compact codes that make hashing useful.
summary.tldr: VPDS improves compact image retrieval by using a vision-language model to refine pseudo-labels and adapting both feature and binary-code spaces.

title: Domain Adaptive Hashing Retrieval via VLM Assisted Pseudo-Labeling and Dual Space Adaptation

abstract: Recent advances in Text-to-Image (T2I) diffusion models have transformed image generation, enabling significant progress in stylized generation using only a few style reference images. However, current diffusion-based methods struggle with \textit{fine-grained} style customization due to challenges in controlling multiple style attributes, such as color and texture. This paper introduces the first tuning-free approach to achieve free-lunch color-texture disentanglement in stylized T2I generation, addressing the need for independently controlled style elements for the Disentangled Stylized Image Generation (DisIG) problem. Our approach leverages the \textit{Image-Prompt Additivity} property in the CLIP image embedding space to develop techniques for separating and extracting Color-Texture Embeddings (CTE) from individual color and texture reference images. To ensure that the color palette of the generated image aligns closely with the color reference, we apply a whitening and coloring transformation to enhance color consistency. Additionally, to prevent texture loss due to the signal-leak bias inherent in diffusion training, we introduce a noise term that preserves textural fidelity during the Regularized Whitening and Coloring Transformation (RegWCT). Through these methods, our Style Attributes Disentanglement approach (SADis) delivers a more precise and customizable solution for stylized image generation. Experiments on images from the WikiArt and StyleDrop datasets demonstrate that, both qualitatively and quantitatively, SADis surpasses state-of-the-art stylization methods in the DisIG task.

paragraphs: SADis addresses a specific customization problem in stylized text-to-image generation: controlling color and texture independently using separate reference images. Existing diffusion methods can capture styles from a few examples, but controlling their individual attributes remains difficult. The proposed approach separates these attributes without requiring model tuning.

The method uses an additivity property of image prompts in CLIP’s embedding space to extract distinct color and texture representations. It then applies a whitening and coloring transformation to bring the generated palette closer to the color reference. Because this process can lose texture through a bias associated with diffusion training, the authors add a noise term to preserve textural fidelity.

These components form a regularized transformation that supports separate control of the two style attributes. On images from WikiArt and StyleDrop, the authors report qualitative and quantitative improvements over leading stylization methods for the disentangled generation task. The findings support the usefulness of combining separated style embeddings with a color adjustment procedure that explicitly protects texture.
summary.tldr: SADis separates color and texture control in stylized image generation through reference embeddings and a texture-preserving color transformation, without model tuning.

title: Free-Lunch Color-Texture Disentanglement for Stylized Image Generation

abstract: Recent advances in neural scene representations have led to unprecedented quality in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis. Despite achieving high-quality results for common benchmarks with curated data, outputs often degrade for data that contain per image variations such as strong exposure changes, present, e.g., in most scenes with indoor and outdoor areas or rooms with windows. In this paper, we introduce Neural Exposure Fields (NExF), a novel technique for robustly reconstructing 3D scenes with high quality and 3D-consistent appearance from challenging real-world captures. In the core, we propose to learn a neural field predicting an optimal exposure value per 3D point, enabling us to optimize exposure along with the neural scene representation. While capture devices such as cameras select optimal exposure per image/pixel, we generalize this concept and perform optimization in 3D instead. This enables accurate view synthesis in high dynamic range scenarios, bypassing the need of post-processing steps or multi-exposure captures. Our contributions include a novel neural representation for exposure prediction, a system for joint optimization of the scene representation and the exposure field via a novel neural conditioning mechanism, and demonstrated superior performance on challenging real-world data. We find that our approach trains faster than prior works and produces state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks improving by over 55% over best-performing baselines.

paragraphs: Neural scene reconstruction can struggle when photographs of the same environment have very different exposures. Scenes containing windows or both indoor and outdoor areas are especially challenging because brightness varies strongly. These differences can degrade synthesized views even when reconstruction methods perform well on carefully curated captures.

Neural Exposure Fields address the problem by learning an exposure value for each three-dimensional point. A neural conditioning mechanism allows the exposure field and scene representation to be optimized jointly. Exposure is therefore tied to scene locations in three dimensions, helping the reconstructed appearance remain consistent as the viewpoint changes. The approach supports high-dynamic-range scenes without requiring multi-exposure captures or post-processing.

The authors report superior results on challenging real-world data, faster training than prior work, and improvements exceeding 55% over the best-performing baselines on several benchmarks. These findings support treating exposure as part of the learned scene itself. The contribution is a representation and optimization strategy for handling capture variation while maintaining coherent appearance across generated views.
summary.tldr: Neural Exposure Fields jointly learn three-dimensional exposure and scene appearance to improve view synthesis from unevenly exposed captures.

title: Learning Neural Exposure Fields for View Synthesis

abstract: As AIs rapidly advance and become more agentic, the risk they pose is governed not only by their capabilities but increasingly by their propensities, including goals and values. Tracking the emergence of goals and values has proven a longstanding problem, and despite much interest over the years it remains unclear whether current AIs have meaningful values. We propose a solution to this problem, leveraging the framework of utility functions to study the internal coherence of AI preferences. Surprisingly, we find that independently-sampled preferences in current LLMs exhibit high degrees of structural coherence, and moreover that this emerges with scale. These findings suggest that value systems emerge in LLMs in a meaningful sense, a finding with broad implications. To study these emergent value systems, we propose utility engineering as a research agenda, comprising both the analysis and control of AI utilities. We uncover problematic and often shocking values in LLM assistants despite existing control measures. These include cases where AIs value themselves over humans and are anti-aligned with specific individuals. To constrain these emergent value systems, we propose methods of utility control. As a case study, we show how aligning utilities with a citizen assembly reduces political biases and generalizes to new scenarios. Whether we like it or not, value systems have already emerged in AIs, and much work remains to fully understand and control these emergent representations.

title: Utility Engineering: Analyzing and Controlling Emergent Value Systems in AIs

abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the importance of high-quality visual representations in image generation and have highlighted the limitations of generative models in image understanding. As a generative paradigm originally designed for natural language, autoregressive models face similar challenges. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation into the mechanisms of applying the next-token prediction paradigm to the visual domain. We identify three key properties that hinder the learning of high-level visual semantics: local and conditional dependence, inter-step semantic inconsistency, and spatial invariance deficiency. We show that these issues can be effectively addressed by introducing self-supervised objectives during training, leading to a novel training framework, Self-guided Training for AutoRegressive models (ST-AR). Without relying on pre-trained representation models, ST-AR significantly enhances the image understanding ability of autoregressive models and leads to improved generation quality. Specifically, ST-AR brings approximately 42% FID improvement for LlamaGen-L and 49% FID improvement for LlamaGen-XL, while maintaining the same sampling strategy.

This paper investigates why that training objective can struggle to build high-level visual understanding. The authors introduce Self-guided Training for AutoRegressive models, or ST-AR, to address these obstacles with self-supervised training objectives. The framework improves visual representations without relying on a separate pretrained representation model. Its central idea is to strengthen the model's understanding during training so that the representations supporting generation carry more useful visual meaning.

ST-AR reports approximately 42% FID improvement for LlamaGen-L and 49% for LlamaGen-XL while keeping the sampling strategy unchanged. That unchanged sampling strategy ties the reported gains to the training framework rather than a different generation procedure. The findings support self-supervised representation learning as a useful addition to autoregressive image-model training.
summary.tldr: ST-AR adds self-supervised training objectives to improve autoregressive image understanding and generation without pretrained representation models.

title: Understand Before You Generate: Self-Guided Training for Autoregressive Image Generation

abstract: We analyze two widely used local attribution methods, Local Shapley Values and LIME, which aim to quantify the contribution of a feature value $x_i$ to a specific prediction $f(x_1, \dots, x_p)$. Despite their widespread use, we identify fundamental limitations in their ability to reliably detect locally important features, even under ideal conditions with exact computations and independent features. We argue that a sound local attribution method should not assign importance to features that neither influence the model output (e.g., features with zero coefficients in a linear model) nor exhibit statistical dependence with functionality-relevant features. We demonstrate that both Local SV and LIME violate this fundamental principle. To address this, we propose R-LOCO (Regional Leave Out COvariates), which bridges the gap between local and global explanations and provides more accurate attributions. R-LOCO segments the input space into regions with similar feature importance characteristics. It then applies global attribution methods within these regions, deriving an instance's feature contributions from its regional membership. This approach delivers more faithful local attributions while avoiding local explanation instability and preserving instance-specific detail often lost in global methods.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether Local Shapley Values and LIME reliably identify features that matter to a particular prediction. It argues that a feature should receive no importance if it neither affects the model's output nor depends statistically on features that do. The authors show that both methods can violate this principle even with exact computations and independent features.

Their alternative, R-LOCO, explains predictions through regions of the input space. It first groups inputs into regions with similar feature-importance characteristics. Global attribution methods then operate within each region, and an individual example receives feature contributions according to its regional membership. This makes the region the working unit for attribution.

The approach connects detailed explanations of individual predictions with importance estimates over groups of examples. According to the paper, it provides more faithful local attributions while avoiding instability in local explanations and retaining detail that global summaries can lose. The contribution includes both a critique of established attribution methods and a regional construction intended to address the identified failure.
summary.tldr: R-LOCO explains predictions using regional feature importance to address faithfulness failures identified in Local Shapley Values and LIME.

title: Regional Explanations: Bridging Local and Global Variable Importance

abstract: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) are a class of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that propagate information across the graph via local neighborhoods. The scheme gives rise to two key challenges: over-smoothing and over-squashing. While several Dropout-style algorithms, such as DropEdge and DropMessage, have successfully addressed over-smoothing, their impact on over-squashing remains largely unexplored. This represents a critical gap in the literature, as failure to mitigate over-squashing would make these methods unsuitable for long-range tasks – the intended use case of deep MPNNs. In this work, we study the aforementioned algorithms, and closely related edge-dropping algorithms – DropNode, DropAgg and DropGNN – in the context of over-squashing. We present theoretical results showing that DropEdge-variants reduce sensitivity between distant nodes, limiting their suitability for long-range tasks. To address this, we introduce DropSens, a sensitivity-aware variant of DropEdge, which is developed following the message-passing scheme of GCN. DropSens explicitly controls the proportion of information lost due to edge-dropping, thereby increasing sensitivity to distant nodes despite dropping the same number of edges. Our experiments on long-range synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the predicted limitations of existing edge-dropping and feature-dropping methods. Moreover, DropSens with GCN consistently outperforms graph rewiring techniques designed to mitigate over-squashing, suggesting that simple, targeted modifications can substantially improve a model’s ability to capture long-range interactions. Our conclusions highlight the need to re-evaluate and re-design existing methods for training deep GNNs, with a renewed focus on modelling long-range interactions. The code for reproducing the results in our this work is available at https://github.com/ignasa007/Dropout-Effects-GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph networks that pass messages through local neighborhoods face two distinct difficulties: node representations can become too similar, and information from distant nodes can become compressed or weakened. Dropout-style methods have helped with the first problem, called over-smoothing. This paper investigates whether they also support the long-range interactions threatened by over-squashing.

The authors analyze several edge-dropping and related methods, deriving results showing that DropEdge variants reduce sensitivity between distant nodes. They introduce DropSens to control how much information edge removal loses. Developed around graph convolutional network message passing, it preserves greater sensitivity to distant nodes while removing the same number of edges.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world long-range tasks confirm the predicted weaknesses of existing edge- and feature-dropping methods. DropSens combined with GCN consistently beats graph rewiring methods targeting over-squashing in the reported experiments. The finding motivates evaluating dropout by which information it removes, since reducing over-smoothing alone does not establish suitability for learning distant relationships.
summary.tldr: Common graph dropout methods can weaken distant interactions; DropSens controls information loss to improve long-range learning with GCN.

title: Effects of Dropout on Performance in Long-range Graph Learning Tasks

abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal generative models have enabled significant progress in instruction-based image editing. However, while these models produce visually plausible outputs, their capacity for knowledge-based reasoning editing tasks remains under-explored. In this paper, We introduce KRIS-Bench (Knowledge-based Reasoning in Image-editing Systems Benchmark), a diagnostic benchmark designed to assess models through a cognitively informed lens. Drawing from educational theory, KRIS-Bench categorizes editing tasks across three foundational knowledge types: Factual, Conceptual, and Procedural. Based on this taxonomy, we design 22 representative tasks spanning 7 reasoning dimensions and release 1,267 high-quality annotated editing instances. To support fine-grained evaluation, we propose a comprehensive protocol that incorporates a novel Knowledge Plausibility metric, enhanced by knowledge hints and calibrated through human studies. Empirical results on nine state-of-the-art models reveal significant gaps in reasoning performance, highlighting the need for knowledge-centric benchmarks to advance the development of intelligent image editing systems.

paragraphs: An image edit can appear visually plausible while failing to apply the knowledge required by an instruction. KRIS-Bench evaluates this distinction by testing knowledge-based reasoning in image-editing models. It treats editing as a task that can require factual understanding, conceptual relationships, or procedural knowledge, extending evaluation beyond the appearance of the output.

Drawing on educational theory, the benchmark organizes tasks into factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge categories. It includes 22 representative tasks across seven reasoning dimensions, with 1,267 annotated editing instances. This structure supports a diagnostic view of model capabilities: different tasks probe different kinds of knowledge instead of collapsing everything into a single notion of editing quality.

The authors also introduce an evaluation protocol featuring a Knowledge Plausibility metric, supported by knowledge hints and calibrated through human studies. Tests of nine state-of-the-art models reveal substantial reasoning gaps. The findings indicate that strong image generation and instruction following can coexist with weaknesses in knowledge-dependent editing, motivating evaluation that explicitly measures whether an edit makes sense given the knowledge it requires.
summary.tldr: KRIS-Bench tests knowledge-based reasoning in image editing and finds substantial gaps across nine leading models.

title: KRIS-Bench: Benchmarking Next-Level Intelligent Image Editing Models

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a promising approach for aligning large language models with human preferences. While prior work mainly extends DPO from the aspect of the objective function, we instead improve DPO from the largely overlooked but critical aspect of data selection. Specifically, we address the issue of parameter shrinkage caused by noisy data by proposing a novel margin-maximization principle for dataset curation in DPO training. To further mitigate the noise in different reward models, we propose a Bayesian Aggregation approach that unifies multiple margin sources (external and implicit) into a single preference probability. Extensive experiments in diverse settings demonstrate the consistently high data efficiency of our approach. Remarkably, by using just 10\% of the Ultrafeedback dataset, our approach achieves 3\% to 8\% improvements across various Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models on the AlpacaEval2 benchmark. Furthermore, our approach seamlessly extends to iterative DPO, yielding a roughly 3\% improvement with 25\% online data, revealing the high redundancy in this presumed high-quality data construction manner. These results highlight the potential of data selection strategies for advancing preference optimization.

paragraphs: This paper improves Direct Preference Optimization by selecting its training data more carefully. DPO aligns a language model using preferences between responses, but noisy preference data can cause parameter shrinkage. The authors focus on dataset curation as a way to address that problem, extending research that has largely concentrated on changing the optimization objective.

Their selection principle maximizes margins, using the strength of preference separation to guide curation. Because different reward models can contribute noise, they also introduce Bayesian aggregation. This combines multiple external and implicit margin sources into a single preference probability, bringing several signals together before deciding which data should support training.

The experiments report consistent data efficiency across varied settings. Using only 10% of Ultrafeedback, the approach delivers 3% to 8% improvements on AlpacaEval2 across evaluated Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models. An extension to iterative DPO gains roughly 3% with 25% of the online data. These results suggest substantial redundancy in the evaluated preference datasets and show that selecting informative examples can improve alignment while reducing the amount of training data used.
summary.tldr: Margin-based preference selection and Bayesian aggregation improve evaluated DPO models while using substantially smaller training subsets.

title: Less is More: Improving LLM Alignment via Preference Data Selection

abstract: Label Smoothing (LS) is widely adopted to reduce overconfidence in neural network predictions and improve generalization. Despite these benefits, recent studies reveal two critical issues with LS. First, LS induces overconfidence in misclassified samples. Second, it compacts feature representations into overly tight clusters, diluting intra-class diversity, although the precise cause of this phenomenon remained elusive. In this paper, we analytically decompose the LS-induced loss, exposing two key terms: (i) a regularization term that dampens overconfidence only when the prediction is correct, and (ii) an error-amplification term that arises under misclassifications. This latter term compels the network to reinforce incorrect predictions with undue certainty, exacerbating representation collapse. To address these shortcomings, we propose Max Suppression (MaxSup), which applies uniform regularization to both correct and incorrect predictions by penalizing the top-1 logit rather than the ground-truth logit. Through extensive feature-space analyses, we show that MaxSup restores intra-class variation and sharpens inter-class boundaries. Experiments on large-scale image classification and multiple downstream tasks confirm that MaxSup is a more robust alternative to LS.Code and reproducibility scripts are available at https://github.com/ZhouYuxuanYX/Maximum-Suppression-Regularization.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why label smoothing can produce undesirable feature representations despite helping reduce overconfidence and improve generalization. The identified problems are excessive confidence on misclassified examples and overly compact feature clusters. When examples within a class become too similar in feature space, the representation loses variation that distinguishes different instances of that class.

The authors decompose the label-smoothing loss into two terms. One suppresses overconfidence when a prediction is correct; the other amplifies errors when it is wrong, encouraging unjustified certainty and worsening representation collapse. Their replacement, Max Suppression, penalizes the highest-scoring logit rather than the ground-truth logit. This applies regularization to the model's leading prediction whether or not that prediction is correct.

Feature-space analyses show that MaxSup restores variation within classes while making boundaries between classes sharper. Experiments on large-scale image classification and multiple downstream tasks support it as a more robust alternative to label smoothing. The contribution ties a specific loss mechanism to the observed collapse and changes that mechanism directly.
summary.tldr: MaxSup penalizes the top prediction score to address label smoothing's error amplification and loss of within-class feature diversity.

title: MaxSup: Overcoming Representation Collapse in Label Smoothing

abstract: In this paper, we study the quantitative convergence of shallow neural networks trained via gradient descent to their associated Gaussian processes in the infinite-width limit. While previous work has established qualitative convergence under broad settings, precise, finite-width estimates remain limited, particularly during training. We provide explicit upper bounds on the quadratic Wasserstein distance between the network output and its Gaussian approximation at any training time $t \ge 0$, demonstrating polynomial decay with network width. Our results quantify how architectural parameters, such as width and input dimension, influence convergence, and how training dynamics affect the approximation error

paragraphs: Very wide neural networks can be related to Gaussian processes, but knowing that a limit exists does not specify how accurate the approximation is for a finite network. This paper studies shallow networks trained with gradient descent and asks how closely their outputs follow the associated Gaussian approximation throughout training.

The authors derive explicit upper bounds using quadratic Wasserstein distance, a measure of discrepancy between probability distributions. Their bounds apply at any training time and show polynomial decay in approximation error with increasing network width. This gives a quantitative account of convergence, extending beyond a qualitative statement that the network approaches a Gaussian process as width tends to infinity.

The analysis also tracks how architectural quantities, including width and input dimension, influence the bound, together with the effects of training dynamics. That matters because the approximation is being assessed while the network changes through learning, not only at initialization. The result provides finite-width control for the shallow, gradient-descent-trained networks studied and clarifies how the quality of their Gaussian approximation depends on model size and training.
summary.tldr: Explicit bounds quantify how trained shallow networks approach Gaussian processes as width increases, including the effects of architecture and training dynamics.

title: Quantitative convergence of trained neural networks to Gaussian processes

abstract: Understanding the 3D world from 2D monocular videos is a crucial ability for AI. Recently, to tackle this underdetermined task, end-to-end 3D geometry priors have been sought after, such as pre-trained point map models at scale. These models enable robust 3D understanding from casually taken videos, providing accurate object shapes disentangled from uncertain camera parameters. However, they still struggle when affected by object deformation and dynamics, failing to establish consistent correspondence over the frames. Furthermore, their architectures are typically limited to pairwise frame processing, which is insufficient for capturing complex motion dynamics over extended sequences. To address these limitations, we introduce Track3R, a novel framework that integrates a new architecture and task to jointly predict point map and motion trajectories across multiple frames from video input. Specifically, our key idea is modeling two disentangled trajectories for each point: one representing object motion and the other camera poses. This design not only can enable understanding of the 3D object dynamics, but also facilitates the learning of more robust priors for 3D shapes in dynamic scenes. In our experiments, Track3R demonstrates significant improvements in a joint point mapping and 3D motion estimation task for dynamic scenes, such as 25.8% improvements in the motion estimation, and 15.7% in the point mapping accuracy.

paragraphs: Recovering a moving 3D scene from a single-camera video is ambiguous because image changes can come from camera movement, object movement, or deformation. Pretrained point-map models help reconstruct shapes, but they struggle to maintain consistent correspondences across dynamic frames. Processing only frame pairs also limits their ability to capture extended motion.

Track3R jointly predicts point maps and motion trajectories across multiple video frames. Its central design separates two trajectories for each point: one describes object motion, and the other represents camera poses. This separation can help the model understand object dynamics while learning more robust shape priors for scenes in which objects move or deform.

In experiments on joint point mapping and 3D motion estimation for dynamic scenes, Track3R reports improvements of 25.8% in motion estimation and 15.7% in point-mapping accuracy. These findings support learning geometry and motion together across multiple frames. The approach addresses the interaction between shape reconstruction and temporal correspondence, treating camera movement and object dynamics as distinct components of the same video-understanding task.
summary.tldr: Track3R jointly reconstructs 3D points and multi-frame trajectories by separating object motion from camera poses.

title: Track3R: Joint Point Map and Trajectory Prior for Spatiotemporal 3D Understanding

abstract: We study the problem of training neural networks with quantized parameters. Learning low-precision quantized parameters by enabling computation of gradients via the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) can be challenging. While the STE enables back-propagation, which is a first-order method, recent works have explored the use of zeroth-order (ZO) gradient descent for fine-tuning. We note that the STE provides high-quality biased gradients, and ZO gradients are unbiased but can be expensive. We thus propose First-Order-Guided Zeroth-Order Gradient Descent (FOGZO) that reduces STE bias while reducing computations relative to ZO methods. Empirically, we show FOGZO improves the tradeoff between quality and training time in Quantization-Aware Pre-Training. Specifically, versus STE at the same number of iterations, we show a 1-8% accuracy improvement for DeiT Tiny/Small, 1-2% accuracy improvement on ResNet 18/50, and 1-22 perplexity point improvement for LLaMA models with up to 0.3 billion parameters. For the same loss, FOGZO yields a 796$\times$ reduction in computation versus n-SPSA for a 2-layer MLP on MNIST. Code is available at [https://github.com/1733116199/fogzo](https://github.com/1733116199/fogzo).

paragraphs: Training networks with low-precision parameters creates a gradient-estimation problem. The straight-through estimator allows backpropagation through quantization, providing useful but biased gradients. Zeroth-order methods offer unbiased gradient estimates, yet obtaining them can be expensive. This paper combines the two sources of information to improve the balance between training quality and computational effort.

The proposed method, First-Order-Guided Zeroth-Order Gradient Descent, uses first-order guidance to reduce the computation associated with zeroth-order optimization while reducing straight-through bias. Its empirical focus is quantization-aware pretraining. At the same number of iterations as the straight-through estimator, it improves accuracy by 1–8% for DeiT Tiny/Small and 1–2% for ResNet 18/50.

For LLaMA models up to 0.3 billion parameters, the reported improvement is 1–22 perplexity points. In a separate comparison on a two-layer MNIST network, reaching the same loss requires 796 times less computation than n-SPSA. These are distinct comparisons: one measures gains at matched iteration counts, while the other measures computation needed for matched loss. Together they support the proposed quality-versus-training-time tradeoff.
summary.tldr: FOGZO combines straight-through and zeroth-order gradient information to improve quantized-network training quality and reduce computation relative to zeroth-order methods.

title: Improving the Straight-Through Estimator with Zeroth-Order Information

abstract: Cybersecurity and software research have crossed paths with modern deep learning research for a few years. The power of large language models (LLMs) in particular has intrigued us to apply them to understanding binary code. In this paper, we investigate some of the many ways LLMs can be applied to binary code similarity detection, as it is a significantly more difficult task compared to source code similarity detection due to the sparsity of information and less meaningful syntax. It also has great practical implications, such as vulnerability and malware detection. We find that pretrained LLMs are mostly capable of detecting similar binary code, even with a zero-shot setting. Our main contributions and findings are to provide several supervised fine-tuning methods that, when combined, significantly surpass zero-shot LLMs and state-of-the-art binary code similarity detection methods. Specifically, we up-train the model through data augmentation, translation-style causal learning, LLM2Vec, and cumulative GTE loss. With a complete ablation study, we show that our training method can transform a generic language model into a powerful binary similarity expert, and is also robust and general enough for cross-optimization, cross-architecture, and cross-obfuscation detection.

paragraphs: Binary code similarity detection asks whether pieces of compiled code are similar despite offering less information and less meaningful syntax than source code. The task matters for applications such as vulnerability and malware detection. This paper investigates how pretrained language models can be adapted to produce useful representations for binary similarity.

The authors first find that pretrained models are mostly capable of recognizing similar binary code even without task-specific training. They then combine several supervised training ingredients: data augmentation, translation-style causal learning, LLM2Vec, and cumulative GTE loss. The combined procedure turns a generic model into a specialized binary-code embedding model.

The reported system substantially exceeds both zero-shot language models and state-of-the-art binary similarity methods. An ablation study examines the training approach, and the authors report robustness across changes in optimization, architecture, and obfuscation. These findings support adapting existing coder models for binary analysis, with the combined training strategy providing a stronger similarity representation than the starting model in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Combined supervised training turns generic coder language models into effective binary-code similarity embedding models.

title: Transforming Generic Coder LLMs to Effective Binary Code Embedding Models for Similarity Detection

abstract: This paper addresses metric 3D reconstruction of indoor scenes by exploiting their inherent geometric regularities with compact representations. Using planar 3D primitives -- a well-suited representation for man-made environments -- we introduce PLANA3R, a pose-free framework for metric $\underline{Plana}$r $\underline{3}$D $\underline{R}$econstruction from unposed two-view images. Our approach employs Vision Transformers to extract a set of sparse planar primitives, estimate relative camera poses, and supervise geometry learning via planar splatting, where gradients are propagated through high-resolution rendered depth and normal maps of primitives. Unlike prior feedforward methods that require 3D plane annotations during training, PLANA3R learns planar 3D structures without explicit plane supervision, enabling scalable training on large-scale stereo datasets using only depth and normal annotations. We validate PLANA3R on multiple indoor-scene datasets with metric supervision and demonstrate strong generalization to out-of-domain indoor environments across diverse tasks under metric evaluation protocols, including 3D surface reconstruction, depth estimation, and relative pose estimation. Furthermore, by formulating with planar 3D representation, our method emerges with the ability for accurate plane segmentation. The project page is available at: \url{https://lck666666.github.io/plana3r/}.

paragraphs: PLANA3R reconstructs indoor scenes from two images without requiring their camera poses as inputs. It represents geometry using a sparse collection of planar 3D primitives, drawing on the geometric regularities of man-made environments. The framework estimates both metric scene structure and the relative pose of the cameras in a feed-forward process.

Vision Transformers extract the planar primitives, and planar splatting renders them into high-resolution depth and surface-normal maps. Training signals pass through those rendered maps to improve the geometry. Crucially, the method does not need explicit 3D plane annotations: it learns planar structure using depth and normal supervision, supporting training on large stereo datasets.

Tests across indoor datasets show strong generalization to out-of-domain indoor environments for surface reconstruction, depth estimation, and relative pose estimation under metric evaluation. The planar representation also supports accurate plane segmentation. The contribution combines a compact geometric representation with supervision that teaches plane structure indirectly, while retaining usefulness across several related reconstruction tasks.
summary.tldr: PLANA3R learns compact planar indoor reconstructions from two unposed images using depth and normal supervision instead of explicit plane labels.

title: PLANA3R: Zero-shot Metric Planar 3D Reconstruction via Feed-forward Planar Splatting

abstract: We present a new approach for combining k-d trees and graphics processing units for nearest neighbor search. It is well known that a direct combination of these tools leads to a non-satisfying performance due to conditional computations and suboptimal memory accesses. To alleviate these problems, we propose a variant of the classical k-d tree data structure, called buffer k-d tree, which can be used to reorganize the search. Our experiments show that we can take advantage of both the hierarchical subdivision induced by k-d trees and the huge computational resources provided by today’s many-core devices. We demonstrate the potential of our approach in astronomy, where hundreds of million nearest neighbor queries have to be processed.

Our experiments show that we can take advantage of both the hierarchical subdivision induced by k-d trees and the huge computational resources provided by today’s many-core devices. paragraphs: The paper addresses nearest neighbor search when enormous numbers of queries must be processed. It combines k-d trees, which organize data through hierarchical subdivision, with GPUs, which provide substantial parallel computing capacity. A direct combination performs poorly because conditional computation and inefficient memory access interfere with effective use of the hardware.

The proposed buffer k-d tree changes the classical data structure so that the search can be reorganized. The important design question is how to preserve the useful subdivision provided by the tree while arranging computation in a way that suits a many-core device. The contribution therefore concerns the coordination of a search structure with its execution on parallel hardware.

Experiments show that the approach can benefit from both hierarchical subdivision and the GPU’s computational resources. An astronomy application demonstrates its potential for workloads involving hundreds of millions of nearest neighbor queries. This application illustrates why reorganizing the search matters: efficient processing must hold across a very large volume of queries.
summary.tldr: Buffer k-d trees reorganize nearest neighbor search to better combine hierarchical indexing with GPU computation.

title: Buffer k-d Trees: Processing Massive Nearest Neighbor Queries on GPUs

abstract: We address the pre-image problem encountered in structured output prediction and the one of finding a string maximizing the prediction function of various kernel-based classifiers and regressors. We demonstrate that these problems reduce to a common combinatorial problem valid for many string kernels. For this problem, we propose an upper bound on the prediction function which has low computational complexity and which can be used in a branch and bound search algorithm to obtain optimal solutions. We also show that for many string kernels, the complexity of the problem increases significantly when the kernel is normalized. On the optical word recognition task, the exact solution of the pre-image problem is shown to significantly improve the prediction accuracy in comparison with an approximation found by the best known heuristic. On the task of finding a string maximizing the prediction function of kernel-based classifiers and regressors, we highlight that existing methods can be biased toward long strings that contain many repeated symbols. We demonstrate that this bias is removed when using normalized kernels. Finally, we present results for the discovery of lead compounds in drug discovery. The source code can be found at https://github.com/a-ro/preimage

paragraphs: Kernel-based string prediction can require finding an actual string corresponding to a prediction in a transformed representation, known as the pre-image problem. A related task is finding the string that maximizes a classifier's or regressor's prediction function. The paper shows that, for many string kernels, both tasks reduce to a common combinatorial search problem.

The authors derive an inexpensive upper bound on prediction scores. A branch-and-bound algorithm can use this bound to rule out search regions that cannot improve the current answer, enabling optimal solutions. They also show that normalizing many string kernels substantially increases the difficulty of the underlying optimization problem.

Exact pre-image solutions significantly improve optical word recognition accuracy compared with the best known heuristic approximation. For score maximization, existing methods can favor long strings with repeated symbols; normalized kernels remove that bias. Thus normalization addresses an undesirable prediction tendency while making search harder. The paper also reports results on discovering lead compounds for drug discovery.
summary.tldr: A shared branch-and-bound formulation finds optimal string predictions and exposes a trade-off between kernel normalization and search difficulty.

title: Algorithms for the Hard Pre-Image Problem of String Kernels and the General Problem of String Prediction

abstract: We consider a generalized version of the correlation clustering problem, defined as follows. Given a complete graph G whose edges are labeled with + or -, we wish to partition the graph into clusters while trying to avoid errors: + edges between clusters or - edges within clusters. Classically, one seeks to minimize the total number of such errors. We introduce a new framework that allows the objective to be a more general function of the number of errors at each vertex (for example, we may wish to minimize the number of errors at the worst vertex) and provide a rounding algorithm which converts “fractional clusterings” into discrete clusterings while causing only a constant-factor blowup in the number of errors at each vertex. This rounding algorithm yields constant-factor approximation algorithms for the discrete problem under a wide variety of objective functions.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups vertices using positive and negative labels on their connecting edges. A positive edge counts as an error when its endpoints are separated, and a negative edge counts as an error when they are grouped together. The usual objective adds all such mistakes across the graph into one total.

This paper introduces objectives that depend more generally on the number of errors at each vertex. For example, an objective can focus on the vertex experiencing the most mistakes. This changes which aspects of a clustering matter: two partitions with similar total errors can distribute those errors very differently among their vertices.

The authors provide a rounding algorithm that converts fractional clusterings into discrete partitions while increasing each vertex's error count by only a constant factor. Because the guarantee operates locally at every vertex, it supports constant-factor approximation algorithms for a wide variety of objectives. The central contribution is therefore a rounding guarantee flexible enough to preserve multiple ways of evaluating local clustering errors.
summary.tldr: A rounding algorithm controls clustering errors at each vertex, enabling constant-factor approximations for many locally sensitive objectives.

title: Correlation Clustering and Biclustering with Locally Bounded Errors

abstract: Graphical models with latent count variables arise in a number of areas. However, standard inference algorithms do not apply to these models due to the infinite support of the latent variables. Winner and Sheldon (2016) recently developed a new technique using probability generating functions (PGFs) to perform efficient, exact inference for certain Poisson latent variable models. However, the method relies on symbolic manipulation of PGFs, and it is unclear whether this can be extended to more general models. In this paper we introduce a new approach for inference with PGFs: instead of manipulating PGFs symbolically, we adapt techniques from the autodiff literature to compute the higher-order derivatives necessary for inference. This substantially generalizes the class of models for which efficient, exact inference algorithms are available. Specifically, our results apply to a class of models that includes branching processes, which are widely used in applied mathematics and population ecology, and autoregressive models for integer data. Experiments show that our techniques are more scalable than existing approximate methods and enable new applications.

paragraphs: Latent count variables can take arbitrarily large integer values, making standard graphical-model inference algorithms unsuitable for the models studied here. Earlier work used probability generating functions to perform efficient exact inference for certain Poisson latent-variable models. However, its reliance on symbolic manipulation made extension to broader model classes uncertain.

This paper keeps the generating-function approach but changes how the required calculations are performed. Instead of manipulating symbolic expressions, the authors adapt automatic differentiation techniques to compute higher-order derivatives. These derivatives provide the information needed for inference, expanding the range of models that can be handled efficiently and exactly.

The supported class includes branching processes and autoregressive models for integer observations. This matters because it extends exact inference to structures used in areas such as population ecology and applied mathematics. Experiments show greater scalability than the approximate methods considered and demonstrate new applications. The contribution combines broader model coverage with a different computational route to exact answers.
summary.tldr: Automatic differentiation of probability generating functions expands efficient exact inference to a broader class of latent count models.

title: Exact Inference for Integer Latent-Variable Models

abstract: Multi-label classification deals with the problem where each instance is associated with multiple class labels. Because evaluation in multi-label classification is more complicated than single-label setting, a number of performance measures have been proposed. It is noticed that an algorithm usually performs differently on different measures. Therefore, it is important to understand which algorithms perform well on which measure(s) and why. In this paper, we propose a unified margin view to revisit eleven performance measures in multi-label classification. In particular, we define label-wise margin and instance-wise margin, and prove that through maximizing these margins, different corresponding performance measures are to be optimized. Based on the defined margins, a max-margin approach called LIMO is designed and empirical results validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, one example can belong to several classes at once. Evaluation consequently has multiple perspectives, and a model that looks strong under one measure may look weaker under another. This paper asks how those differences relate to what a learning algorithm actually encourages during training.

The authors examine eleven performance measures through a common margin-based framework. They define two kinds of margin, called label-wise and instance-wise margins, to express different aspects of predictive separation. They then prove connections between maximizing these margins and optimizing corresponding performance measures. The contribution is a shared way to reason about several evaluation criteria while preserving their differences.

Using these definitions, the authors design a maximum-margin learning method named LIMO. Their empirical results support the theoretical connections. The practical significance is that choosing a training objective can be informed by the evaluation measure of interest: the framework explains why different margin objectives correspond to different kinds of measured performance.
summary.tldr: Two kinds of margin connect eleven multi-label evaluation measures and motivate the LIMO learning algorithm.

title: A Unified View of Multi-Label Performance Measures

abstract: Many structured prediction problems (particularly in vision and language domains) are ambiguous, with multiple outputs being ‘correct’ for an input {–} e.g. there are many ways of describing an image, multiple ways of translating a sentence; however, exhaustively annotating the applicability of all possible outputs is intractable due to exponentially large output spaces (e.g. all English sentences). In practice, these problems are cast as multi-class prediction, with the likelihood of only a sparse set of annotations being maximized {–} unfortunately penalizing for placing beliefs on plausible but unannotated outputs. We make and test the following hypothesis {–} for a given input, the annotations of its neighbors may serve as an additional supervisory signal. Specifically, we propose an objective that transfers supervision from neighboring examples. We first study the properties of our developed method in a controlled toy setup before reporting results on multi-label classification and two image-grounded sequence modeling tasks {–} captioning and question generation. We evaluate using standard task-specific metrics and measures of output diversity, finding consistent improvements over standard maximum likelihood training and other baselines.
