paragraphs: An image can have several valid descriptions, and a sentence can have several valid translations. Training datasets usually record only a small fraction of these possibilities because exhaustively listing them is impractical. Maximizing the likelihood of the recorded answers alone can consequently penalize a model for assigning probability to plausible answers that were never annotated.

The paper tests the hypothesis that annotations attached to neighboring inputs can supply additional supervision. Its proposed objective transfers supervisory information between neighboring examples, expanding the evidence available for an input beyond its own sparse annotations. The approach treats nearby examples as a possible source of valid output variation.

The authors first study the method in a controlled toy setting, then evaluate multi-label classification, image captioning, and image-grounded question generation. They assess both task-specific performance and output diversity, reporting consistent improvements over standard maximum-likelihood training and other baselines. These results support neighbor-based supervision as a way to learn multiple plausible outputs in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Transferring supervision from neighboring examples improves reported task performance and output diversity when valid answers are sparsely annotated.

title: Learn from Your Neighbor: Learning Multi-modal Mappings from Sparse Annotations

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are pow- erful generative models based on providing feed- back to a generative network via a discriminator network. However, the discriminator usually as- sesses individual samples. This prevents the dis- criminator from accessing global distributional statistics of generated samples, and often leads to mode dropping: the generator models only part of the target distribution. We propose to feed the discriminator with mixed batches of true and fake samples, and train it to predict the ratio of true samples in the batch. The latter score does not depend on the order of samples in a batch. Rather than learning this invariance, we introduce a generic permutation-invariant discriminator ar- chitecture. This architecture is provably a uni- versal approximator of all symmetric functions. Experimentally, our approach reduces mode col- lapse in GANs on two synthetic datasets, and obtains good results on the CIFAR10 and CelebA datasets, both qualitatively and quantitatively.

The latter score does not depend on the order of samples in a batch. Rather than learning this invariance, we introduce a generic permutation-invariant discriminator ar- chitecture. Experimentally, our approach reduces mode col- lapse in GANs on two synthetic datasets, and obtains good results on the CIFAR10 and CelebA datasets, both qualitatively and quantitatively.

paragraphs: A GAN's discriminator usually judges generated examples individually. That limits its access to statistics describing a collection of generated samples, which can contribute to mode dropping: the generator represents only part of the target distribution. This paper changes the discriminator's task so that it receives information about batches as a whole.

The proposed discriminator takes a mixture of real and generated examples and predicts the fraction that is real. Because this fraction does not depend on sample order, the authors build permutation invariance directly into the architecture. They prove that the architecture can universally approximate symmetric functions, giving it broad representational capacity for functions whose outputs ignore ordering.

Experiments show reduced mode collapse on two synthetic datasets and good qualitative and quantitative results on CIFAR10 and CelebA. These findings support batch-level feedback as a way to address missing distributional diversity. The approximation theorem concerns what the discriminator architecture can represent; the reduction in collapse is established empirically in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: A permutation-invariant discriminator predicts the real-sample fraction in mixed batches and empirically reduces GAN mode collapse.

title: Mixed batches and symmetric discriminators for GAN training

abstract: The seminal work of Dwork et al. [ITCS 2012] introduced a metric-based notion of individual fairness: given a task-specific similarity metric, their notion required that every pair of similar individuals should be treated similarly. In the context of machine learning, however, individual fairness does not generalize from a training set to the underlying population. We show that this can lead to computational intractability even for simple fair-learning tasks. With this motivation in mind, we introduce and study a relaxed notion of approximate metric-fairness : for a random pair of individuals sampled from the population, with all but a small probability of error, if they are similar then they should be treated similarly. We formalize the goal of achieving approximate metric-fairness simultaneously with best-possible accuracy as Probably Approximately Correct and Fair (PACF) Learning. We show that approximate metric-fairness does generalize, and leverage these generalization guarantees to construct polynomial-time PACF learning algorithms for the classes of linear and logistic predictors.

paragraphs: Metric-based individual fairness asks that people considered similar by a task-specific metric receive similar treatment. Requiring this for every pair creates a learning difficulty: fairness on training examples does not automatically generalize to the population. The paper shows that this issue can make even simple fair-learning tasks computationally intractable.

The authors relax the requirement to randomly sampled pairs from the population. Similar individuals should receive similar treatment except with a small probability of error. They formalize learning under this requirement as Probably Approximately Correct and Fair learning, combining approximate metric fairness with the goal of best-possible accuracy.

The central result is that this approximate fairness notion does generalize. The authors use that guarantee to construct polynomial-time learning algorithms for linear and logistic predictors. The relaxation matters because it turns a population-wide fairness goal into one that can be learned efficiently for these predictor classes, while explicitly allowing a small probability of fairness violations.
summary.tldr: Allowing a small probability of metric-fairness violations enables generalization guarantees and efficient fair learning for linear and logistic predictors.

title: Probably Approximately Metric-Fair Learning

abstract: Entropy regularization is commonly used to improve policy optimization in reinforcement learning. It is believed to help with exploration by encouraging the selection of more stochastic policies. In this work, we analyze this claim using new visualizations of the optimization landscape based on randomly perturbing the loss function. We first show that even with access to the exact gradient, policy optimization is difficult due to the geometry of the objective function. We then qualitatively show that in some environments, a policy with higher entropy can make the optimization landscape smoother, thereby connecting local optima and enabling the use of larger learning rates. This paper presents new tools for understanding the optimization landscape, shows that policy entropy serves as a regularizer, and highlights the challenge of designing general-purpose policy optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: Entropy regularization encourages a reinforcement-learning policy to remain more stochastic, and its benefits are often attributed to better exploration. This paper examines how entropy also affects the optimization problem itself. It introduces visualizations based on random perturbations of the loss function to study the shape of the policy objective.

The authors first show that policy optimization can remain difficult even when the exact gradient is available. This points to the geometry of the objective as a source of difficulty beyond gradient estimation. They then qualitatively show that, in some environments, higher policy entropy smooths the landscape, connects local optima, and permits larger learning rates.

These findings give entropy a role as an optimization regularizer as well as a commonly used encouragement to explore. The environment-specific qualification matters: the paper demonstrates smoothing in some settings rather than establishing a universal effect. Its contribution combines tools for inspecting policy objectives with evidence that their geometry helps explain training behavior, highlighting why one general-purpose policy optimizer is difficult to design.
summary.tldr: Landscape visualizations suggest that higher policy entropy can ease optimization in some environments by smoothing the objective and allowing larger learning rates.

title: Understanding the Impact of Entropy on Policy Optimization

abstract: We show that standard ResNet architectures can be made invertible, allowing the same model to be used for classification, density estimation, and generation. Typically, enforcing invertibility requires partitioning dimensions or restricting network architectures. In contrast, our approach only requires adding a simple normalization step during training, already available in standard frameworks. Invertible ResNets define a generative model which can be trained by maximum likelihood on unlabeled data. To compute likelihoods, we introduce a tractable approximation to the Jacobian log-determinant of a residual block. Our empirical evaluation shows that invertible ResNets perform competitively with both state-of-the-art image classifiers and flow-based generative models, something that has not been previously achieved with a single architecture.

In contrast, our approach only requires adding a simple normalization step during training, already available in standard frameworks. paragraphs: The paper shows how standard residual network architectures can be made invertible, so their transformations can be reversed. This opens the same architecture to classification, density estimation, and generation. The motivation is architectural flexibility: conventional ways to enforce invertibility often partition dimensions or impose restrictions on the network’s structure.

The proposed approach instead adds a simple normalization step during training using functionality already available in standard frameworks. The resulting invertible networks define a generative model that can learn from unlabeled data through maximum likelihood. Computing those likelihoods requires a residual block’s Jacobian log-determinant, for which the authors introduce a tractable approximation.

In empirical evaluations, invertible residual networks perform competitively with leading image classifiers and flow-based generative models. The significance is that one architecture supports both kinds of modeling with competitive results. The likelihood computation still uses the stated approximation, so architectural invertibility and the numerical method for evaluating likelihood are distinct parts of the contribution.
summary.tldr: A training-time normalization makes ResNets invertible, enabling one architecture to perform competitively in classification and generative modeling.

title: Invertible Residual Networks

abstract: Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) is the leading algorithm for solving large imperfect-information games. It converges to an equilibrium by iteratively traversing the game tree. In order to deal with extremely large games, abstraction is typically applied before running CFR. The abstracted game is solved with tabular CFR, and its solution is mapped back to the full game. This process can be problematic because aspects of abstraction are often manual and domain specific, abstraction algorithms may miss important strategic nuances of the game, and there is a chicken-and-egg problem because determining a good abstraction requires knowledge of the equilibrium of the game. This paper introduces Deep Counterfactual Regret Minimization , a form of CFR that obviates the need for abstraction by instead using deep neural networks to approximate the behavior of CFR in the full game. We show that Deep CFR is principled and achieves strong performance in large poker games. This is the first non-tabular variant of CFR to be successful in large games.

paragraphs: Counterfactual Regret Minimization, or CFR, solves imperfect-information games through repeated traversal of the game tree and converges to an equilibrium. For very large games, a common approach first compresses the game through abstraction, solves that smaller version using tables, and transfers the resulting strategy back to the original game.

The paper explains several problems with this workflow. Abstraction often requires manual, domain-specific decisions and can discard strategically important distinctions. Choosing a good abstraction also creates a circular difficulty: knowing what can safely be simplified may require knowledge of the equilibrium that the algorithm is supposed to discover. These issues motivate learning directly in the full game.

Deep CFR replaces the need for that preliminary abstraction with deep neural networks that approximate CFR’s behavior. The authors present it as a principled method and demonstrate strong performance in large poker games, describing it as the first successful non-tabular CFR variant at that scale. The result supports neural approximation as a practical route to applying CFR beyond explicit tabular representations.
summary.tldr: Deep CFR uses neural networks to approximate CFR in full games, avoiding preliminary abstraction and achieving strong results in large poker games.

title: Deep Counterfactual Regret Minimization

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the qualities of a collection of items by performing noisy comparisons among them. Following the standard paradigm, we assume there is a fixed “comparison graph” and every neighboring pair of items in this graph is compared k times according to the Bradley-Terry-Luce model (where the probability than an item wins a comparison is proportional the item quality). We are interested in how the relative error in quality estimation scales with the comparison graph in the regime where k is large. We show that, asymptotically, the relevant graph-theoretic quantity is the square root of the resistance of the comparison graph. Specifically, we provide an algorithm with relative error decay that scales with the square root of the graph resistance, and provide a lower bound showing that (up to log factors) a better scaling is impossible. The performance guarantee of our algorithm, both in terms of the graph and the skewness of the item quality distribution, significantly outperforms earlier results.

paragraphs: This paper asks how accurately item qualities can be recovered from noisy pairwise comparisons when only certain pairs are compared. The permitted comparisons form a fixed graph. Every neighboring pair is compared k times under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, in which winning probabilities depend on the relative qualities of the two items.

The authors focus on the regime where k is large and identify graph resistance as the relevant feature of the comparison structure. They provide an algorithm whose relative estimation error scales with the square root of that resistance. This ties the quality of estimation to a specific property of how comparisons connect the items.

A lower bound shows that, apart from logarithmic factors, better dependence on graph resistance is impossible in the asymptotic setting studied. The algorithm’s guarantee also improves earlier results in its dependence on the graph and on the skewness of item qualities. Together, the upper and lower bounds explain which aspect of comparison structure governs achievable accuracy when many repeated comparisons are available.
summary.tldr: For many repeated Bradley-Terry-Luce comparisons, graph resistance determines achievable relative estimation accuracy up to logarithmic factors.

title: Graph Resistance and Learning from Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: In this article, we propose a new class of priors for Bayesian inference with multiple Gaussian graphical models. We introduce Bayesian treatments of two popular procedures, the group graphical lasso and the fused graphical lasso, and extend them to a continuous spike-and-slab framework to allow self-adaptive shrinkage and model selection simultaneously. We develop an EM algorithm that performs fast and dynamic explorations of posterior modes. Our approach selects sparse models efficiently and automatically with substantially smaller bias than would be induced by alternative regularization procedures. The performance of the proposed methods are demonstrated through simulation and two real data examples.
originalAbstract: In this article, we propose a new class of priors for Bayesian inference with multiple Gaussian graphical models. We introduce Bayesian treatments of two popular procedures, the group graphical lasso and the fused graphical lasso, and extend them to a continuous spike-and-slab framework to allow self-adaptive shrinkage and model selection simultaneously. We develop an EM algorithm that performs fast and dynamic explorations of posterior modes. Our approach selects sparse models efficiently and automatically with substantially smaller bias than would be induced by alternative regularization procedures. The performance of the proposed methods are demonstrated through simulation and two real data examples.

paragraphs: The paper develops Bayesian methods for jointly estimating multiple Gaussian graphical models, which represent relationships among variables. A central challenge is selecting sparse relationship structures while estimating their strengths. Regularization helps remove weak relationships, but it can also introduce bias by shrinking the relationships that remain too strongly.

The authors give Bayesian treatments of the group graphical lasso and fused graphical lasso, then extend them with continuous spike-and-slab priors. This framework supports adaptive shrinkage and model selection together. Its purpose is to let the amount of shrinkage adjust during inference while determining which relationships belong in the resulting models.

An expectation-maximization algorithm explores posterior modes quickly and dynamically, providing a computational procedure for finding candidate models. The authors report efficient, automatic sparse-model selection with substantially less bias than alternative regularization procedures. Simulations and two real-data examples demonstrate the methods’ performance. The contribution therefore combines a more adaptive statistical formulation with an algorithm designed to make that formulation practical.
summary.tldr: Bayesian spike-and-slab extensions of joint graphical lasso combine adaptive shrinkage and sparse-model selection with reduced estimation bias.

title: Bayesian Joint Spike-and-Slab Graphical Lasso

abstract: Time-frequency (TF) representations provide powerful and intuitive features for the analysis of time series such as audio. But still, generative modeling of audio in the TF domain is a subtle matter. Consequently, neural audio synthesis widely relies on directly modeling the waveform and previous attempts at unconditionally synthesizing audio from neurally generated invertible TF features still struggle to produce audio at satisfying quality. In this article, focusing on the short-time Fourier transform, we discuss the challenges that arise in audio synthesis based on generated invertible TF features and how to overcome them. We demonstrate the potential of deliberate generative TF modeling by training a generative adversarial network (GAN) on short-time Fourier features. We show that by applying our guidelines, our TF-based network was able to outperform a state-of-the-art GAN generating waveforms directly, despite the similar architecture in the two networks.

paragraphs: Audio can be represented as a waveform or as features describing how its frequency content changes over time. The paper investigates generating audio through the second representation, focusing on the short-time Fourier transform. Although these features are useful for analyzing sound, generating features that can be converted back into satisfying audio presents additional challenges.

The authors examine the difficulties involved in synthesizing audio from generated, invertible time-frequency features and provide guidelines for addressing them. They then train a generative adversarial network on short-time Fourier features. This connects their discussion of representation choices to a working synthesis system, testing whether deliberate treatment of the feature domain can improve the resulting audio.

In the reported comparison, the feature-based network outperforms a state-of-the-art GAN that generates waveforms directly, even though the networks have similar architectures. The finding supports time-frequency modeling as a promising route for audio generation. It also shows why the representation and the way it is handled can matter alongside the network architecture.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed generation of short-time Fourier features lets an audio GAN outperform a similarly structured waveform GAN in the reported comparison.

title: Adversarial Generation of Time-Frequency Features with application in audio synthesis

abstract: Pre-training and fine-tuning, e.g., BERT \citep{devlin2018bert}, have achieved great success in language understanding by transferring knowledge from rich-resource pre-training task to the low/zero-resource downstream tasks. Inspired by the success of BERT, we propose MAsked Sequence to Sequence pre-training (MASS) for the encoder-decoder based language generation tasks. MASS adopts the encoder-decoder framework to reconstruct a sentence fragment given the remaining part of the sentence: its encoder takes a sentence with randomly masked fragment (several consecutive tokens) as input, and its decoder tries to predict this masked fragment. In this way, MASS can jointly train the encoder and decoder to develop the capability of representation extraction and language modeling. By further fine-tuning on a variety of zero/low-resource language generation tasks, including neural machine translation, text summarization and conversational response generation (3 tasks and totally 8 datasets), MASS achieves significant improvements over the baselines without pre-training or with other pre-training methods. Especially, we achieve the state-of-the-art accuracy (30.02 in terms of BLEU score) on the unsupervised English-French translation, even beating the early attention-based supervised model \citep{bahdanau2015neural}.
originalAbstract: Pre-training and fine-tuning, e.g., BERT \citep{devlin2018bert}, have achieved great success in language understanding by transferring knowledge from rich-resource pre-training task to the low/zero-resource downstream tasks. Inspired by the success of BERT, we propose MAsked Sequence to Sequence pre-training (MASS) for the encoder-decoder based language generation tasks. MASS adopts the encoder-decoder framework to reconstruct a sentence fragment given the remaining part of the sentence: its encoder takes a sentence with randomly masked fragment (several consecutive tokens) as input, and its decoder tries to predict this masked fragment. In this way, MASS can jointly train the encoder and decoder to develop the capability of representation extraction and language modeling. By further fine-tuning on a variety of zero/low-resource language generation tasks, including neural machine translation, text summarization and conversational response generation (3 tasks and totally 8 datasets), MASS achieves significant improvements over the baselines without pre-training or with other pre-training methods. Especially, we achieve the state-of-the-art accuracy (30.02 in terms of BLEU score) on the unsupervised English-French translation, even beating the early attention-based supervised model \citep{bahdanau2015neural}.

paragraphs: MASS develops pretraining specifically for encoder-decoder language generation. It hides a randomly selected consecutive fragment of a sentence, gives the remaining sentence to an encoder, and trains a decoder to reconstruct the missing fragment. The task connects understanding available text with generating the portion that has been removed.

Because reconstruction uses both components, the pretraining jointly develops the encoder’s representation extraction and the decoder’s language modeling. The pretrained system is then fine-tuned for generation tasks with little or no task-specific training resources. This makes the pretraining objective relevant to the coordinated work an encoder and decoder must perform downstream.

Across translation, summarization, and conversational response generation on eight datasets, MASS significantly improves over the tested baselines without pretraining or with other pretraining methods. For unsupervised English-French translation, the authors report 30.02 BLEU and a state-of-the-art result, exceeding an early attention-based supervised model. These findings support fragment reconstruction as useful preparation for the evaluated low- and zero-resource generation tasks.
summary.tldr: MASS jointly pretrains an encoder and decoder by reconstructing masked sentence fragments, improving low- and zero-resource language generation.

title: MASS: Masked Sequence to Sequence Pre-training for Language Generation

abstract: Over-parameterization is ubiquitous nowadays in training neural networks to benefit both optimization in seeking global optima and generalization in reducing prediction error. However, compressive networks are desired in many real world applications and direct training of small networks may be trapped in local optima. In this paper, instead of pruning or distilling over-parameterized models to compressive ones, we propose a new approach based on differential inclusions of inverse scale spaces. Specifically, it generates a family of models from simple to complex ones that couples a pair of parameters to simultaneously train over-parameterized deep models and structural sparsity on weights of fully connected and convolutional layers. Such a differential inclusion scheme has a simple discretization, proposed as Deep structurally splitting Linearized Bregman Iteration (DessiLBI), whose global convergence analysis in deep learning is established that from any initializations, algorithmic iterations converge to a critical point of empirical risks. Experimental evidence shows that DessiLBI achieve comparable and even better performance than the competitive optimizers in exploring the structural sparsity of several widely used backbones on the benchmark datasets. Remarkably, with early stopping, DessiLBI unveils “winning tickets” in early epochs: the effective sparse structure with comparable test accuracy to fully trained over-parameterized models.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can be easier to optimize, while practical applications often need compact models. This paper develops a training approach that explores sparse structures while also training an over-parameterized network. It generates a family of models progressing from simple to complex, allowing the search for useful structure to accompany the optimization process.

The method couples two sets of parameters to learn the larger model and structural sparsity in fully connected and convolutional layers simultaneously. Its mathematical foundation uses differential inclusions in inverse scale spaces. A discrete version becomes DessiLBI, an iterative training algorithm. The convergence analysis establishes convergence from any initialization to a critical point of empirical risk; it does not claim convergence to a global optimum.

Experiments across several common network backbones and benchmark datasets find performance comparable to, and sometimes better than, competitive optimizers when exploring structural sparsity. Early stopping also reveals sparse structures in early epochs with test accuracy comparable to fully trained over-parameterized models. These observed winning tickets suggest that useful compact structures can emerge during the initial stages of this training process.
summary.tldr: DessiLBI jointly trains large networks and sparse structures, empirically revealing effective sparse subnetworks early in training.

title: DessiLBI: Exploring Structural Sparsity of Deep Networks via Differential Inclusion Paths

abstract: We propose a reward function estimation framework for inverse reinforcement learning with deep energy-based policies. We name our method PQR, as it sequentially estimates the Policy, the Q-function, and the Reward function by deep learning. PQR does not assume that the reward solely depends on the state, instead it allows for a dependency on the choice of action. Moreover, PQR allows for stochastic state transitions. To accomplish this, we assume the existence of one anchor action whose reward is known, typically the action of doing nothing, yielding no reward. We present both estimators and algorithms for the PQR method. When the environment transition is known, we prove that the PQR reward estimator uniquely recovers the true reward. With unknown transitions, we bound the estimation error of PQR. Finally, the performance of PQR is demonstrated by synthetic and real-world datasets.

To accomplish this, we assume the existence of one anchor action whose reward is known, typically the action of doing nothing, yielding no reward. paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks to recover a reward function from behavior. Deep PQR approaches this problem with deep energy-based policies and a sequence of three estimation steps: first the policy, then the Q-function, and finally the reward. This sequence gives the method its name and organizes reward recovery into connected learning problems.

The framework allows rewards to depend on both the state and the chosen action, and it accommodates stochastic state transitions. Its central assumption is that one anchor action has a known reward. The authors give doing nothing with zero reward as a typical example. This known reference is part of the setup that makes their reward-estimation approach possible.

The theoretical result depends on what is known about the environment. With known transitions, the authors prove that the estimator uniquely recovers the true reward. With unknown transitions, they instead bound its estimation error. Synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate PQR's performance. These results distinguish exact recovery under the stated information conditions from bounded-error estimation when transition information must also be handled.
summary.tldr: Deep PQR estimates policies, Q-functions, and rewards sequentially, using an action with known reward to support identifiable reward recovery.

title: Deep PQR: Solving Inverse Reinforcement Learning using Anchor Actions

abstract: This paper presents a framework of successive functional gradient optimization for training nonconvex models such as neural networks, where training is driven by mirror descent in a function space. We provide a theoretical analysis and empirical study of the training method derived from this framework. It is shown that the method leads to better performance than that of standard training techniques.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a framework of successive functional gradient optimization for training nonconvex models such as neural networks, where training is driven by mirror descent in a function space. We provide a theoretical analysis and empirical study of the training method derived from this framework. It is shown that the method leads to better performance than that of standard training techniques.

paragraphs: Training a nonconvex model involves choosing a sequence of changes that improves its behavior. This paper proposes a framework called successive functional gradient optimization for that task, including the training of neural networks. Its defining feature is that mirror descent in a space of functions guides the training process.

The function-space perspective places the model's represented function at the center of the optimization framework. Successive functional gradient steps provide the guidance from which the authors derive a training method for nonconvex models. The approach therefore connects a function-level optimization procedure with the practical task of fitting a model.

The paper supplies both theoretical analysis and an empirical study of the resulting method, and reports better performance than standard training techniques. These two forms of investigation make the proposal more than a change in how training is described: a concrete method is derived and evaluated. The stated result supports functional optimization as a useful source of guidance for nonconvex learning.
summary.tldr: The paper derives a nonconvex training method guided by function-space mirror descent and reports improvements over standard training.

title: Guided Learning of Nonconvex Models through Successive Functional Gradient Optimization

abstract: Normalizing flows are a powerful tool for building expressive distributions in high dimensions. So far, most of the literature has concentrated on learning flows on Euclidean spaces. Some problems however, such as those involving angles, are defined on spaces with more complex geometries, such as tori or spheres. In this paper, we propose and compare expressive and numerically stable flows on such spaces. Our flows are built recursively on the dimension of the space, starting from flows on circles, closed intervals or spheres.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows offer a way to build expressive probability distributions in high dimensions. Much of their development has focused on Euclidean spaces, but some quantities naturally belong to spaces with different geometry. The paper highlights angles as a motivating example and studies flows on tori and spheres.

The authors propose and compare flow constructions designed for those spaces, describing them as expressive and numerically stable. Their construction is recursive in dimension: flows in higher-dimensional spaces are built from lower-dimensional components. The starting components include flows on circles, closed intervals, or spheres, giving the approach a common organizing principle across the geometries considered.

The contribution expands the settings in which flow-based distribution modeling can be formulated around the geometry of the variables themselves. Its emphasis is on constructing suitable distributions and comparing the resulting flows. By connecting higher-dimensional models to simpler geometric building blocks, the paper provides a structured route to expressive probability models beyond the Euclidean setting that dominates the prior literature.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs expressive, numerically stable normalizing flows on tori and spheres through recursion over dimension.

title: Normalizing Flows on Tori and Spheres

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of model-free reinforcement learning for Robust Markov Decision Process (RMDP) with large state spaces. The goal of the RMDPs framework is to find a policy that is robust against the parameter uncertainties due to the mismatch between the simulator model and real-world settings. We first propose the Robust Least Squares Policy Evaluation algorithm, which is a multi-step online model-free learning algorithm for policy evaluation. We prove the convergence of this algorithm using stochastic approximation techniques. We then propose Robust Least Squares Policy Iteration (RLSPI) algorithm for learning the optimal robust policy. We also give a general weighted Euclidean norm bound on the error (closeness to optimality) of the resulting policy. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of our RLSPI algorithm on some benchmark problems from OpenAI Gym.

paragraphs: A policy learned using a simulator may face different conditions in the real world because the simulator’s parameters are uncertain or inaccurate. This paper studies that problem through robust Markov decision processes, whose goal is to find policies that withstand such uncertainty. It focuses on model-free reinforcement learning with large state spaces.

The first contribution is Robust Least Squares Policy Evaluation, an online, multistep method for evaluating a policy. The authors prove that this evaluation algorithm converges using stochastic approximation techniques. Policy evaluation is a building block here: it supplies the assessment needed before policy improvement can be considered.

The paper then introduces Robust Least Squares Policy Iteration to learn a robust policy and provides a weighted Euclidean-norm bound on the resulting policy’s distance from optimality. This gives a quantitative theoretical characterization of policy error. Demonstrations on OpenAI Gym benchmark problems complement the convergence and performance analysis, showing the proposed iteration method operating on practical reinforcement-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: Robust least-squares policy evaluation and iteration address uncertain dynamics with convergence and policy-error guarantees.

title: Robust Reinforcement Learning using Least Squares Policy Iteration with Provable Performance Guarantees

abstract: In few-shot imitation, an agent is given a few demonstrations of a previously unseen task, and must then successfully perform that task. We propose a novel approach to learning few-shot-imitation agents that we call demonstration-conditioned reinforcement learning (DCRL). Given a training set consisting of demonstrations, reward functions and transition distributions for multiple tasks, the idea is to work with a policy that takes demonstrations as input, and to train this policy to maximize the average of the cumulative reward over the set of training tasks. Relative to previously proposed few-shot imitation methods that use behaviour cloning or infer reward functions from demonstrations, our method has the disadvantage that it requires reward functions at training time. However, DCRL also has several advantages, such as the ability to improve upon suboptimal demonstrations, to operate given state-only demonstrations, and to cope with a domain shift between the demonstrator and the agent. Moreover, we show that DCRL outperforms methods based on behaviour cloning by a large margin, on navigation tasks and on robotic manipulation tasks from the Meta-World benchmark.

paragraphs: Few-shot imitation asks an agent to perform a previously unseen task after seeing only a few demonstrations. This paper trains such agents with demonstration-conditioned reinforcement learning, or DCRL. The policy receives demonstrations as part of its input, allowing the examples to inform which task it should perform.

Training uses multiple tasks with demonstrations, reward functions, and transition distributions. The policy learns to maximize average cumulative reward across those tasks. Because the objective rewards successful behavior, the method can improve on suboptimal demonstrations instead of being limited to reproducing them. The authors also identify the ability to use demonstrations containing only states and to handle a domain shift between demonstrator and agent.

This approach has an explicit requirement: reward functions must be available during training. The paper presents that as a disadvantage relative to earlier methods based on behavior cloning or inferring rewards from demonstrations. In the reported navigation and Meta-World robotic manipulation experiments, DCRL substantially outperforms behavior-cloning methods. The results support using demonstrations to condition a reward-trained policy for few-shot task execution.
summary.tldr: DCRL trains policies to use demonstrations as task inputs, outperforming behavior cloning while requiring reward functions during training.

title: Demonstration-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Few-Shot Imitation

abstract: Stochastic Neural Networks (SNNs) that inject noise into their hidden layers have recently been shown to achieve strong robustness against adversarial attacks. However, existing SNNs are usually heuristically motivated, and often rely on adversarial training, which is computationally costly. We propose a new SNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance without relying on adversarial training, and enjoys solid theoretical justification. Specifically, while existing SNNs inject learned or hand-tuned isotropic noise, our SNN learns an anisotropic noise distribution to optimize a learning-theoretic bound on adversarial robustness. We evaluate our method on a number of popular benchmarks, show that it can be applied to different architectures, and that it provides robustness to a variety of white-box and black-box attacks, while being simple and fast to train compared to existing alternatives.

paragraphs: Stochastic neural networks inject noise into hidden layers and can achieve strong resistance to adversarial attacks. Existing designs often choose noise heuristically and may still rely on computationally expensive adversarial training. This paper proposes a stochastic network whose noise distribution is learned using a theoretical robustness objective.

The main distinction is the shape of that noise. Isotropic noise treats directions uniformly, whereas the proposed anisotropic distribution can vary by direction. The network learns this distribution by optimizing a learning-theoretic bound on adversarial robustness. This provides a principled target for noise design, connecting the random perturbations inside the network to an explicit robustness analysis.

The authors report leading performance without adversarial training on the benchmarks they evaluate. They also demonstrate applicability across different architectures and robustness against several white-box and black-box attacks. Training is described as simple and fast relative to existing alternatives. Together, these findings support learned directional noise as a practical robustness mechanism, with theoretical motivation and empirical evidence across multiple tested conditions.
summary.tldr: Learning direction-dependent hidden-layer noise from a robustness bound yields strong reported adversarial robustness without adversarial training.

title: Weight-covariance alignment for adversarially robust neural networks

abstract: Black-box variational inference algorithms use stochastic sampling to analyze diverse statistical models, like those expressed in probabilistic programming languages, without model-specific derivations. While the popular score-function estimator computes unbiased gradient estimates, its variance is often unacceptably large, especially in models with discrete latent variables. We propose a stochastic natural gradient estimator that is as broadly applicable and unbiased, but improves efficiency by exploiting the curvature of the variational bound, and provably reduces variance by marginalizing discrete latent variables. Our marginalized stochastic natural gradients have intriguing connections to classic coordinate ascent variational inference, but allow parallel updates of variational parameters, and provide superior convergence guarantees relative to naive Monte Carlo approximations. We integrate our method with the probabilistic programming language Pyro and evaluate real-world models of documents, images, networks, and crowd-sourcing. Compared to score-function estimators, we require far fewer Monte Carlo samples and consistently convergence orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Black-box variational inference fits approximate distributions across many statistical models without requiring a custom derivation for each one. A common tool, the score-function gradient estimator, is unbiased but can be extremely noisy, especially with discrete latent variables. That variance makes learning inefficient even when the estimator is correct on average.

The paper proposes an equally broadly applicable, unbiased stochastic natural-gradient estimator. It uses curvature information from the variational objective and marginalizes discrete latent variables to provably reduce variance. The method connects to classic coordinate-ascent variational inference while allowing parallel parameter updates, and it has stronger convergence guarantees than naive Monte Carlo approximations.

The authors integrate the approach into Pyro and evaluate models involving documents, images, networks, and crowdsourcing. Compared with score-function estimators, the method needs far fewer Monte Carlo samples and converges orders of magnitude faster in the reported evaluations. The contribution combines a theoretical variance reduction with a practical route to faster inference across diverse probabilistic models.
summary.tldr: Marginalized natural-gradient estimators reduce variance and substantially accelerate black-box variational inference in the reported evaluations.

title: Marginalized Stochastic Natural Gradients for Black-Box Variational Inference

abstract: In real-world multi-agent systems, agents with different capabilities may join or leave without altering the team’s overarching goals. Coordinating teams with such dynamic composition is challenging: the optimal team strategy varies with the composition. We propose COPA, a coach-player framework to tackle this problem. We assume the coach has a global view of the environment and coordinates the players, who only have partial views, by distributing individual strategies. Specifically, we 1) adopt the attention mechanism for both the coach and the players; 2) propose a variational objective to regularize learning; and 3) design an adaptive communication method to let the coach decide when to communicate with the players. We validate our methods on a resource collection task, a rescue game, and the StarCraft micromanagement tasks. We demonstrate zero-shot generalization to new team compositions. Our method achieves comparable or better performance than the setting where all players have a full view of the environment. Moreover, we see that the performance remains high even when the coach communicates as little as 13% of the time using the adaptive communication strategy.

paragraphs: COPA studies teams whose members can join or leave while the overall objective stays the same. Because agents have different capabilities, a strategy suitable for one team composition may become unsuitable for another. The challenge is to adapt coordination to the available players without needing to learn every possible team configuration separately.

The framework assumes a coach can observe the whole environment while individual players have only partial views. The coach distributes individual strategies to coordinate them. Both coach and players use attention mechanisms, and a variational objective regularizes learning. An adaptive communication method lets the coach decide when to send information, making communication timing part of the coordination approach.

Experiments cover resource collection, a rescue game, and StarCraft micromanagement. The authors demonstrate generalization to new team compositions without additional training and report performance comparable to or better than a setting where every player sees the full environment. Performance also remains high when the coach communicates as little as 13% of the time in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: COPA uses a globally informed coach and adaptive communication to coordinate partially informed players as team composition changes.

title: Coach-Player Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Team Composition

abstract: Probabilistic programming uses programs to express generative models whose posterior probability is then computed by built-in inference engines. A challenging goal is to develop general purpose inference algorithms that work out-of-the-box for arbitrary programs in a universal probabilistic programming language (PPL). The densities defined by such programs, which may use stochastic branching and recursion, are (in general) nonparametric, in the sense that they correspond to models on an infinite-dimensional parameter space. However standard inference algorithms, such as the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm, target distributions with a fixed number of parameters. This paper introduces the Nonparametric Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (NP-HMC) algorithm which generalises HMC to nonparametric models. Inputs to NP-HMC are a new class of measurable functions called “tree representable”, which serve as a language-independent representation of the density functions of probabilistic programs in a universal PPL. We provide a correctness proof of NP-HMC, and empirically demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing approaches on several nonparametric examples.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs describe generative models and rely on inference engines to compute posterior distributions. Programs with random branching or recursion can define models whose parameter space is infinite-dimensional. This creates a mismatch with standard Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which is designed to target distributions with a fixed number of parameters.

The paper introduces Nonparametric Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to extend HMC to this broader model setting. Its inputs are a newly defined class of measurable functions called tree representable functions. These provide a representation of probabilistic program densities that does not depend on a particular programming language, separating the inference method from the syntax used to express a model.

The authors prove the algorithm's correctness and report significant performance gains over existing approaches on several nonparametric examples. The contribution therefore addresses both the formal validity and the practical promise of extending HMC beyond fixed-dimensional models. It advances the stated goal of general-purpose inference for expressive probabilistic programs through a specific representation and accompanying algorithm.
summary.tldr: NP-HMC extends Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to nonparametric probabilistic programs using tree representable densities, with a correctness proof and empirical gains.

title: Nonparametric Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: We study exploration in stochastic multi-armed bandits when we have access to a divisible resource that can be allocated in varying amounts to arm pulls. We focus in particular on the allocation of distributed computing resources, where we may obtain results faster by allocating more resources per pull, but might have reduced throughput due to nonlinear scaling. For example, in simulation-based scientific studies, an expensive simulation can be sped up by running it on multiple cores. This speed-up however, is partly offset by the communication among cores, which results in lower throughput than if fewer cores were allocated to run more trials in parallel. In this paper, we explore these trade-offs in two settings. First, in a fixed confidence setting, we need to find the best arm with a given target success probability as quickly as possible. We propose an algorithm which trades off between information accumulation and throughput and show that the time taken can be upper bounded by the solution of a dynamic program whose inputs are the gaps between the sub-optimal and optimal arms. We also prove a matching hardness result. Second, we present an algorithm for a fixed deadline setting, where we are given a time deadline and need to maximize the probability of finding the best arm. We corroborate our theoretical insights with simulation experiments that show that the algorithms consistently match or outperform baseline algorithms on a variety of problem instances.

paragraphs: Finding the best option in a stochastic bandit requires repeated measurements, but those measurements may share a divisible computing budget. Giving more resources to one measurement can finish it sooner while reducing total throughput because parallel speedups are imperfect. The paper studies how to allocate resources while learning which option is best.

For a fixed confidence target, the goal is to identify the best arm as quickly as possible. The proposed algorithm balances information accumulation against throughput. Its completion time is upper-bounded using a dynamic program whose inputs are the performance gaps between the optimal arm and the others. A matching hardness result complements this guarantee.

The paper also introduces an algorithm for a fixed deadline, where the objective is to maximize the probability of identifying the best arm before time runs out. Simulations show the algorithms consistently matching or outperforming the tested baselines across varied instances. The results connect statistical exploration decisions with the computational trade-offs governing how quickly evidence can be gathered.
summary.tldr: Adaptive resource allocation balances measurement speed and throughput to improve best-arm identification under confidence or deadline requirements.

title: Resource Allocation in Multi-armed Bandit Exploration: Overcoming Sublinear Scaling with Adaptive Parallelism

abstract: In offline reinforcement learning (RL), we seek to utilize offline data to evaluate (or learn) policies in scenarios where the data are collected from a distribution that substantially differs from that of the target policy to be evaluated. Recent theoretical advances have shown that such sample-efficient offline RL is indeed possible provided certain strong representational conditions hold, else there are lower bounds exhibiting exponential error amplification (in the problem horizon) unless the data collection distribution has only a mild distribution shift relative to the target policy. This work studies these issues from an empirical perspective to gauge how stable offline RL methods are. In particular, our methodology explores these ideas when using features from pre-trained neural networks, in the hope that these representations are powerful enough to permit sample efficient offline RL. Through extensive experiments on a range of tasks, we see that substantial error amplification does occur even when using such pre-trained representations (trained on the same task itself); we find offline RL is stable only under extremely mild distribution shift. The implications of these results, both from a theoretical and an empirical perspective, are that successful offline RL (where we seek to go beyond the low distribution shift regime) requires substantially stronger conditions beyond those which suffice for successful supervised learning.

This work studies these issues from an empirical perspective to gauge how stable offline RL methods are. In particular, our methodology explores these ideas when using features from pre-trained neural networks, in the hope that these representations are powerful enough to permit sample efficient offline RL. paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to evaluate or learn a policy. A central difficulty appears when those data come from a distribution different from the target policy’s distribution. Existing theory allows sample-efficient learning under strong representation conditions, but also identifies settings where errors grow exponentially with the problem horizon unless distribution shift is mild.

This paper investigates those concerns empirically using features from pre-trained neural networks. The motivation is that sufficiently informative representations might support stable learning despite a mismatch between the available data and the target policy. The experiments include representations trained on the very task being studied, giving this possibility a direct test.

Across the evaluated tasks, substantial error amplification persists even with those representations. Stable offline learning is observed only when distribution shift is extremely mild. The findings challenge the expectation that features useful for supervised learning will by themselves support reliable offline reinforcement learning under larger shifts. The authors interpret the evidence as pointing toward substantially stronger requirements for success beyond the low-shift regime.
summary.tldr: Experiments find substantial offline RL error amplification with pre-trained neural features, with stability observed only under extremely mild distribution shift.

title: Instabilities of Offline RL with Pre-Trained Neural Representation

abstract: Decision trees and random forests (RF) are a cornerstone of modern machine learning practice. Due to their tendency to overfit, trees are typically regularized by a variety of techniques that modify their structure (e.g. pruning). We introduce Hierarchical Shrinkage (HS), a post-hoc algorithm which regularizes the tree not by altering its structure, but by shrinking the prediction over each leaf toward the sample means over each of its ancestors, with weights depending on a single regularization parameter and the number of samples in each ancestor. Since HS is a post-hoc method, it is extremely fast, compatible with any tree-growing algorithm and can be used synergistically with other regularization techniques. Extensive experiments over a wide variety of real-world datasets show that HS substantially increases the predictive performance of decision trees even when used in conjunction with other regularization techniques. Moreover, we find that applying HS to individual trees in a RF often improves its accuracy and interpretability by simplifying and stabilizing decision boundaries and SHAP values. We further explain HS by showing that it to be equivalent to ridge regression on a basis that is constructed of decision stumps associated to the internal nodes of a tree. All code and models are released in a full-fledged package available on Github

paragraphs: Decision trees can overfit, and regularization often changes their structure through operations such as pruning. Hierarchical Shrinkage instead adjusts the predictions of an already trained tree. It moves each leaf’s prediction toward sample averages at its ancestor nodes, using information from progressively broader groups of training examples.

The amount of shrinkage depends on one regularization parameter and the number of samples at each ancestor. Because the procedure operates after tree construction, it is fast, compatible with any tree-growing algorithm, and can accompany other regularization methods. The authors also show an equivalence to ridge regression on a collection of decision stumps associated with the tree’s internal nodes, giving the adjustment a familiar statistical interpretation.

Across extensive experiments on real-world datasets, the method substantially improves decision-tree prediction, including when other regularizers are already used. Applied to individual trees in random forests, it often improves accuracy and interpretability by simplifying and stabilizing decision boundaries and SHAP values. The results show that changing a tree’s predictions can improve its behavior while preserving its existing branching structure.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Shrinkage improves trained trees by pulling leaf predictions toward ancestor averages, often benefiting accuracy and interpretability without changing tree structure.

title: Hierarchical Shrinkage: Improving the accuracy and interpretability of tree-based models.

abstract: Second-order optimizers are thought to hold the potential to speed up neural network training, but due to the enormous size of the curvature matrix, they typically require approximations to be computationally tractable. The most successful family of approximations are Kronecker-Factored, block-diagonal curvature estimates (KFAC). Here, we combine tools from prior work to evaluate exact second-order updates with careful ablations to establish a surprising result: Due to its approximations, KFAC is not closely related to second-order updates, and in particular, it significantly outperforms true second-order updates. This challenges widely held believes and immediately raises the question why KFAC performs so well. Towards answering this question we present evidence strongly suggesting that KFAC approximates a first-order algorithm, which performs gradient descent on neurons rather than weights. Finally, we show that this optimizer often improves over KFAC in terms of computational cost and data-efficiency.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization uses curvature information in the hope of accelerating neural network training, but the relevant matrices are often too large to handle directly. KFAC makes this approach tractable through structured approximations. This paper asks whether KFAC’s practical success actually comes from closely reproducing true second-order updates.

The authors evaluate exact second-order updates and use careful ablations to examine the effects of approximation. They find that KFAC is not closely related to those updates and significantly outperforms them in their evaluation. This challenges the explanation that KFAC works well simply because it is a computationally convenient substitute for the exact procedure.

To explain the result, the authors present evidence strongly suggesting that KFAC approximates a different kind of algorithm: first-order gradient descent on neurons rather than individual weights. They also show that this optimizer often improves on KFAC in computational cost and data efficiency. The proposed connection is supported by evidence, while the reported improvements are frequent rather than universal.
summary.tldr: Evidence suggests KFAC’s success is better explained by neuron-level first-order optimization than by approximation of true second-order updates.

title: Gradient Descent on Neurons and its Link to Approximate Second-order Optimization

abstract: Short-term plasticity (STP) is a mechanism that stores decaying memories in synapses of the cerebral cortex. In computing practice, STP has been used, but mostly in the niche of spiking neurons, even though theory predicts that it is the optimal solution to certain dynamic tasks. Here we present a new type of recurrent neural unit, the STP Neuron (STPN), which indeed turns out strikingly powerful. Its key mechanism is that synapses have a state, propagated through time by a self-recurrent connection-within-the-synapse. This formulation enables training the plasticity with backpropagation through time, resulting in a form of learning to learn and forget in the short term. The STPN outperforms all tested alternatives, i.e. RNNs, LSTMs, other models with fast weights, and differentiable plasticity. We confirm this in both supervised and reinforcement learning (RL), and in tasks such as Associative Retrieval, Maze Exploration, Atari video games, and MuJoCo robotics. Moreover, we calculate that, in neuromorphic or biological circuits, the STPN minimizes energy consumption across models, as it depresses individual synapses dynamically. Based on these, biological STP may have been a strong evolutionary attractor that maximizes both efficiency and computational power. The STPN now brings these neuromorphic advantages also to a broad spectrum of machine learning practice. Code is available in https://github.com/NeuromorphicComputing/stpn.

paragraphs: Short-term plasticity stores fading memories in synapses. This paper turns that mechanism into a recurrent neural unit called the STP Neuron, or STPN. Each synapse carries a state that evolves through its own recurrent connection, allowing the connection itself to hold changing information over time.

The formulation makes plasticity trainable through backpropagation through time. The network can therefore learn how to retain and forget information over short periods. Across the reported tests, STPN outperforms all tested alternatives, including RNNs, LSTMs, other fast-weight models, and differentiable-plasticity models. The evaluations span supervised and reinforcement learning, including associative retrieval, maze exploration, Atari games, and MuJoCo robotics.

The authors also calculate that STPN minimizes energy use among the compared models in neuromorphic or biological circuits because it dynamically depresses individual synapses. They suggest that biological short-term plasticity may consequently offer an evolutionary advantage in efficiency and computational power. That biological interpretation is a possibility, while the machine-learning results establish the unit's performance across the tested tasks.
summary.tldr: STP Neurons learn short-term synaptic memory and forgetting, outperforming tested recurrent alternatives and offering calculated energy advantages in neuromorphic or biological circuits.

title: Short-Term Plasticity Neurons Learning to Learn and Forget

abstract: Predicting how a drug-like molecule binds to a specific protein target is a core problem in drug discovery. An extremely fast computational binding method would enable key applications such as fast virtual screening or drug engineering. Existing methods are computationally expensive as they rely on heavy candidate sampling coupled with scoring, ranking, and fine-tuning steps. We challenge this paradigm with EquiBind, an SE(3)-equivariant geometric deep learning model performing direct-shot prediction of both i) the receptor binding location (blind docking) and ii) the ligand’s bound pose and orientation. EquiBind achieves significant speed-ups and better quality compared to traditional and recent baselines. Further, we show extra improvements when coupling it with existing fine-tuning techniques at the cost of increased running time. Finally, we propose a novel and fast fine-tuning model that adjusts torsion angles of a ligand’s rotatable bonds based on closed form global minima of the von Mises angular distance to a given input atomic point cloud, avoiding previous expensive differential evolution strategies for energy minimization.

paragraphs: Predicting where and how a drug-like molecule binds to a protein is a central computational problem in drug discovery. Existing approaches can be expensive because they sample many candidates and then score, rank, and refine them. EquiBind instead predicts the binding location and the molecule’s bound pose and orientation directly.

The model uses SE(3)-equivariant geometric deep learning, connecting its predictions to the spatial structure of the problem. Its direct prediction covers blind docking, where the receptor binding location must also be determined. The authors report substantial speed gains and better quality than traditional and recent baselines. Combining EquiBind with existing refinement techniques improves results further while increasing runtime.

The paper also proposes a fast refinement method for the angles of rotatable ligand bonds. It uses closed-form global minima of a von Mises angular-distance objective relative to an input atomic point cloud. This replaces expensive differential-evolution strategies in that refinement step, adding a geometric adjustment mechanism alongside the direct docking model.
summary.tldr: EquiBind directly predicts protein binding locations and ligand poses, achieving reported speed and quality gains with optional geometric refinement.

title: EquiBind: Geometric Deep Learning for Drug Binding Structure Prediction

abstract: Long-term time series forecasting is challenging since prediction accuracy tends to decrease dramatically with the increasing horizon. Although Transformer-based methods have significantly improved state-of-the-art results for long-term forecasting, they are not only computationally expensive but more importantly, are unable to capture the global view of time series (e.g. overall trend). To address these problems, we propose to combine Transformer with the seasonal-trend decomposition method, in which the decomposition method captures the global profile of time series while Transformers capture more detailed structures. To further enhance the performance of Transformer for long-term prediction, we exploit the fact that most time series tend to have a sparse representation in a well-known basis such as Fourier transform, and develop a frequency enhanced Transformer. Besides being more effective, the proposed method, termed as Frequency Enhanced Decomposed Transformer (FEDformer), is more efficient than standard Transformer with a linear complexity to the sequence length. Our empirical studies with six benchmark datasets show that compared with state-of-the-art methods, Fedformer can reduce prediction error by 14.8% and 22.6% for multivariate and univariate time series, respectively. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/MAZiqing/FEDformer.

paragraphs: Forecasting becomes harder as predictions extend further into the future. This paper identifies two problems with Transformer-based forecasting: substantial computational cost and difficulty capturing a time series' overall profile, such as its trend. FEDformer addresses both by combining seasonal-trend decomposition with a Transformer that also works with frequency information.

The decomposition handles the broad structure of the series, while the Transformer captures finer details. The frequency component uses the observation that many time series have sparse representations in bases such as the Fourier basis. This gives the model another way to represent temporal structure while supporting complexity that grows linearly with sequence length.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets report prediction-error reductions of 14.8% for multivariate forecasting and 22.6% for univariate forecasting relative to state-of-the-art methods. The results support combining an explicit representation of broad temporal patterns with learned detailed structure. The reported efficiency and accuracy gains apply to the proposed architecture and evaluations, while the frequency design is motivated by sparsity that many, rather than all, time series exhibit.
summary.tldr: FEDformer combines seasonal-trend decomposition and frequency-enhanced Transformers to improve long-term forecasting with linear sequence-length complexity.

title: FEDformer: Frequency Enhanced Decomposed Transformer for Long-term Series Forecasting

abstract: The goal of coreset selection in supervised learning is to produce a weighted subset of data, so that training only on the subset achieves similar performance as training on the entire dataset. Existing methods achieved promising results in resource-constrained scenarios such as continual learning and streaming. However, most of the existing algorithms are limited to traditional machine learning models. A few algorithms that can handle large models adopt greedy search approaches due to the difficulty in solving the discrete subset selection problem, which is computationally costly when coreset becomes larger and often produces suboptimal results. In this work, for the first time we propose a continuous probabilistic bilevel formulation of coreset selection by learning a probablistic weight for each training sample. The overall objective is posed as a bilevel optimization problem, where 1) the inner loop samples coresets and train the model to convergence and 2) the outer loop updates the sample probability progressively according to the model’s performance. Importantly, we develop an efficient solver to the bilevel optimization problem via unbiased policy gradient without trouble of implicit differentiation. We theoretically prove the convergence of this training procedure and demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm against various coreset selection methods in various tasks, especially in more challenging label-noise and class-imbalance scenarios.

paragraphs: Coreset selection aims to replace a full training dataset with a weighted subset that yields similar model performance. Selecting that subset is a discrete optimization problem. Existing approaches for large models often use greedy search, which can become expensive as the subset grows and can produce suboptimal selections.

The paper replaces direct subset search with a continuous probabilistic formulation that learns a selection weight for each training example. Its two-level procedure samples coresets and trains the model to convergence in the inner loop. The outer loop then adjusts the sampling probabilities according to the resulting model performance, linking selection decisions to how well the selected data supports learning.

The authors develop an efficient solver using unbiased policy gradients, avoiding implicit differentiation, and prove convergence of the training procedure. Experiments report better results than various coreset selection methods across multiple tasks, especially with noisy labels and class imbalance. The contribution is a way to learn a distribution over useful subsets through their training outcomes.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic bilevel method learns which training examples to sample, improving coreset selection especially under label noise and class imbalance.

title: Probabilistic Bilevel Coreset Selection

abstract: Self-supervised learning has achieved a great success in the representation learning of visual and textual data. However, the current methods are mainly validated on the well-curated datasets, which do not exhibit the real-world long-tailed distribution. Recent attempts to consider self-supervised long-tailed learning are made by rebalancing in the loss perspective or the model perspective, resembling the paradigms in the supervised long-tailed learning. Nevertheless, without the aid of labels, these explorations have not shown the expected significant promise due to the limitation in tail sample discovery or the heuristic structure design. Different from previous works, we explore this direction from an alternative perspective, i.e., the data perspective, and propose a novel Boosted Contrastive Learning (BCL) method. Specifically, BCL leverages the memorization effect of deep neural networks to automatically drive the information discrepancy of the sample views in contrastive learning, which is more efficient to enhance the long-tailed learning in the label-unaware context. Extensive experiments on a range of benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of BCL over several state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/BCL.

paragraphs: Self-supervised representation learning is often evaluated on carefully curated datasets, while real data can have a long tail of infrequent categories. Without labels, identifying those rare examples is difficult. This makes it harder to transfer supervised strategies that rebalance losses or redesign models around known category frequencies.

Boosted Contrastive Learning approaches the problem through the data used in contrastive learning. It uses neural networks' memorization behavior to automatically regulate the information discrepancy between different views of a sample. The learning signal therefore depends on how those views differ, with memorization helping drive that difference in a setting where category labels are unavailable.

The motivation is to improve long-tailed learning without relying on explicit discovery of rare labeled categories or heuristic architectural choices. Experiments across several benchmark datasets show that the approach is effective relative to several state-of-the-art methods. These results support the usefulness of manipulating sample-view information through memorization for the tested self-supervised learning problems.
summary.tldr: Boosted Contrastive Learning uses memorization to regulate differences between sample views and improve self-supervised learning on long-tailed data.

title: Contrastive Learning with Boosted Memorization

abstract: Decoding seen images from brain activities has been an absorbing field. However, the reconstructed images still suffer from low quality with existing studies. This can be because our visual system is not like a camera that ”remembers” every pixel. Instead, only part of the information can be perceived with our selective attention, and the brain ”guesses” the rest to form what we think we see. Most existing approaches ignored the brain completion mechanism. In this work, we propose to reconstruct seen images with both the visual perception and the brain completion process, and design a simple, yet effective visual decoding framework to achieve this goal. Specifically, we first construct a shared discrete representation space for both brain signals and images. Then, a novel self-supervised token-to-token inpainting network is designed to implement visual content completion by building context and prior knowledge about the visual objects from the discrete latent space. Our approach improved the quality of visual reconstruction significantly and achieved state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: This paper studies reconstructing viewed images from brain activity. It motivates its approach with the possibility that low reconstruction quality partly reflects a mismatch between existing methods and human vision. Selective attention captures only some visual information, while a completion process helps form the perceived scene from those cues.

The proposed framework combines visual perception with content completion. It first builds a shared discrete representation space for images and brain signals. A self-supervised token-to-token inpainting network then learns context and prior knowledge about visual objects within that space, supplying the content-completion component of the reconstruction process.

The authors report a significant improvement in reconstruction quality and state-of-the-art performance. The findings support combining decoded visual cues with learned completion when producing reconstructed images. The brain-completion account serves as the motivation for this design; the stated empirical result concerns the quality of the resulting visual reconstructions produced by the shared representation and inpainting framework.
summary.tldr: A shared brain-image representation and self-supervised inpainting model improve visual reconstruction by combining decoded cues with learned content completion.

title: Rethinking Visual Reconstruction: Experience-Based Content Completion Guided by Visual Cues

abstract: Recent work has shown that leveraging learned predictions can improve the running time of algorithms for bipartite matching and similar combinatorial problems. In this work, we build on this idea to improve the performance of the widely used Ford-Fulkerson algorithm for computing maximum flows by seeding Ford-Fulkerson with predicted flows. Our proposed method offers strong theoretical performance in terms of the quality of the prediction. We then consider image segmentation, a common use-case of flows in computer vision, and complement our theoretical analysis with strong empirical results.
