paragraphs: The maximum-flow problem asks how much flow a network can carry under its constraints. Ford-Fulkerson is a widely used algorithm for computing that quantity. This paper explores whether learned predictions can make it faster by supplying a useful starting flow before the algorithm performs its remaining work.

The approach seeds Ford-Fulkerson with predicted flows. Its motivation is that a prediction may capture part of the structure of a good solution, giving the algorithm a more useful starting point. The authors provide theoretical performance results expressed in terms of prediction quality, connecting the computational benefit to how informative the supplied prediction is.

The paper also evaluates the method on image segmentation, a computer vision application of network flows. Strong empirical results complement the theoretical analysis in that setting. The contribution is a way to incorporate predictions into an established combinatorial algorithm, with an explicit analysis of prediction quality and an application demonstrating practical value. The stated theory makes prediction quality part of the performance story rather than assuming every prediction is equally helpful.
summary.tldr: Seeding Ford-Fulkerson with predicted flows yields prediction-quality-dependent performance guarantees and strong image-segmentation results.

title: Predictive Flows for Faster Ford-Fulkerson

abstract: Prompt-based learning has emerged as a successful paradigm in natural language processing, where a single general-purpose language model can be instructed to perform any task specified by input prompts. Yet task specification in robotics comes in various forms, such as imitating one-shot demonstrations, following language instructions, and reaching visual goals. They are often considered different tasks and tackled by specialized models. We show that a wide spectrum of robot manipulation tasks can be expressed with multimodal prompts, interleaving textual and visual tokens. Accordingly, we develop a new simulation benchmark that consists of thousands of procedurally-generated tabletop tasks with multimodal prompts, 600K+ expert trajectories for imitation learning, and a four-level evaluation protocol for systematic generalization. We design a transformer-based robot agent, VIMA, that processes these prompts and outputs motor actions autoregressively. VIMA features a recipe that achieves strong model scalability and data efficiency. It outperforms alternative designs in the hardest zero-shot generalization setting by up to $2.9\times$ task success rate given the same training data. With $10\times$ less training data, VIMA still performs $2.7\times$ better than the best competing variant. Code and video demos are available at https://vimalabs.github.io

VIMA brings a wide range of manipulation tasks into a common format: prompts that interleave text and visual tokens. This lets different forms of task instruction enter the same robot agent.

The authors build a simulation benchmark with thousands of procedurally generated tabletop tasks, more than 600,000 expert trajectories, and four levels of generalization evaluation. VIMA uses a transformer to process multimodal prompts and generate motor actions autoregressively. The benchmark and agent together provide a way to study both learning efficiency and transfer to unfamiliar tasks.

In the hardest zero-shot generalization setting, VIMA achieves up to 2.9 times the task success rate of alternative designs using the same training data. With ten times less training data, it still performs 2.7 times better than the best competing variant. These reported comparisons support the proposed design’s data efficiency and generalization within the simulation benchmark.
summary.tldr: VIMA uses interleaved text and visual prompts to guide one robot agent across manipulation tasks, with strong generalization and data efficiency in simulation.

title: VIMA: Robot Manipulation with Multimodal Prompts

abstract: Diffusion models exhibited tremendous progress in image and video generation, exceeding GANs in quality and diversity. However, they are usually trained on very large datasets and are not naturally adapted to manipulate a given input image or video. In this paper we show how this can be resolved by training a diffusion model on a single input image or video. Our image/video-specific diffusion model (SinFusion) learns the appearance and dynamics of the single image or video, while utilizing the conditioning capabilities of diffusion models. It can solve a wide array of image/video-specific manipulation tasks. In particular, our model can learn from few frames the motion and dynamics of a single input video. It can then generate diverse new video samples of the same dynamic scene, extrapolate short videos into long ones (both forward and backward in time) and perform video upsampling. Most of these tasks are not realizable by current video-specific generation methods.

paragraphs: Diffusion models usually learn from large datasets, while manipulating a particular image or video calls for sensitivity to that specific input. SinFusion explores training a diffusion model on just one image or video. The resulting model specializes in the input's appearance and, for video, its dynamics while retaining diffusion models' conditioning capabilities.

This specialization supports a range of image- and video-specific manipulation tasks. For video, the method can learn motion and dynamics from a few frames, then generate diverse new samples of the same dynamic scene. These capabilities show how learning from one input can support several forms of generation and manipulation tied to that input. The authors state that most of the demonstrated tasks are unavailable in the video-specific generation methods they compare against. The focus is therefore on flexible modeling of an individual scene, with learned appearance and motion reused to create new variations and temporal extensions.
summary.tldr: SinFusion trains on a single image or video to support input-specific generation, manipulation, temporal extension, and video upsampling.

title: SinFusion: Training Diffusion Models on a Single Image or Video

abstract: We here present a stepping stone towards a deeper understanding of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the form of a theory of learning in linear CNNs. Through analyzing the gradient descent equations, we discover that the evolution of the network during training is determined by the interplay between the dataset structure and the convolutional network structure. We show that linear CNNs discover the statistical structure of the dataset with non-linear, ordered, stage-like transitions, and that the speed of discovery changes depending on the relationship between the dataset and the convolutional network structure. Moreover, we find that this interplay lies at the heart of what we call the "dominant frequency bias", where linear CNNs arrive at these discoveries using only the dominant frequencies of the different structural parts present in the dataset. We furthermore provide experiments that show how our theory relates to deep, non-linear CNNs used in practice. Our findings shed new light on the inner working of CNNs, and can help explain their shortcut learning and their tendency to rely on texture instead of shape.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear convolutional neural networks as a tractable step toward understanding CNN learning. By analyzing gradient descent, the authors connect training behavior to the interaction between the dataset's statistical structure and the network's convolutional structure. The resulting account makes both the data and the architecture central to explaining what is learned.

They show that discoveries of statistical structure occur through ordered, stage-like transitions, even though the network itself is linear. The speed of those discoveries depends on the relationship between dataset and network structure. They also identify a dominant frequency bias: the network makes these discoveries using only the dominant frequencies associated with different structural parts of the data.

Experiments examine how the theory relates to deep nonlinear CNNs used in practice. The authors suggest that the findings can help explain shortcut learning and a preference for texture over shape. The theoretical result concerns linear CNNs, while the experiments provide a connection to more complex networks and the interpretation offers a possible explanation of their behavior.
summary.tldr: A theory of linear CNNs links staged learning and dominant-frequency bias to interactions between dataset structure and convolutional architecture.

title: Linear CNNs Discover the Statistical Structure of the Dataset Using Only the Most Dominant Frequencies

abstract: In reinforcement learning, the advantage function is critical for policy improvement, but is often extracted from a learned Q-function. A natural question is: Why not learn the advantage function directly? In this work, we introduce VA-learning, which directly learns advantage function and value function using bootstrapping, without explicit reference to Q-functions. VA-learning learns off-policy and enjoys similar theoretical guarantees as Q-learning. Thanks to the direct learning of advantage function and value function, VA-learning improves the sample efficiency over Q-learning both in tabular implementations and deep RL agents on Atari-57 games. We also identify a close connection between VA-learning and the dueling architecture, which partially explains why a simple architectural change to DQN agents tends to improve performance.

paragraphs: The advantage function is important for improving a reinforcement learning policy, yet it is often obtained indirectly from a learned Q-function. This paper asks whether learning advantage directly would be more effective. Its proposed VA-learning method learns both the advantage function and the value function without explicitly referring to Q-functions.

VA-learning uses bootstrapping, so its learning updates depend on existing estimates, and it supports off-policy learning. The authors establish theoretical guarantees similar to those of Q-learning. This provides a theoretical basis for changing which quantities the algorithm learns directly, while retaining guarantees comparable to the established approach.

Experiments show improved sample efficiency over Q-learning in both tabular implementations and deep reinforcement learning agents on Atari-57. The paper also identifies a close connection to the dueling architecture. That connection partially explains why the architectural change can improve DQN performance. Together, the results support direct value-and-advantage learning as an efficient alternative in the evaluated settings and clarify part of an existing architectural benefit.
summary.tldr: VA-learning directly learns values and advantages, with Q-learning-like guarantees and improved sample efficiency in tabular and Atari-57 experiments.

title: VA-learning as a more efficient alternative to Q-learning

abstract: Recently, test-time adaptation (TTA) has been proposed as a promising solution for addressing distribution shifts. It allows a base model to adapt to an unforeseen distribution during inference by leveraging the information from the batch of (unlabeled) test data. However, we uncover a novel security vulnerability of TTA based on the insight that predictions on benign samples can be impacted by malicious samples in the same batch. To exploit this vulnerability, we propose Distribution Invading Attack (DIA), which injects a small fraction of malicious data into the test batch. DIA causes models using TTA to misclassify benign and unperturbed test data, providing an entirely new capability for adversaries that is infeasible in canonical machine learning pipelines. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate the high effectiveness of our attack on multiple benchmarks across six TTA methods. In response, we investigate two countermeasures to robustify the existing insecure TTA implementations, following the principle of security by design. Together, we hope our findings can make the community aware of the utility-security tradeoffs in deploying TTA and provide valuable insights for developing robust TTA approaches.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model during inference using an unlabeled batch, helping it respond to unfamiliar data distributions. This paper identifies a security consequence of that shared adaptation process: malicious inputs in a batch can affect predictions on other inputs that are benign and have not themselves been modified.

The proposed Distribution Invading Attack injects a small fraction of malicious data into the test batch. By exploiting the adaptation mechanism, it causes misclassification of unperturbed benign samples. The important distinction is where the attack acts: it changes the batch used for adaptation, creating an indirect route to influence predictions on separate samples.

Evaluations across multiple benchmarks and six adaptation methods demonstrate high attack effectiveness. The authors also investigate two countermeasures intended to strengthen existing implementations, following a security-by-design principle. The findings expose a utility-security tradeoff in the evaluated adaptation pipelines: using incoming data to improve predictions can also let malicious batch members influence them. They motivate considering this interaction when designing robust test-time adaptation.
summary.tldr: Malicious samples can exploit test-time adaptation to cause errors on untouched benign samples in the same batch.

title: Uncovering Adversarial Risks of Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Recent work has highlighted the complex influence training hyperparameters, e.g., the number of training epochs, can have on the prunability of machine learning models. Perhaps surprisingly, a systematic approach to predict precisely how adjusting a specific hyperparameter will affect prunability remains elusive. To address this gap, we introduce a phenomenological model grounded in the statistical mechanics of learning. Our approach uses temperature-like and load-like parameters to model the impact of neural network (NN) training hyperparameters on pruning performance. A key empirical result we identify is a sharp transition phenomenon: depending on the value of a load-like parameter in the pruned model, increasing the value of a temperature-like parameter in the pre-pruned model may either enhance or impair subsequent pruning performance. Based on this transition, we build a three-regime model by taxonomizing the global structure of the pruned NN loss landscape. Our model reveals that the dichotomous effect of high temperature is associated with transitions between distinct types of global structures in the post-pruned model. Based on our results, we present three case-studies: 1) determining whether to increase or decrease a hyperparameter for improved pruning; 2) selecting the best model to prune from a family of models; and 3) tuning the hyperparameter of the Sharpness Aware Minimization method for better pruning performance.

paragraphs: Removing parts of a neural network can produce a smaller model, but how well pruning works depends on how the original network was trained. This paper addresses the difficulty of predicting that dependence. It introduces a phenomenological model, grounded in statistical mechanics, that represents training influences through temperature-like and load-like parameters.

The central empirical observation is a sharp transition. Depending on the load-like parameter of the pruned network, increasing the temperature-like parameter before pruning can either help or hurt subsequent performance. The authors organize this behavior into three regimes based on the global structure of the pruned network’s loss landscape. Their explanation connects the opposing effects of temperature to transitions between those structures.

The framework matters because a training adjustment need not have the same pruning effect everywhere. The paper illustrates its use through three case studies: choosing which direction to adjust a hyperparameter, selecting a model to prune, and tuning Sharpness Aware Minimization for better pruning performance.
summary.tldr: A three-regime model explains why the same kind of training adjustment can improve or impair subsequent network pruning.

title: A Three-regime Model of Network Pruning

abstract: In this paper, we focus on single-demonstration imitation learning (IL), a practical approach for real-world applications where acquiring multiple expert demonstrations is costly or infeasible and the ground truth reward function is not available. In contrast to typical IL settings with multiple demonstrations, single-demonstration IL involves an agent having access to only one expert trajectory. We highlight the issue of sparse reward signals in this setting and propose to mitigate this issue through our proposed Transition Discriminator-based IL (TDIL) method. TDIL is an IRL method designed to address reward sparsity by introducing a denser surrogate reward function that considers environmental dynamics. This surrogate reward function encourages the agent to navigate towards states that are proximal to expert states. In practice, TDIL trains a transition discriminator to differentiate between valid and non-valid transitions in a given environment to compute the surrogate rewards. The experiments demonstrate that TDIL outperforms existing IL approaches and achieves expert-level performance in the single-demonstration IL setting across five widely adopted MuJoCo benchmarks as well as the "Adroit Door" robotic environment.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a task from a single expert demonstration when the true reward function is unavailable. This setting matters when collecting multiple demonstrations is expensive or impractical. With only one example trajectory, useful reward signals can be sparse, leaving the learner with little guidance about how to approach expert behavior.

Transition Discriminator-based Imitation Learning, or TDIL, creates a denser substitute reward that accounts for the environment's dynamics. It trains a discriminator to distinguish valid transitions from invalid ones and uses that information to compute rewards. The reward encourages movement toward states proximal to expert states, connecting progress toward the demonstration with transitions supported by the environment.

In experiments across five MuJoCo benchmarks and the Adroit Door robotic environment, TDIL outperforms existing imitation-learning approaches and reaches expert-level performance using a single demonstration. These results support dynamics-aware proximity as a useful source of learning guidance. The contribution is a way to extract more actionable reward information from a scarce expert example.
summary.tldr: TDIL uses environment-aware proximity to expert states to provide denser rewards for learning from one demonstration.

title: Expert Proximity as Surrogate Rewards for Single Demonstration Imitation Learning

abstract: The ability of deep networks to learn superior representations hinges on leveraging the proper inductive biases, considering the inherent properties of datasets. In tabular domains, it is critical to effectively handle heterogeneous features (both categorical and numerical) in a unified manner and to grasp irregular functions like piecewise constant functions. To address the challenges in the self-supervised learning framework, we propose a novel pretext task based on the classical binning method. The idea is straightforward: reconstructing the bin indices (either orders or classes) rather than the original values. This pretext task provides the encoder with an inductive bias to capture the irregular dependencies, mapping from continuous inputs to discretized bins, and mitigates the feature heterogeneity by setting all features to have category-type targets. Our empirical investigations ascertain several advantages of binning: capturing the irregular function, compatibility with encoder architecture and additional modifications, standardizing all features into equal sets, grouping similar values within a feature, and providing ordering information. Comprehensive evaluations across diverse tabular datasets corroborate that our method consistently improves tabular representation learning performance for a wide range of downstream tasks. The codes are available in https://github.com/kyungeun-lee/tabularbinning.

paragraphs: Tabular datasets combine numerical and categorical features, and their relationships can change abruptly rather than smoothly. These properties create challenges for learning useful representations without task labels. This paper proposes a self-supervised training task that uses binning to make the learning objective better reflect those characteristics of tabular data.

Instead of reconstructing each original feature value, the model predicts the bin to which that value belongs, treating the bin as an ordered index or a class. This gives all features category-type prediction targets and groups similar numerical values together. Mapping continuous inputs into discrete bins also encourages the encoder to capture irregular dependencies, including relationships resembling piecewise constant functions.

The authors investigate several benefits of this approach, including its handling of irregular functions, compatibility with encoder architectures and other modifications, and use of ordering information. Evaluations across varied tabular datasets show consistent improvements in representation learning for a wide range of downstream tasks. The findings suggest that changing the reconstruction target can supply useful structure for learning from heterogeneous tables.
summary.tldr: Predicting feature bins instead of original values improves self-supervised representations across the evaluated tabular tasks.

title: Binning as a Pretext Task: Improving Self-Supervised Learning in Tabular Domains

abstract: Traditional studies emphasize the significance of context information in improving matting performance. Consequently, deep learning-based matting methods delve into designing pooling or affinity-based context aggregation modules to achieve superior results. However, these modules cannot well handle the context scale shift caused by the difference in image size during training and inference, resulting in matting performance degradation. In this paper, we revisit the context aggregation mechanisms of matting networks and find that a basic encoder-decoder network without any context aggregation modules can actually learn more universal context aggregation, thereby achieving higher matting performance compared to existing methods. Building on this insight, we present AEMatter, a matting network that is straightforward yet very effective. AEMatter adopts a Hybrid-Transformer backbone with appearance-enhanced axis-wise learning (AEAL) blocks to build a basic network with strong context aggregation learning capability. Furthermore, AEMatter leverages a large image training strategy to assist the network in learning context aggregation from data. Extensive experiments on five popular matting datasets demonstrate that the proposed AEMatter outperforms state-of-the-art matting methods by a large margin. The source code is available at https://github.com/aipixel/AEMatter.

paragraphs: Image matting relies on contextual information to distinguish foreground contributions from the surrounding image. Many deep learning approaches explicitly gather that context through pooling or affinity-based modules. This paper identifies a difficulty with those designs: differences between training and inference image sizes change the scale of context and can degrade performance.

The authors find that a basic encoder-decoder network without dedicated context aggregation modules can learn more universal context aggregation. They build AEMatter around this observation, using a Hybrid-Transformer backbone and appearance-enhanced axis-wise learning blocks. The architecture is intended to give the network strong capacity to learn contextual relationships from data.

A large-image training strategy further supports this learning process. The resulting approach combines architecture and training scale to address context aggregation, rather than treating a specialized aggregation module as the essential ingredient. Experiments on five popular matting datasets report large improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support revisiting how context is acquired, particularly when image size changes between the examples used for training and those processed during inference.
summary.tldr: AEMatter learns context aggregation through its backbone and large-image training, improving matting across five datasets.

title: Revisiting Context Aggregation for Image Matting

abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) model incorporates the power of multiple submodels via gating functions to achieve greater performance in numerous regression and classification applications. From a theoretical perspective, while there have been previous attempts to comprehend the behavior of that model under the regression settings through the convergence analysis of maximum likelihood estimation in the Gaussian MoE model, such analysis under the setting of a classification problem has remained missing in the literature. We close this gap by establishing the convergence rates of density estimation and parameter estimation in the softmax gating multinomial logistic MoE model. Notably, when part of the expert parameters vanish, these rates are shown to be slower than polynomial rates owing to an inherent interaction between the softmax gating and expert functions via partial differential equations. To address this issue, we propose using a novel class of modified softmax gating functions which transform the input before delivering them to the gating functions. As a result, the previous interaction disappears and the parameter estimation rates are significantly improved.

paragraphs: A mixture-of-experts classifier combines several predictive models using a gate that determines their contributions. Although related regression models had received theoretical attention, the paper addresses a gap for classification: how quickly maximum likelihood estimation recovers the predictive distribution and model parameters as the amount of data increases.

The authors establish convergence rates for mixtures with softmax gating and multinomial logistic experts. They identify a problematic case in which some expert parameters vanish. In that setting, interactions between the gating function and expert functions can produce convergence slower than polynomial rates. These interactions are expressed through partial differential equations, connecting the statistical difficulty to the mathematical structure of the model.

To address this behavior, the paper introduces a class of modified softmax gates that transform inputs before applying the gating functions. The modification removes the identified interaction and substantially improves parameter estimation rates. The result explains a specific source of slow estimation and shows how changing the gate can improve the theoretical behavior of this classification model.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies slow estimation in softmax-gated classification mixtures and introduces modified gates that improve parameter convergence rates.

title: A General Theory for Softmax Gating Multinomial Logistic Mixture of Experts

abstract: We study the matroid semi-bandits problem, where at each round the learner plays a subset of $K$ arms from a feasible set, and the goal is to maximize the expected cumulative linear rewards. Existing algorithms have per-round time complexity at least $\Omega(K)$, which becomes expensive when $K$ is large. To address this computational issue, we propose FasterCUCB whose sampling rule takes time sublinear in $K$ for common classes of matroids: $\mathcal{O}(D\text{ polylog}(K)\text{ polylog}(T))$ for uniform matroids, partition matroids, and graphical matroids, and $\mathcal{O}(D\sqrt{K}\text{ polylog}(T))$ for transversal matroids. Here, $D$ is the maximum number of elements in any feasible subset of arms, and $T$ is the horizon. Our technique is based on dynamic maintenance of an approximate maximum-weight basis over inner-product weights. Although the introduction of an approximate maximum-weight basis presents a challenge in regret analysis, we can still guarantee an upper bound on regret as tight as CUCB in the sense that it matches the gap-dependent lower bound by Kveton et al. (2014a) asymptotically.

paragraphs: In a matroid semi-bandit problem, a learner repeatedly selects a feasible subset of available arms to maximize accumulated expected reward. When the number of arms is large, even choosing the next subset can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces FasterCUCB to reduce the cost of that selection step for several common matroid classes.

The method dynamically maintains an approximate maximum-weight basis with weights expressed through inner products. For uniform, partition, and graphical matroids, its sampling rule costs D times polylogarithmic factors in K and T. For transversal matroids, it costs D times the square root of K and a polylogarithmic factor in T. Here K is the number of arms, D the largest feasible subset size, and T the horizon.

Using an approximate basis makes the regret analysis more difficult, but the authors retain a bound as tight as CUCB's in the stated asymptotic, gap-dependent sense. It matches the corresponding lower bound asymptotically. The contribution combines faster selection with strong learning guarantees; the computational bounds explicitly retain their dependence on subset size.
summary.tldr: FasterCUCB reduces sampling costs for common matroids while retaining asymptotically tight gap-dependent regret guarantees.

title: Matroid Semi-Bandits in Sublinear Time

abstract: Model extraction is to obtain a cloned model that replicates the functionality of a black-box victim model solely through query-based access. Present defense strategies exhibit shortcomings, manifesting as: (1) computational or memory inefficiencies during deployment; or (2) dependence on expensive defensive training methods that mandate the re-training of the victim model; or (3) watermarking-based methods only passively detect model theft without actively preventing model extraction. To address these limitations, we introduce an innovative Bayesian active watermarking technique to fine-tune the victim model and learn the watermark posterior distribution conditioned on input data. The fine-tuning process aims to maximize the log-likelihood on watermarked in-distribution training data for preserving model utility while simultaneously maximizing the change of model’s outputs on watermarked out-of-distribution data, thereby achieving effective defense. During deployment, a watermark is randomly sampled from the estimated watermark posterior. This watermark is then added to the input query, and the victim model returns the prediction based on the watermarked input query to users. This proactive defense approach requires only slight fine-tuning of the victim model without the need of full re-training and demonstrates high efficiency in terms of memory and computation during deployment. Rigorous theoretical analysis and comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method.
originalAbstract: Model extraction is to obtain a cloned model that replicates the functionality of a black-box victim model solely through query-based access. Present defense strategies exhibit shortcomings, manifesting as: (1) computational or memory inefficiencies during deployment; or (2) dependence on expensive defensive training methods that mandate the re-training of the victim model; or (3) watermarking-based methods only passively detect model theft without actively preventing model extraction. To address these limitations, we introduce an innovative Bayesian active watermarking technique to fine-tune the victim model and learn the watermark posterior distribution conditioned on input data. The fine-tuning process aims to maximize the log-likelihood on watermarked in-distribution training data for preserving model utility while simultaneously maximizing the change of model’s outputs on watermarked out-of-distribution data, thereby achieving effective defense. During deployment, a watermark is randomly sampled from the estimated watermark posterior. This watermark is then added to the input query, and the victim model returns the prediction based on the watermarked input query to users. This proactive defense approach requires only slight fine-tuning of the victim model without the need of full re-training and demonstrates high efficiency in terms of memory and computation during deployment. Rigorous theoretical analysis and comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Model extraction attempts to clone a model’s behavior using only queries to its interface. The paper targets shortcomings in existing defenses, including costly deployment, expensive retraining, and watermarking that detects theft without actively obstructing extraction. It proposes Bayesian active watermarking as a defense that changes how the protected model handles incoming queries.

The method lightly fine-tunes the victim model while learning an input-conditioned posterior distribution over watermarks. Its training objectives preserve predictive utility on watermarked in-distribution examples and encourage output changes on watermarked out-of-distribution examples. At deployment, it samples a watermark from the learned posterior, adds it to the query input, and returns the model’s prediction for that modified input.

This couples randomized query processing with training intended to preserve useful predictions while resisting cloning. The authors report that it requires only slight fine-tuning rather than full retraining and has low memory and computation overhead during deployment. Theoretical analysis and experimental results support the defense’s effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Bayesian active watermarking samples input-dependent watermarks to resist model extraction while aiming to preserve utility with modest training and deployment costs.

title: Defense against Model Extraction Attack by Bayesian Active Watermarking

abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been successfully used to discover sparse and human-interpretable representations of the latent activations of language models (LLMs). However, we would ultimately like to understand the computations performed by LLMs and not just their representations. The extent to which SAEs can help us understand computations is unclear because they are not designed to “sparsify” computations in any sense, only latent activations. To solve this, we propose Jacobian sparse autoencoders (JSAEs), which yield not only sparsity in the input and output activations of a given model component but also sparsity in the computation (formally, the Jacobian) connecting them. With a naïve implementation, the Jacobians in LLMs would be computationally intractable due to their size. Our key technical contribution is thus finding an efficient way of computing Jacobians in this setup. We find that JSAEs extract a relatively large degree of computational sparsity while preserving downstream LLM performance approximately as well as traditional SAEs. We also show that JSAEs achieve a greater degree of computational sparsity on pre-trained LLMs than on the equivalent randomized LLM. This shows that the sparsity of the computational graph appears to be a property that LLMs learn through training, and suggests that JSAEs might be more suitable for understanding learned transformer computations than standard SAEs.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders can reveal compact, interpretable features in a language model’s internal activations. Understanding those features leaves another question: how does the model transform one set of features into another? This paper introduces Jacobian sparse autoencoders to make the connections involved in that computation sparse as well as the input and output representations.

The relevant object is the Jacobian, which describes how changes in inputs affect outputs. JSAEs encourage sparsity in this mapping for a model component. Since directly computing the required Jacobians in language models would be prohibitively large, the authors develop an efficient computation method that makes the approach tractable.

Experiments find substantial computational sparsity while preserving downstream performance approximately as well as conventional sparse autoencoders. Pretrained language models also exhibit more computational sparsity under this approach than equivalent randomized models. This suggests that the sparse computational structure reflects something acquired during training. The results motivate JSAEs as potentially better tools for investigating learned transformer computations, rather than establishing that they fully explain those computations.
summary.tldr: Jacobian sparse autoencoders expose sparse relationships between model features, offering a way to study learned computations as well as representations.

title: Jacobian Sparse Autoencoders: Sparsify Computations, Not Just Activations

abstract: We propose a Weighted Autoregressive Varying gatE (WAVE) attention mechanism equipped with both Autoregressive (AR) and Moving-average (MA) components. It can adapt to various attention mechanisms, enhancing and decoupling their ability to capture long-range and local temporal patterns in time series data. In this paper, we first demonstrate that, for the time series forecasting (TSF) task, the previously overlooked decoder-only autoregressive Transformer model can achieve results comparable to the best baselines when appropriate tokenization and training methods are applied. Moreover, inspired by the ARMA model from statistics and recent advances in linear attention, we introduce the full ARMA structure into existing autoregressive attention mechanisms. By using an indirect MA weight generation method, we incorporate the MA term while maintaining the time complexity and parameter size of the underlying efficient attention models. We further explore how indirect parameter generation can produce implicit MA weights that align with the modeling requirements for local temporal impacts. Experimental results show that WAVE attention that incorporates the ARMA structure consistently improves the performance of various AR attentions on TSF tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting requires capturing both longer-range patterns and local temporal effects. The paper first shows that decoder-only autoregressive Transformers can match strong forecasting baselines when suitable tokenization and training methods are used. This establishes that the architecture’s forecasting performance depends meaningfully on how the task is presented and trained.

The authors then introduce WAVE, an attention mechanism that incorporates both autoregressive and moving-average components, inspired by statistical ARMA models. The aim is to enhance and separate the handling of long-range and local patterns. An indirect weight-generation method adds the moving-average component while maintaining the time complexity and parameter size of the underlying efficient attention mechanism.

The paper also examines how those indirectly generated weights can match the modeling needs of local temporal effects. Experiments show consistent improvements across several autoregressive attention mechanisms and report state-of-the-art forecasting results. The contribution is therefore both an architectural addition and an efficiency result: richer temporal modeling is incorporated without changing the stated complexity or parameter size of the efficient attention models.
summary.tldr: WAVE adds an efficiently generated moving-average component to autoregressive attention, improving time-series forecasting across tested attention mechanisms.

title: WAVE: Weighted Autoregressive Varying Gate for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: The quest for Continual Learning (CL) seeks to empower neural networks with the ability to learn and adapt incrementally. Central to this pursuit is addressing the stability-plasticity dilemma, which involves striking a balance between two conflicting objectives: preserving previously learned knowledge and acquiring new knowledge. While numerous CL methods aim to achieve this trade-off, they often overlook the impact of network architecture on stability and plasticity, restricting the trade-off to the parameter level. In this paper, we delve into the conflict between stability and plasticity at the architectural level. We reveal that under an equal parameter constraint, deeper networks exhibit better plasticity, while wider networks are characterized by superior stability. To address this architectural-level dilemma, we introduce a novel framework denoted Dual-Arch, which serves as a plug-in component for CL. This framework leverages the complementary strengths of two distinct and independent networks: one dedicated to plasticity and the other to stability. Each network is designed with a specialized and lightweight architecture, tailored to its respective objective. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Dual-Arch enhances the performance of existing CL methods while being up to 87% more compact in terms of parameters.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to acquire new knowledge while preserving what it learned earlier. These goals are often described as plasticity and stability. This paper argues that network architecture deserves attention alongside parameter-level learning methods, because the shape of a network can influence how well it serves each goal.

Under an equal parameter budget, the authors find that deeper networks show better plasticity, whereas wider networks show better stability. Dual-Arch uses these complementary tendencies in two distinct, independent networks. One has a lightweight architecture specialized for learning new information, while the other has a lightweight architecture specialized for preserving previous knowledge.

The framework is designed as a plug-in for existing continual-learning methods. Extensive experiments show improved performance while using up to 87% fewer parameters. The findings make architecture an additional means of managing the stability-plasticity trade-off: separately designed networks can serve the two objectives more effectively in the evaluated settings, without requiring a larger overall parameter footprint.
summary.tldr: Dual-Arch pairs architectures specialized for learning and retention, improving continual-learning methods while being up to 87% smaller.

title: Rethinking the Stability-Plasticity Trade-off in Continual Learning from an Architectural Perspective

abstract: When optimising for conditional value at risk (CVaR) using policy gradients (PG), current methods rely on discarding a large proportion of trajectories, resulting in poor sample efficiency. We propose a reformulation of the CVaR optimisation problem by capping the total return of trajectories used in training, rather than simply discarding them, and show that this is equivalent to the original problem if the cap is set appropriately. We show, with empirical results in an number of environments, that this reformulation of the problem results in consistently improved performance compared to baselines. We have made all our code available here: https://github.com/HarryMJMead/cvar-return-capping.

paragraphs: Conditional value at risk, or CVaR, focuses policy optimization on the poor-return part of the outcome distribution. Existing policy-gradient methods for this objective discard a large share of collected trajectories. The paper identifies this loss of usable training experience as a cause of poor sample efficiency.

The proposed reformulation caps the total return assigned to trajectories used in training instead of simply throwing those trajectories away. This changes how collected experience enters the optimization problem. The authors show that the reformulated problem is equivalent to the original CVaR problem when the cap is chosen appropriately, so that choice is central to the equivalence claim.

Across experiments in several environments, return capping consistently improves performance relative to the tested baselines. The results support retaining trajectories through a suitable transformation of their returns as a way to improve CVaR policy-gradient training. The contribution combines a conditional theoretical equivalence with empirical evidence that this reformulation makes better use of the experience collected during learning.
summary.tldr: Capping trajectory returns yields an equivalent CVaR optimization problem when the cap is appropriate and improves performance in the reported experiments.

title: Return Capping: Sample Efficient CVaR Policy Gradient Optimisation

abstract: We analyze nonlinearly preconditioned gradient methods for solving smooth minimization problems. We introduce a generalized smoothness property, based on the notion of abstract convexity, that is broader than Lipschitz smoothness and provide sufficient first- and second-order conditions. Notably, our framework encapsulates algorithms associated with the gradient clipping method and brings out novel insights for the class of $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions that has received widespread interest recently, thus allowing us to extend beyond already established methods. We investigate the convergence of the proposed method in both the convex and nonconvex setting.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for gradient methods that transform the gradient nonlinearly before using it to minimize a smooth function. The motivation is to analyze such updates under a smoothness condition broader than the usual Lipschitz requirement. A broader condition can bring additional objective functions and update rules into the same convergence analysis.

The authors formulate their generalized smoothness property using abstract convexity. They provide sufficient conditions involving first-order and second-order information, giving ways to establish that a function fits the framework. These conditions are sufficient criteria, so the stated result does not make them necessary requirements for every function that could satisfy the generalized property.

The framework includes algorithms associated with gradient clipping and gives new insights into the class of (L0,L1)-smooth functions. It also supports methods beyond those already established in that setting. The authors investigate convergence for both convex and nonconvex minimization. The contribution is a common analytical foundation connecting nonlinear gradient transformations, generalized smoothness, and convergence across these two optimization settings.
summary.tldr: A generalized smoothness framework supports convergence analysis of nonlinear gradient transformations, including methods related to gradient clipping.

title: Nonlinearly Preconditioned Gradient Methods under Generalized Smoothness

abstract: Real-world human decision-making often relies on strategic planning, where high-level goals guide the formulation of sub-goals and subsequent actions, as evidenced by domains such as healthcare, business, and urban policy. Despite notable successes in controlled settings, conventional reinforcement learning (RL) follows a bottom-up paradigm, which can struggle to adapt to real-world complexities such as sparse rewards and limited exploration budgets. While methods like hierarchical RL and environment shaping provide partial solutions, they frequently rely on either ad-hoc designs (e.g. choose the set of high-level actions) or purely data-driven discovery of high-level actions that still requires significant exploration. In this paper, we introduce a top-down framework for RL that explicitly leverages human-like strategy to reduce sample complexity, guide exploration, and enable high-level decision-making. We first formalize the Strategy Problem, which frames policy generation as finding distributions over policies that balance specificity and value. Building on this definition, we propose the Strategist agent—an iterative framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to synthesize domain knowledge into a structured representation of actionable strategies and sub-goals. We further develop a reward shaping methodology that translates these strategies expressed in natural language into quantitative feedback for RL methods. Empirically, we demonstrate a significantly faster convergence than conventional PPO. Taken together, our findings highlight that top-down strategic exploration opens new avenues for enhancing RL on real-world decision problems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can struggle when rewards are sparse and opportunities to explore are limited. Discovering useful high-level actions from experience may itself require substantial exploration, while manually designing them can be ad hoc. This paper develops a top-down approach in which strategies guide the creation of sub-goals and subsequent action learning.

They then introduce Strategist, an iterative framework that uses language models to turn domain knowledge into structured, actionable strategies and sub-goals. A reward-shaping method converts these natural-language strategies into quantitative feedback that reinforcement-learning methods can use.

The empirical results show significantly faster convergence than conventional PPO. This supports the usefulness of strategic guidance for making exploration more productive in the evaluated settings. The contribution links three pieces that need to work together: a formal description of strategy, a way to construct strategies from knowledge, and a mechanism for translating them into learning signals.
summary.tldr: Strategist turns language-model-generated strategies into sub-goals and shaped rewards, yielding faster convergence than conventional PPO in the reported experiments.

title: Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation

abstract: Fast adversarial training (FAT) aims to enhance the robustness of models against adversarial attacks with reduced training time, however, FAT often suffers from compromised robustness due to insufficient exploration of adversarial space. In this paper, we develop a loss function to mitigate the problem of degraded robustness under FAT. Specifically, we derive a quadratic upper bound (QUB) on the adversarial training (AT) loss function and propose to utilize the bound with existing FAT methods. Our experimental results show that applying QUB loss to the existing methods yields significant improvement of robustness. Furthermore, using various metrics, we demonstrate that this improvement is likely to result from the smoothened loss landscape of the resulting model.

paragraphs: Fast adversarial training aims to improve resistance to adversarial attacks while reducing training time. Its speed can come with weaker robustness because the training process does not sufficiently explore the adversarial space. This paper addresses that problem by changing the loss used during training, providing a modification that can accompany existing fast methods.

The authors derive a quadratic upper bound on the adversarial training loss. An upper bound provides a quantity that bounds the original objective from above; here, the proposed bound becomes a training loss used with fast adversarial training procedures. The contribution therefore focuses on the optimization objective within those procedures.

Experiments show significant robustness improvements when the quadratic upper-bound loss is applied to existing methods. The authors also examine several metrics and find evidence suggesting that a smoother loss landscape likely explains the gains. This proposed explanation remains qualified: the results support smoothing as a likely mechanism, alongside the directly reported empirical improvement in adversarial robustness.
summary.tldr: A quadratic upper-bound loss improves existing fast adversarial training methods, with evidence suggesting smoother loss landscapes help explain the gains.

title: Quadratic Upper Bound for Boosting Robustness

abstract: Data selection has emerged as a crucial downstream application of data valuation, yet the theoretical foundations for using data values in selection remain underexplored. We reformulate data selection as a sequential decision-making problem where the optimal selection sequence arises from dynamic programming, and data values can be understood as encodings of this optimal sequence. This framework unifies and reinterprets existing methods like Data Shapley through the lens of approximate dynamic programming, revealing them as myopic linear approximations to the sequential problem. We further analyze how selection optimality degrades with utility curvature under submodularity, explaining when and why these approximations fail. To bridge theory and practice, we propose an efficient bipartite graph-based surrogate that preserves submodular structure while enabling scalable greedy selection with provable guarantees. Experiments on classical ML benchmarks and large-scale LLM fine-tuning data selection demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/frankhlchi/SeqDataVal

paragraphs: This paper examines how data values should guide the selection of training examples. It formulates selection as a sequence of decisions, with dynamic programming defining the optimal sequence. Within this framework, a data value can encode information about that sequence, connecting the meaning of an example’s value to the choices made around it.

The framework reinterprets methods such as Data Shapley as myopic linear approximations to the sequential problem. Under submodularity, the authors analyze how utility curvature degrades selection optimality, explaining when these approximations can fail. This makes interactions among selection decisions central to understanding the usefulness of assigned values.

For scalable selection, the authors propose a bipartite graph surrogate that preserves submodular structure and supports greedy selection with provable guarantees. Experiments on classical machine-learning benchmarks and large-scale language-model fine-tuning report substantial improvements over existing approaches. The contribution connects a sequential theory of data value to a practical approximation whose structure supports both efficient computation and formal selection guarantees.
summary.tldr: A sequential-decision view explains limitations of existing data values and motivates scalable, guaranteed greedy data selection.

title: Unifying and Optimizing Data Values for Selection via Sequential Decision-Making

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely deployed in industry, making their intellectual property valuable. However, protecting GNNs from unauthorized use remains a challenge. Watermarking offers a solution by embedding ownership information into models. Existing watermarking methods have two limitations: First, they rarely focus on graph data or GNNs. Second, the de facto backdoor-based method relies on manipulating training data, which can introduce ownership ambiguity through misclassification and vulnerability to data poisoning attacks that can interrupt the backdoor mechanism. Our explanation-based watermarking inherits the strengths of backdoor-based methods (e.g., black-box verification) without data manipulation, eliminating ownership ambiguity and data dependencies. In particular, we watermark GNN explanations such that these explanations are statistically distinct from others, so ownership claims must be verified through statistical significance. We theoretically prove that, even with full knowledge of our method, locating the watermark is NP-hard. Empirically, our method demonstrates robustness to fine-tuning and pruning attacks. By addressing these challenges, our approach significantly advances GNN intellectual property protection.

paragraphs: Watermarking embeds ownership information in a model so that unauthorized use can be investigated. This paper focuses on graph neural networks and the problems of backdoor-based watermarks, which manipulate training data. Such methods can make ownership claims ambiguous through misclassification and can depend on data mechanisms vulnerable to poisoning.

The proposed method embeds a watermark in the model’s explanations, making them statistically distinguishable from other explanations. Verification therefore requires a statistically significant ownership signal. The approach retains black-box verification while avoiding training-data manipulation, which the authors identify as removing the associated ownership ambiguity and data dependencies.

The paper proves that locating the watermark is NP-hard even when the method itself is fully known. This is a computational hardness result, rather than a statement that discovery is impossible in every instance. Experiments additionally show robustness against fine-tuning and pruning attacks. Together, the theory and experiments support explanations as a carrier of ownership information that can be checked externally and can survive the tested model modifications.
summary.tldr: The method watermarks graph neural network explanations for statistical ownership verification and shows robustness to fine-tuning and pruning.

title: Watermarking Graph Neural Networks via Explanations for Ownership Protection

abstract: Current computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP) methods often treat retrosynthesis as solved once a single feasible route is identified, focusing primarily on convergence or shortest-path metrics. This view is misaligned with real-world practice, where chemists must balance competing objectives such as cost, sustainability, toxicity, and overall yield. To address this, we formulate synthesis planning as a multi-objective search problem and introduce MORetro$^\ast$, an algorithm that generates a Pareto front of synthesis routes to explicitly capture trade-offs between user-defined criteria. MORetro$^\ast$ uses weighted scalarization and solution-informed sampling to efficiently navigate the combinatorial search space and prioritize promising trade-offs. Building on multi-objective A$^\ast$-search, we provide optimality guarantees showing that, for a fixed single-step model, MORetro$^\ast$ recovers the true Pareto front under admissibility. Across multiple retrosynthesis benchmarks, MORetro$^\ast$ produces diverse, high-quality Pareto fronts, uncovering solutions overlooked by single-objective approaches and better aligning CASP outputs with industrial decision-making.

To address this, we formulate synthesis planning as a multi-objective search problem and introduce MORetro$^\ast$, an algorithm that generates a Pareto front of synthesis routes to explicitly capture trade-offs between user-defined criteria. MORetro$^\ast$ uses weighted scalarization and solution-informed sampling to efficiently navigate the combinatorial search space and prioritize promising trade-offs. Across multiple retrosynthesis benchmarks, MORetro$^\ast$ produces diverse, high-quality Pareto fronts, uncovering solutions overlooked by single-objective approaches and better aligning CASP outputs with industrial decision-making.

paragraphs: Finding a feasible route to synthesize a molecule leaves important practical choices unresolved. Chemists may need to balance cost, toxicity, sustainability, and yield, so a shortest route need not be the most useful one. This paper formulates synthesis planning as a search over multiple objectives and introduces MORetro* to expose the resulting trade-offs.

The algorithm seeks a Pareto front: routes for which improving one objective requires worsening another. It combines weighted scalarization, which combines criteria using weights, with sampling informed by solutions already found. These mechanisms guide exploration toward promising compromises in a combinatorial search space, allowing the output to present several useful alternatives under user-defined criteria.

Building on multi-objective A* search, the authors prove recovery of the true Pareto front for a fixed single-step model under admissibility. The guarantee therefore depends on those stated conditions. Across retrosynthesis benchmarks, MORetro* produces diverse, high-quality fronts and finds solutions missed by single-objective methods. Its practical contribution is to make competing preferences visible within the planning output.
summary.tldr: MORetro* searches for synthesis routes that express competing practical objectives, with conditional guarantees of recovering the true Pareto front.

title: From Feasible to Practical: Pareto-Optimal Synthesis Planning

abstract: Empirical successes show that regularization improves the stability and efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL), with applications in robotics and post-training of large language models. Yet, theoretical analyses of regularized Markov decision processes (MDPs) have mostly been confined to the standard RL setting. In this work, we investigate regularized MDPs through the lens of robust RL. We introduce a doubly regularized MDP framework that combines policy and dynamics regularizations, enabling robust policy learning while naturally accommodating continuous action spaces. Within this framework, we develop an optimism-based online algorithm and provide the first finite-sample regret guarantees in both tabular and linear settings. Our results show that algorithms for doubly regularized MDPs are as sample-efficient as well-studied robust MDP algorithms, while additionally benefiting from the flexibility of soft policies. We further design practical algorithmic variants for both settings and demonstrate empirically that our approach efficiently and effectively handles function approximation and exploration in large state-action spaces, achieving robust performances.

In this work, we investigate regularized MDPs through the lens of robust RL. We introduce a doubly regularized MDP framework that combines policy and dynamics regularizations, enabling robust policy learning while naturally accommodating continuous action spaces. Within this framework, we develop an optimism-based online algorithm and provide the first finite-sample regret guarantees in both tabular and linear settings. Our results show that algorithms for doubly regularized MDPs are as sample-efficient as well-studied robust MDP algorithms, while additionally benefiting from the flexibility of soft policies. We further design practical algorithmic variants for both settings and demonstrate empirically that our approach efficiently and effectively handles function approximation and exploration in large state-action spaces, achieving robust performances.

Within this framework, the authors develop an online algorithm based on optimism and establish finite-sample regret guarantees for both tabular and linear settings. Their results show sample efficiency comparable to established robust Markov decision process algorithms, with the additional flexibility of soft policies that distribute probability over actions.

The authors also develop practical variants for the two settings and evaluate their ability to handle function approximation and exploration in large state-action spaces. The experiments report efficient learning and robust performance. The contribution combines a theoretical account of doubly regularized learning with empirical evidence that the framework can support practical robust reinforcement learning beyond small, explicitly enumerated problems.
summary.tldr: Regularizing both policies and dynamics yields a robust reinforcement learning framework with finite-sample guarantees and practical algorithmic variants.

title: Doubly Regularized Markov Decision Processes for Robust Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce Finslerian Reinforcement Learning (FiRL), an RL framework that makes directional costs explicit and improves robustness to tail risk. FiRL incorporates a Finsler metric into the locomotion cost, expressing effort as $F(x,v)$ that depends on the state $x$ and motion $v$, so it can capture uphill versus downhill asymmetry, lateral slip, and other direction-dependent effects. To handle rare but catastrophic outcomes, FiRL optimizes a Conditional Value-at-Risk ($CVaR_\alpha$) objective. We derive the corresponding risk-sensitive Bellman equation and show that the resulting CVaR–Finsler Bellman operator is a $\gamma$-contraction. This guarantees a unique fixed-point value function, while the underlying Finsler cost induces an asymmetric path cost $d_F$ that satisfies a triangle inequality despite directional asymmetry. We then develop a FiRL actor–critic algorithm to learn policies under this anisotropic, risk-averse objective. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robot trials, FiRL demonstrates safer and more energy-efficient locomotion behavior than strong baselines such as risk-neutral PPO. For instance, on a $12^\circ$ sloped Hopper task, FiRL reduces worst-case ($CVaR_{0.1}$) impact forces by over 35% and total energy cost by 15%, while also improving success rate.

title: Learning Anisotropic Value Geometry with Finsler Reinforcement Learning

abstract: DNA language models are increasingly used to represent genomic sequence, yet their effectiveness depends critically on how raw nucleotides are converted into model inputs. Unlike natural language, DNA offers no canonical boundaries, making fixed tokenizations a brittle design choice under shifts, indels, and local repeats. We introduce DNAChunker, a masked DNA language model that incorporates a learnable adaptive segmentation module to produce context-dependent, variable-length units. Building on a dynamic segmentation procedure, DNAChunker learns to allocate finer granularity to functionally enriched regions while compressing repetitive or redundant sequence. We pretrain DNAChunker on the human reference genome and evaluate it across five benchmarks, where it consistently improves over strong fixed-tokenization baselines. Further analyses and ablations indicate that unlike fixed tokenizations, segmentation is learned in a biologically-informed, mutation-resilient manner.

paragraphs: DNA language models need to turn nucleotide sequences into units they can process, but DNA lacks a canonical equivalent of word boundaries. A fixed segmentation can be brittle when sequences shift or contain insertions, deletions, and repeated regions. DNAChunker makes the choice of boundaries a learned part of the model.

Its masked language model includes an adaptive segmentation module that creates variable-length units according to sequence context. The learned procedure allocates smaller units to regions enriched for biological function and compresses repetitive or redundant stretches. This lets the representation devote finer resolution to some parts of a sequence without forcing that same granularity everywhere.

The authors pretrain the model on the human reference genome and evaluate it on five benchmarks, reporting consistent improvements over strong models with fixed tokenization. Additional analyses and ablations indicate that the learned segmentation reflects biological information and is resilient to mutations. The contribution is therefore both a representation method and evidence that learning where to divide DNA can improve how genomic language models use their inputs.
summary.tldr: DNAChunker learns context-dependent DNA segments, improving benchmark performance while allocating finer resolution to functionally enriched regions.

title: DNACHUNKER: Learnable Tokenization for DNA Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in audio deepfake detection have been driven by increasingly large speech foundation models and growing amounts of synthetic data. Despite strong benchmark performance, it remains unclear how detection capability scales with model capacity and training data under realistic deployment conditions involving distribution shift, signal corruption, and unseen synthesis pipelines. In this work, we present the first systematic study of scaling laws in post-training audio deepfake detection, focusing on fine-tuning regimes rather than large-scale pretraining. Using a controlled family of speech foundation models with shared architecture and pretraining, we analyze how detection performance, robustness, and generalization evolve as a function of model size and training data scale. Our results reveal a fundamental asymmetry between performance scaling and robustness scaling in audio deepfake detection, suggesting increasing model capacity alone is insufficient for achieving reliable real-world generalization.

This paper studies scaling during fine-tuning, focusing on detection performance alongside robustness and generalization.

The experiments use a controlled family of speech models that share architecture and pretraining, while examining model size and training-data scale. The evaluation considers distribution shifts, corrupted signals, and synthesis pipelines absent from training. This setup places ordinary detection gains and behavior under unfamiliar conditions within the same scaling study.

The central finding is an asymmetry between performance scaling and robustness scaling. Better detection performance as resources increase does not imply matching progress in resilience to deployment changes. The authors therefore conclude that increasing model capacity alone is insufficient for reliable real-world generalization. The work clarifies why model size and data quantity need to be assessed against several dimensions of detector quality.
summary.tldr: Audio deepfake detection performance and robustness scale differently, making larger models alone insufficient for reliable generalization.

title: Scaling Behavior in Model Fine-tuning for Audio DeepFake Detection

abstract: We study the discrete Bertrand pricing game with a non-increasing demand function. The game has $n \ge 2$ players who simultaneously choose prices from the set $1/k, 2/k, \ldots, 1$, where $k\in\mathbb{N}$. The player who sets the lowest price captures the entire demand; if multiple players tie for the lowest price, they split the demand equally. We study the Bertrand paradox, where classical theory predicts low prices, yet real markets often sustain high prices. To understand this gap, we analyze a repeated-game model in which firms set prices using no-regret learners. Our goal is to characterize the equilibrium outcomes that can arise under different no-regret learning guarantees. We are particularly interested in questions such as whether no-external-regret learners can converge to undesirable high-price outcomes, and how stronger guarantees such as no-swap regret shape the emergence of competitive low-price behavior. We address these and related questions through a theoretical analysis, complemented by experiments that support the theory and reveal surprising phenomena for no-swap regret learners.

Its focus is how different learning guarantees shape the equilibrium outcomes that can emerge over repeated interaction.

The model has at least two firms choosing simultaneously from a finite price grid, with demand that does not increase as price rises. The lowest-priced firm receives all demand; firms tied for the lowest price split it equally. These rules define the competitive setting in which the authors compare external-regret and stronger swap-regret guarantees.

The analysis asks whether external-regret learners can approach undesirable high-price outcomes and how swap-regret guarantees influence competitive low-price behavior. Theoretical results are accompanied by experiments that support the analysis and reveal surprising behavior among swap-regret learners. The contribution is an examination of how learning rules affect pricing equilibria within this specified game, connecting algorithmic guarantees to the economic question behind the Bertrand paradox.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how external-regret and swap-regret learning shape equilibria in a repeated discrete Bertrand pricing game.

title: Revisiting the Bertrand Paradox via Equilibrium Analysis of No-regret Learners

abstract: The adversarial robustness of attributions is a fundamental requirement for reliable explainability in deep learning, yet existing approaches typically rely on computationally expensive explicit regularization. In this work, we show that attribution robustness can arise implicitly from the learning dynamics of standard stochastic gradient descent. We theoretically motivate this effect through connections between parameter-space and input-space curvature, and validate it across architectures, datasets, and attribution methods, with negligible computational overhead. In contrast, we prove that such robustness gains often does not transfer to attention-based attribution under softmax normalization, due to inherent entropy constraints, and we validate this limitation experimentally. Finally, we show that replacing softmax attention with kernel-based attention restores the robustness gains in transformer models. Our results highlight learning dynamics as a principled and practical mechanism for robust explainability, and reveal fundamental limitations of attention-based attribution under normalization.

paragraphs: Attribution methods explain predictions by assigning importance to parts of an input. For these explanations to be reliable, they should resist adversarial manipulation. Existing approaches often encourage that robustness with explicit regularization, which can be computationally expensive. This paper investigates whether ordinary training dynamics can provide robustness implicitly.

The authors connect curvature in parameter space with curvature in input space to theoretically motivate robustness arising through stochastic gradient descent. They validate the effect across architectures, datasets, and attribution methods, reporting negligible computational overhead. This makes learning dynamics themselves a practical mechanism for improving the stability of explanations.

The paper also identifies a specific boundary: these robustness gains often fail to transfer to attention-based attribution when attention uses softmax normalization. The authors link this failure to inherent entropy constraints, proving and experimentally validating the limitation. Replacing softmax with kernel-based attention restores the gains in the studied transformer models. The results therefore connect robust attribution to both training dynamics and the normalization used by the explanation mechanism.
summary.tldr: Standard training dynamics can improve attribution robustness, while kernel-based attention addresses a softmax-related barrier to those gains in transformers.

title: Improving Adversarial Robustness of Attribution via Implicit Regularization

abstract: We introduce Flower, a neural architecture for learning PDE solution operators built entirely from multihead warps. Aside from pointwise channel mixing and a multiscale scaffold, Flowers use no Fourier multipliers, no dot-product attention, and no convolutional mixing. Each head predicts a displacement field and warps the mixed input features. Motivated by physics and computational efficiency, displacements are predicted pointwise, without any spatial aggregation, and nonlocality enters only through sparse sampling at source coordinates, one per head. Stacking warps in multiscale residual blocks yields Flowers, which implement adaptive, global interactions at linear cost. We theoretically motivate this design through three complementary lenses: flow maps for conservation laws, waves in inhomogeneous media, and a kinetic-theoretic continuum limit. Flowers achieve excellent performance on a broad suite of 2D and 3D time-dependent PDE benchmarks, particularly flows and waves. A compact 17M-parameter model consistently outperforms Fourier, convolution, and attention-based baselines of similar size, while a 150M-parameter variant improves over recent transformer-based foundation models with much more parameters, data, and training compute.

paragraphs: Flowers are neural models for learning the operators that produce solutions to partial differential equations. Their main building block is a multihead warp: each head predicts a displacement and samples input features at the resulting source coordinate. This makes adaptive movement through the feature field the basis of information exchange.

Displacements are predicted pointwise, without aggregating spatial neighborhoods. Each head obtains nonlocal information through one source sample, and stacked multiscale residual blocks build global interactions at linear cost. The architecture also uses pointwise channel mixing and a multiscale scaffold. The authors motivate the design through conservation-law flow maps, waves in varying media, and a kinetic-theoretic continuum limit.

On two- and three-dimensional time-dependent PDE benchmarks, particularly flows and waves, a 17-million-parameter model consistently beats similarly sized Fourier, convolutional, and attention-based alternatives. A 150-million-parameter version also improves on recent Transformer foundation models using more parameters, data, and compute. These comparisons support sparse adaptive warping as an effective architecture for the evaluated physical solution operators.
summary.tldr: Flowers learn PDE solution operators through sparse adaptive warps, delivering strong benchmark performance with linear-cost global interactions.

title: Flowers: A Warp Drive for Neural PDE Solvers

abstract: Tabular data is one of the most fundamental and widely used formats for representing structured information. Classical machine learning algorithms continue to achieve substantial success in extracting predictive patterns and constructing accurate models from structured data; however, representation learning approaches that extend language-model-based methods to the tabular setting have opened new opportunities. Nevertheless, conventional tokenization procedures and token embedding mechanisms are not well-suited to numerical variables, as they fail to preserve key numerical properties, including proximity structure and ordinal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TabularBERT, a Transformer-based model that discretizes numerical variables via binning-based tokenization and learns representations that account for numerical proximity and ordinal information while capturing conditional dependencies among variables through masked self-supervised pretraining. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed approach, highlighting the benefits of language-model-based representation learning in the tabular domain.
